entries.text: Characters # characters Personnel records and field status Archive online All characters Independent MSF Government Private Eye Magiarchy Magi Academy Police The Church Household Personnel archive / 18 records Characters Character profiles, affiliations, abilities, and connections across the story. 18 records visible Archive online MSF · 001 Chibi preview Fionn's biological daughter and displaced heir Lynleit MSF Magiarchy Fionn's daughter, an MSF officer and Magus who becomes a fugitive after Helena accuses her of his murder. Heir-director Strategist Magi IND · 002 Arc 1 · Chibi Independent operator and later MSF director Kyrien Independent Opening MSF Later director A non-Magus who begins as Lynleit's secret recruit and later becomes director of MSF. Tradecraft Survival Intelligence MSF · 003 Chibi preview Political usurper Helena MSF Fionn's wife and Lynleit's stepmother. She takes control of MSF after his assassination and accuses Lynleit of the murder. IND · 004 Chibi preview Mercenary assassin and secret bodyguard Tien Independent A professional mercenary and assassin concealed by Helena as her private bodyguard, Tien removes her enemies quietly and cleanly. ARC · 005 Chibi preview Magiarch and MSF founder Fionn MSF Magiarchy Lynleit's biological father, publicly the director of MSF and secretly the country's Magiarch, Fionn faces a foreign magical conflict disguised as political chaos inside Narvea. FLD · 006 Chibi preview Ducal Guard field agent and bodyguard Heyk Government The sole survivor of a paramilitary unit massacred inside Vilen's quarantined park, later recruited into the Ducal Guard under Drake and Sherie. FLD · 007 Chibi preview Diplomat in training and covert negotiator Sherie Government Drake's niece and diplomatic apprentice, Sherie combines his strategic instruction with the charm and quick judgment he cannot easily bring into a room himself. FLD · 008 Chibi preview Official for Special Assignments Drake Government State Councillor, the Duke's trusted troubleshooter, and Sherie's uncle. His warnings about the disappearances are dismissed at Court. ARC · 009 Chibi preview MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard Felix MSF Lynleit's playful friend and bodyguard, trusted by Fionn. Felix handles hacking and communications for the field team. ARC · 010 Chibi preview MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard Reiner MSF Lynleit's stern friend and bodyguard, trusted by Fionn. Reiner is a powerfully built protection specialist who holds exposed positions and confronts threats directly. ARC · 011 Chibi preview Criminology student and procedural investigator Yulia Independent A top criminology student who checks Hiyu's theories against evidence and reluctantly accompanies him into Vilen's quarantined park. ARC · 012 Chibi preview Criminology student and intuitive investigator Hiyu Independent A criminology student who suspects magic behind the disappearances and enters Vilen's quarantined park with Yulia to find proof. ARC · 013 Chibi preview Independent magical examiner and private investigator Natalia Private Eye Magiarchy Former Academy A former Magi Academy professor who left a restrictive academic career to pursue independent research. Private cases fund that work, turning her one-woman office into a discreet practice for magical deviations, personal afflictions, and edge cases. ARC · 014 L Chibi unavailable Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally Lester Independent A demiholumn, half human and half Holumn, who remains outside Natalia's one-woman business but sometimes does the impossible on her behalf. ARC · 015 Chibi preview Magi Academy student Myka Magi Academy Magiarchy A young Magus studying at the Magi Academy who relies on her aunt Natalia for academic advice, personal reassurance, and a view of magical inquiry beyond institutional limits. PLC · 016 Chibi preview Police inspector Inspector Leo Police A police inspector whose missing-person investigation reaches the edge of a quarantine controlled by authorities above his clearance. CHR · 017 Chibi preview Church special envoy Father Mikhail The Church A Church special envoy and formidable field operative whose mission in Cardiff forces him to survive several Magi threats before Lynleit reaches him. HSE · 018 Chibi preview Grey cat of the Director's House Ash Household A grey male cat who enters Lynleit's family home uninvited, survives her clumsy attempt to remove him, and decides to remain. ? Narrative architecture One crisis, two explanations Underlying conflict What the country sees A political conspiracy Disappearances, illegal material movement, court tension, and strife inside MSF suggest a domestic coup aimed at Narvea and Ducal authority. Coup rumors Institutional mistrust MSF power struggle masks → What drives it A magical conflict Foreign Magiarchates, church actors, and criminal Magi all remain plausible participants in the pressure surrounding Fionn. Their struggle is translated into political chaos that ordinary investigators can recognize but cannot fully explain. entries.title: World
entries.text: World # world-index Places, institutions, and authorities 8 full records Setting archive The systems behind the story A 21st-century world where modern cities and intelligence work coexist with inherited titles, old institutions, and hidden magic. Read the setting foundation . Records 08 Institution notes 01 Terms at a glance Magic The supernatural force within reality, including psyche and soul. Magecraft The trained discipline through which Magi act on conditions reality can support. Miracle-making The Church's forbidden category for acts resembling wizardry or imitating sacred deeds. Holumn A supernatural manifestation that may be a body, phenomenon, event, will, or curse. The Spill The continuing crisis in which Holumn manifestations exceed ordinary containment. Narvean fog A recurring regional hazard, intensified by certain Holumn incidents during the Spill. Suppression doctrine Church-sanctioned measures to contain public knowledge of magic. 01 Primary records Established foundations Explore the places, organizations, and phenomena recorded in the archive. N PLACE · STATE Full record The Duchy of Narvea The main country of the story, held together by constitutional balance, diplomatic tradition, regional identities, and competing centers of authority. Open country profile → III PLACE · RESIDENCE Location record The Director's House A three-floor hillside family home with a river outlook, glass garden rooms, and a discreet residential role in MSF's command life. Open the house record → MSF ORGANIZATION · PRIVATE INTELLIGENCE Foundation record MSF A private intelligence contractor selling services to the government while retaining control of its succession, inner workings, and concentrated force in Turon. Open agency record → † INSTITUTION · RELIGION Foundation record The Church Every church head knows the Magi exist and commands special envoys whose priesthood conceals political, intelligence, combat, and covert operational training. Open institutional record → M FRAMEWORK · MAGICAL GOVERNANCE Full record The Magiarchy The territorial order of the Magi, alongside their ancient pagan traditions, including the Cult of Inanna. Open magical order → H PHENOMENON · HIDDEN WORLD Evidence-linked record Holumns Psychic pressure can take the form of a creature, weather, an event, a disembodied will, or a curse. Victims and witnesses describe what each manifestation does. Open the Holumn archive → L INDUSTRY · FIREARMS Initial archive Weapons Narvean firearms, their design families, specifications, and use by MSF, police, and military officers. Open weapons archive → IA MATERIAL CULTURE · ANOMALOUS OBJECTS Object archive Items & Artefacts Story-relevant objects and nonhuman holdings whose properties, custody, and history carry consequences outside the Weapons and Holumn archives. Open items archive → 02 Education Magi Academy The Academy teaches magecraft. Natalia was a professor there and Lynleit's favourite teacher. Myka studies there and turns to Natalia when she encounters dangers within the institution. ✎ Page notes World Use notes to identify which institution should receive the next full record.

entries.text: After the Failed Attempt · v1 · Archived Chapter 03 · The Hidden Wager After Kyrien's failed attack on an MSF-protected politician nearly harms Lynleit, she questions him without revealing that she was present and converts his prison risk into a secret alliance. Kyrien's attempt on an MSF-protected politician fails because the target secretly belongs to the Magi world. Lynleit is present and almost harmed during the attempt, but Kyrien does not know she was there and she never tells him. Lynleit takes control of his interrogation and offers conditional freedom in exchange for becoming her secret helper. She recruits him because her intuition warns her that a danger she cannot yet identify is approaching. Lynleit later tells only Felix and Reiner, while even Fionn remains outside the compartment. Reiner trusts Lynleit's judgment, while Felix accepts the decision without trusting Kyrien. Chapter 03: After the Failed Attempt Placeholder draft built only from confirmed scene facts. The dialogue, location details, and connective action will be replaced or revised when final chapter material is available. The Protection Failure The politician is under MSF protection when Kyrien makes the attempt. It fails for a reason he could not have anticipated: the target belongs to the hidden world of Magi. Lynleit is present during the attempt and is almost harmed by it. Kyrien does not know she was there. Lynleit never tells him. The Interview Room Kyrien now faces prison, and the police office gives him no reason to expect another outcome. Lynleit enters the interrogation knowing that the man opposite her nearly injured or killed her without intending to. To Kyrien, the personal edge in her questions has no visible source. Lynleit enters the interrogation with authority that has not yet been explained. She does not offer forgiveness. She offers conditional freedom. Kyrien may avoid prison if he becomes her secret helper. The arrangement leaves him confined to her demands, useful precisely because Helena does not know he belongs to Lynleit's circle. The Warning Lynleit cannot prove that a crisis is coming. Her suspicion of Helena is built from a tense family history, things she has noticed but not yet explained, and an intuition that tells her the present balance will not hold. Recruiting Kyrien is a high-risk answer to a danger she cannot name. Fionn's assassination is still far away. Lynleit does not foresee the event itself, but she acts with the conviction that she will soon need an ally her enemies cannot anticipate. The Compartment Lynleit later tells only Felix and Reiner. Even Fionn remains uninformed. Both friends see Kyrien as a possible danger to her. Reiner accepts the arrangement because he trusts Lynleit's judgment. Felix yields because Reiner's decision leaves him in the minority, but his distrust of Kyrien remains. The wager stays hidden. Much later, when Fionn is assassinated and Helena moves against Lynleit, the danger she sensed finally takes visible form. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner

entries.text: After the Failed Attempt · v3 · Current Chapter 03 · The Hidden Wager Years of work buy Kyrien proof but no justice. After his failed attack on the Prosecutor General, Lynleit questions him and offers confidential service while his lawyer negotiates the terms. Kyrien funds years of legal work while supporting his mother. Credible evidence is found, but a closed review protects the prosecutor. After an interval, strangers humiliate his mother in a shop. He decides to kill the prosecutor only after getting her home and attending to her needs. The newly appointed Prosecutor General survives the dinner attack. Kyrien escapes immediate capture, sees no unmistakable magic, and is detained later. Lynleit nearly suffers harm at the dinner but conceals her attendance during questioning. With his lawyer present, Kyrien describes his family's treatment without confessing. Lynleit helps confirm his mother's welfare. His refusal to repeat his mother's apology suggests how difficult the humiliation remains to discuss. inferred Lynleit privately recognizes suppression and her need for an ally outside her circle. Kyrien accepts paid confidential work subject to legal review of release, care, and employment terms. Lynleit tells Felix and Reiner, not Fionn. Reiner trusts her judgment; Felix accepts without trusting Kyrien. Chapter 03: After the Failed Attempt The invoices The lawyer had put the old statement beside the copy used in the prosecution. Kyrien could see the difference without understanding the notes in the margins. "That isn't what he said." "No." He looked at her. She had been careful with him for so long that the unqualified answer took a moment to register. "Can you prove that?" "We have the original, the amendment, and the record of who received each. This one doesn't depend on anybody remembering correctly." Kyrien rubbed a mark on his cuff. He had come straight from work; there had been nowhere to wash properly, and the mark was dry now. "And the other allegations?" She brought out another folder. There had always been another allegation. His father would answer one, sometimes with records from the very office accusing him, and a fresh question would arrive before the answer had done any good. By the end, even people who believed him asked why he could not leave it alone. After his death, the papers had supplied an answer for him. Shame. Instability. Fear of what might be uncovered next. Kyrien had paid people to examine those answers. He took extra shifts, found work between them, and learned which expenses could wait. Each month he put his mother's bills beside the solicitor's account and worked out what was left. Sometimes the solicitor's account waited too. She continued answering his calls. He brought documents, remembered who had visited the house, corrected a date when he knew it was wrong. When she explained an application he did not understand, he asked her to explain it again. The legal work was hers. Now an independent inquiry had accepted enough of it to examine the senior prosecutor. "The preliminary review supports us," she said. "Important evidence was knowingly distorted. That is what they have found." On the way home, Kyrien bought the tea his mother preferred. He had been buying the cheaper one and telling himself she had not noticed. She noticed this one immediately. "Was it on offer?" "No." She turned the packet over, checking anyway. For a while, the folder on his kitchen table contained something other than a bill. The closed review The lawyer did not put the two statements in front of him this time. "They haven't disproved them," she said. Kyrien waited. "The review went into closed session. The prosecutor's conduct has been accepted under a confidential national-security mandate. We cannot challenge what we are not permitted to examine." "They examined it." "Yes." "And they have our evidence." "Yes." She went through the remaining routes with him. He wrote down the first two, then stopped when she explained why neither could reach the decision that mattered. She let him keep the pen. He asked for copies of everything they were allowed to retain. The prosecutor's vindication was public. So was the suggestion that a malicious campaign had tried to ruin an honourable man. The altered statement stayed in the folder. One of his father's old contacts met him afterward. Kyrien had trusted him enough to bring the papers. "Your father was wronged," the man said quietly. Kyrien pushed the folder toward him. The man did not open it. "There are consequences this country cannot afford." "For whom?" He received no useful answer. He took the folder home because the copies had cost money. He continued working. His mother still needed meals, clean clothes, company on the bad days, and to be left alone on the days she could manage. There were mornings when she had already washed the cups before he got up. There were evenings when she sat in the same chair until he asked whether she had eaten. He kept paying what he owed the lawyer. For a time, he still called. The shopping His mother wanted to go to the shop herself. Kyrien offered to carry the bag. She considered that, then gave him the heavier one and kept the small cloth bag she always used for bread. Inside, she checked the tea before putting it back. At the counter she was counting change when a customer recognized her. "Aren't you the commander's wife?" Her hand stopped over the coins. "Yes." "I saw they cleared the prosecutor. Terrible business. All that trouble, and for what? Compensation?" Kyrien took the bag from the counter. "We're leaving." His mother did not move. "My husband didn't... The evidence wasn't..." "Well, they've looked at it, haven't they?" The shopkeeper glanced at the people waiting behind her. "Please. There's no need to make a scene." He was speaking to her. One customer watched. Another studied the shelves behind the till. Kyrien gathered the loose coins, paid, and stood beside his mother until she would take his arm. Outside she tried to open the bread bag. Her fingers kept missing the fold. "I'm sorry. I thought I could manage the shopping." "You can." "I shouldn't have answered." He held the bag open for her. At home she wanted the bread put away before she sat down. He did that, made her tea, and found the programme she had missed. When she asked whether he was going to work, he told her the time of his shift. Only after she had settled did he take the prosecutor's photograph out of the folder. He meant to kill him. His mother would still need someone to come home. He knew that while he looked at the photograph, and afterward, when he put it away and left for work. He arranged for a neighbour his mother already knew to stay during his longer absences and left her number beside the telephone. His mother complained that neither of them could make tea properly and then asked when the neighbour was coming again. The appointment The senior prosecutor became Prosecutor General. A formal dinner marked the appointment; surviving the supposed smear campaign was mentioned as a recommendation for the office. MSF supplied part of the security. Lynleit attended, spoke civilly to a man she disliked, and was almost harmed when Kyrien's attempt failed. Kyrien got away. His father's old contacts and the practical knowledge he had inherited had helped him prepare, but something at the dinner had escaped his understanding. He had seen nothing he could identify as magic. He went back to work. The police came later. His history supplied a motive. The incident supplied questions. They did not yet have the evidence to turn their certainty into a conclusive case. The interview Kyrien had counted the screws in the table bracket twice when the door opened. The woman who came in carried a slim file. She did not ask where to sit. His lawyer pulled her own chair a little closer to his. "Lynleit. MSF. We assisted with security at the dinner." The investigating officer introduced her for the record. His lawyer asked what part of the questioning required the contractor's presence, listened to the answer, and made a note. "You can ask," she said. "He may decline to answer." Lynleit sat opposite him. Her file was much thinner than his father's had been. "Did you follow the appointment?" "It was on the news." "You had a particular interest." "So did the news." She waited. He looked at the officer, then back at her. "You understand why we're speaking to you." "My lawyer explained." "Your complaint against the prosecutor was dismissed." "The evidence wasn't." For the first time she opened the file. "No," she said. "It wasn't." He did not help her with the silence that followed. She asked about his work, the dinner, and people who had known his father. When a question moved from what he knew to where he had been, his lawyer touched the edge of her notebook. "I won't answer that." Lynleit looked at the notebook. Then she asked whether he understood how many people had been working at the dinner. "Catering staff. Drivers. Security. People who had no part in your father's case." "Is that a question?" his lawyer asked. "Did he give any thought to them?" "You're asking him to accept your account of his involvement." Lynleit shut the file with one hand. Not loudly, but before the lawyer had finished speaking. Kyrien looked at that hand. "I didn't say I was there." "I heard you." "Then ask me something I can answer." She watched him for long enough that he began to wish he had left the last sentence out. Then she drew out a payment schedule. "These are yours?" His lawyer checked it before he did. "Copies we supplied with the complaint," she said. "To answer the allegation that he was financing it with somebody else's money." Lynleit placed the employment records beside it. "You changed shifts here. Took a second job here. This payment arrived in three parts." "Four," Kyrien said. She found the small entry at the bottom. "Four." He had forgotten that one. He remembered it now: getting home too late, his mother still awake, the envelope under a plate so he would not leave it behind in the morning. "You were still paying your lawyers after the review." "They were still answering." His lawyer lowered her eyes to the schedule. "Then something changed." Kyrien looked at the table. "What happened?" He rubbed his thumb along the seam of his cuff. The shift he had missed would have paid the neighbour and most of the next bill. "They started on my mother." "Who did?" "A man in a shop." Lynleit looked up from the papers. He had given her the wrong sort of answer. She had been ready for a name, perhaps another official. He could see her waiting for him to supply one. "She was buying bread," he said. The lawyer did not interrupt. He told them about the coins, the shopkeeper, and getting his mother outside. He stopped before repeating what she had said to him. "And after that?" Lynleit asked. "I took her home." "Did you..." "I took her home." She left the question unfinished. "Is someone with her now?" "Our neighbour. Until six." The answer came too quickly. He sat back. "Why?" "Because it's nearly six." She looked at his lawyer. "Can you find out whether the neighbour can stay?" The officer agreed to a break, and the lawyer used the number Kyrien had left with her. The neighbour could stay. His mother had eaten. She wanted to know whether he had his key. "Yes," he said, although nobody on the telephone could hear him. What Lynleit knew Lynleit read the review heading again while the lawyer spoke quietly to her client. She knew the sort of restricted authority that could keep a witness out of court without ever calling him a witness. The file before her had begun with a commander who survived an arrest gone wrong, then filled with allegations that changed whenever he answered them. Its last pages protected the people who had arranged the case. Suppression. The word belonged to reports she was permitted to read and Kyrien was not. She turned over one of his receipts. The late charge was smaller than the price of her lunch. She could still remember where she had been standing at the dinner, and how little had separated her from the attack. Disliking the prosecutor had been easier before that. Across the table, Kyrien asked when he could go home. Lynleit could recommend a release arrangement. She could not make the evidence disappear, and she could not promise what the police would do with evidence they might find tomorrow. She also could not shake the thought that she would need him. Helena knew her officers, her friends, the people Fionn trusted. Recently she had begun asking about visits and journeys that had never interested her before. Lynleit had explanations for each question. None explained why she kept remembering them together. She asked the investigating officer for a separate discussion with Kyrien and his representative once the recorded interview was over. "About what?" "Work." The offer The lawyer stayed. Kyrien had expected Lynleit to object; instead she put a different sheet between them and waited while the lawyer read it. The door was closed. The formal questioning had ended. Nothing she offered here would erase the record they had already made. "MSF can request an arrangement under its government contract," Lynleit said. "I can put you forward for it. That means work, supervision, and a case that remains open. It doesn't mean I own the police." "Does your father?" Kyrien asked. "He owns MSF." "That's not what I asked." "It's the answer you're getting." His lawyer turned the sheet over. "Who approves release?" "The responsible authorities. Not me. I can recommend it, provide the undertaking, and argue that continued detention serves no useful purpose." "And if he declines your employment?" "You continue pursuing his release without our support." "Which I will," the lawyer told him. Lynleit nodded, once. Kyrien looked at the sheet. She was not offering him a clean name. She had brought a way to get home sooner and made herself part of it. "What work?" "Watching. Checking things. Telling me when an explanation doesn't fit what you've seen. Sometimes going somewhere without advertising who sent you." "You have people for that." "People know who they are." "And you think nobody knows who I am?" "They know whose son you are. They don't know you work for me." "I don't." "Not yet." His lawyer made a mark beside a paragraph. "Payment?" Lynleit gave her the employment terms. The lawyer asked another question, and then a third. Kyrien waited until the figures were on paper before doing the arithmetic. "This has to replace the shifts I lose," he said. "Not be paid whenever you decide the work was useful." "Regular pay. Expenses separately." "My mother can't stay alone for days." "Then before you're away, someone she knows has to be able to stay. Put the cost in the expenses." "She chooses who." "Yes." "And if nobody can?" Lynleit looked at him rather than the lawyer. "You tell me before you go. We change the assignment." He had answers to the questions he had expected to fight about. He trusted them less for arriving so readily. "What happens when you don't need me?" "If the arrangement works, I'll help you get clear of the scrutiny you can actually get clear of. I won't promise immunity." "Can I leave?" His lawyer put her pen down. "We'll need that in writing. Along with the release conditions, who can change them, and what happens if employment ends." "Agreed," Lynleit said. Kyrien looked at her. "You haven't answered." "You can leave the work. I can't promise that every protection attached to it survives your leaving." His lawyer kept the sheet on her side of the table. "He will not sign this version. Bring the complete terms. I review them, and I remain his representative." "Of course." "And no questions about the dinner disguised as an assignment." Lynleit's mouth tightened. "Understood." Kyrien had watched officials agree pleasantly before. He looked at the written rate again, then at the clock. "I'll do the work," he said. "If the terms say what you've said." "They will." "My lawyer checks." "I heard her." Lynleit gathered the papers she had brought. His lawyer kept the proposed terms, with the unsigned page folded to the front. Before leaving, Lynleit asked whether he had any other questions. "Can I speak to my mother myself?" She went to ask the officer. The people she told Later, Felix stood with the back of a chair between his hands while Reiner read the short account Lynleit had given them. "You recruited him." "Yes." "The man from the dinner." "There was more than one man at the dinner." "Lynleit." She stopped sorting the papers. "I need someone Helena hasn't already counted." "She hasn't counted plenty of people. Most haven't tried to kill somebody beside you." Reiner looked up. "Does he know you were there?" "No." "Your father?" "Doesn't know about the arrangement. And won't hear it from us." Felix let go of the chair. Reiner set the account down. "You trust him?" "No. I think he'll do the work." He considered that for a while. "All right." Felix turned toward him. "That's all?" "I trust her judgment. It doesn't mean we stop watching." "Good," Felix said. "Because I wasn't going to." Lynleit slid the account back into its folder. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner

entries.title: Before the First Bell
entries.subtitle: Chapter 01 · Vanishing Point
entries.text: Before the First Bell Chapter 01 · Vanishing Point Lynleit and Fionn attend private negotiations at a church before dawn while their MSF escort waits outside and wonders why. Lynleit and Fionn arrive at a church before dawn for private negotiations. Felix and Reiner wait outside as the family's security detail. Lynleit leaves the meeting early and visibly irritated. Felix and Reiner seek gossip, but Lynleit redirects them with a playful tease. A report of another disappearance appears while the meeting is in progress. Chapter 01: Before the First Bell Working draft based on the confirmed opening scene. Dialogue and exact staging remain provisional. 05:17 The first week of September had arrived without deciding whether it belonged to summer or autumn. The city was dark when the MSF car turned onto Saint Orison Street. Rain from the previous night still rested in the joins between the stones, and the church at the end of the road seemed to have collected more darkness than the buildings around it. Its windows were unlit. Its bell had not yet marked the hour. Felix slowed at the iron gate. "This is the address?" Reiner checked the card in his hand for the third time. "Saint Orison Cathedral. East entrance." "A cathedral. At this hour." From the rear seat, Lynleit looked past them toward the steps. She had said little since they left MSF headquarters. Her coat was buttoned neatly, her expression composed, and the file resting across her knees had not been opened once. Fionn sat beside her with his eyes closed. "The east entrance," he said. Felix glanced at the empty street. "Of course. Much less suspicious than the front." Lynleit looked at him through the mirror. "Your gift for discretion remains one of the agency's better-kept secrets." "Thank you." "That was not praise." "I accepted it before the correction." Reiner hid a smile behind the route card. They drove around the cathedral and stopped beside a narrow door set into the oldest part of the stonework. A priest was already waiting beneath the arch. He wore no coat despite the cold. Fionn stepped out first. Lynleit followed, taking the file with her. Felix reached for his door. The priest raised one hand. "The officers will remain outside." Felix paused with the door half open. "We are their security detail." "You are expected to wait." Reiner looked to Fionn. "Director?" Fionn did not appear surprised. "Stay with the car." "Sir, if this is a negotiation, we should at least clear the room." "The room has already been cleared." The priest opened the door. Warm amber light touched the wet stones, then narrowed as Fionn entered. Lynleit stopped before following him. "Try not to investigate the clergy while we are inside," she said. Felix leaned against the open car door. "How long will you be?" "I don't know. Stay warm." Then she disappeared into the church, and the door closed behind her. Outside At 05:31, Felix decided the meeting concerned money. At 05:38, he revised this to blackmail. At 05:46, after a delivery van passed without stopping and a light appeared in one high window, he proposed that Fionn had joined a secret monastic order and intended to leave MSF to Lynleit before breakfast. Reiner remained beside the car, arms folded. "You could ask him when he comes out." "And spoil it?" Across the street, a newspaper bundle landed outside a closed kiosk. The top page loosened in the wind. For a moment, Felix could read part of the headline. SECOND VOLUNTEER MISSING NEAR VILEN PARKLAND The page folded over itself before he could see the rest. "They closed another path through the park," he said. Reiner followed his glance. "Drainage works." "In September?" "Rain happens in September." "People also happen in September. They usually do not vanish into landscaping projects." Reiner looked back toward the church door. "You are supposed to be watching the entrance." Felix sighed and obeyed. The bell still had not rung. An Early Exit At 05:53, the side door opened. Lynleit came out alone. She descended the steps with the same measured pace she used when crossing the operations floor, but the file was now held too tightly beneath one arm. Her mouth was set. Felix straightened. Reiner opened the rear door for her. "Is the Director following?" "Eventually." She did not get into the car. Felix and Reiner exchanged a look. Lynleit noticed it immediately. "No," she said. Felix placed a hand against his chest. "I have not asked anything." "You have asked several things. You simply used your face." "Then my face would appreciate clarification. Why is the director of an intelligence foundation negotiating with a church before sunrise?" "Perhaps he is confessing the budget." "Reiner said money too." "I said no such thing," Reiner replied. Felix continued. "We were refused entry. The priest knew we were coming. You left early, and you look as though somebody inside suggested something very stupid with complete confidence." Lynleit looked back at the closed door. She turned back to them. "You are both remarkably interested in private church business." "Occupational concern," Felix said. "Of course. Should I ask whether the priest has time to arrange a ceremony for you? You are already dressed, and Reiner has spent the entire morning pretending not to enjoy your company." Reiner went still. Felix smiled. "Would MSF cover the reception?" "Only if you classify it as a training exercise." "I object to this entire conversation," Reiner said. "Noted," Lynleit replied. "Felix, put his objection in the wedding file." "We have a wedding file?" "We do now." The cathedral bell struck once. The side door opened again, and Fionn stepped into the morning with the priest behind him. Whatever expression he had worn inside was gone before he reached the first step. He looked from Lynleit to Felix, then to Reiner. "Did I miss something?" "Felix and Reiner are considering a church wedding," Lynleit said. "We are not," Reiner replied. Fionn considered this with the gravity of an official report. "Then I appear to have missed very little." He entered the car. Lynleit followed without looking back at the church. As Felix pulled away from the curb, the morning traffic reports announced a new diversion around the park. The explanation was maintenance. The estimated reopening date was left unspecified. Nobody in the car commented on it. Lynleit,Fionn,Felix,Reiner

entries.title: Doom Has an Address · v4 · Superseded
entries.subtitle: Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1
entries.text: Doom Has an Address · v4 · Superseded Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 Natalia works through a shared curse with a pen-and-paper example, failed self-observation, and stories from her own life. Lynleit follows the lesson, disputes its conclusion, and seeks Father Mikhail's second opinion. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects the fatal solution, consults other Magi, and searches Magiarchal records and prohibited theurgical procedures for an alternative. Natalia uses a two-name diagram, her failed decision diary, and her experience after leaving the Academy to explain why a change of identity must go deeper than its description. She introduces the ego hypothesis and quotes Jung. Lynleit jokes with Natalia, works through the examples, and keeps the diagram; Natalia proposes reciprocal attachment as a possible change, not a guaranteed cure. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds the proposed method from Kyrien and investigates their relationship as a possible procedure. Lynleit attempts to initiate an encounter but does not fully cross the boundary between them. The curse begins weakening the following morning and is later gone. Lynleit's unread pages and repeated denials suggest that she still wants Kyrien now that the curse is gone. inferred Kyrien knows about Lynleit's attempt, her refusal to explain it, and the curse's decline, but lacks enough information to connect them. The incomplete attempt and its aftermath change both identities enough for the curse to lose its hold. Doom Has an Address The condition The Holumn was eventually destroyed. That was the first mistake. Lynleit and Kyrien did not understand what they were fighting until after they had already killed it. Destroying the creature completed the final part of its mechanism: its own terminal condition passed to whoever had caused its death. They had destroyed it together. There was still only one curse, attached to both of them. Their bodies began to weaken. Sleep stopped restoring them properly, and minor injuries healed too slowly. Lynleit found her magecraft increasingly exhausting. Kyrien began stopping on stairs. Within days, ordinary exertion had become difficult for both of them. The Magi who examined the curse gave them several weeks. Attempts to suppress it produced a second discovery. Removing it from Lynleit brought relief only until the attachment to Kyrien restored it. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. One of them could survive if the other died first. Lynleit rejected the answer. She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "Natalia?" "I'm here. Find something to write on." Lynleit pulled a sheet out from under a report. "Should I put my name at the top?" "Twice, if it helps." "It rarely helped with your marking." "Two names, then. Yours and Kyrien's." Lynleit wrote them side by side. "Join them," Natalia said. "Now cross yours out." The pen stopped. "On the paper, Lynleit." "I know. I was enjoying the lesson." "If I gave that sheet to someone who knew Kyrien, could they still find you?" "Through him." "And if you crossed out his name instead?" "They could ask me." "There. Suppression rubs out part of the address. It leaves someone who can supply the missing part." Lynleit looked at the line between the names. She had drawn it through an old calculation. "So they keep treating us as separate patients." "Which is a sensible place to begin. Unfortunately, you have already tested it." "Several times." "And nearly exhausted yourselves proving the same thing. Keep that sheet. We're going to stop repeating it." Lynleit drew a small, unfriendly face beside her name. "This is older than your Holumn," Natalia continued. "The mechanism, I mean. People have been trying to move a death from one person to another for a very long time." "With results?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. A fatal omen threatened the king, so another man occupied his place and received his fate." "Comforting." "The useful question is why the omen would accept the substitute. It wasn't looking for the king's face. It recognized a position someone else could occupy." Lynleit turned the pen over. "This one hid its death in us." "Exactly." She stopped drawing. "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. I was very pleased with them." "Always a warning." "Eventually I noticed that the woman in the notebooks was wonderfully reasonable. She never ate because she was bored. Never postponed a letter because she disliked the recipient. She had excellent reasons for everything." "You should introduce us." "I couldn't. I'd made her up. "It showed me where to look. It didn't explain every disagreement. Some days I was simply tired." Lynleit divided the space below the quotation into two columns. "Expectation and result." "Yes. Changing clothes certainly won't help." "A pity. I could have been cured before lunch." "You're still looking for a procedure you can complete without anything happening to you." "I'm prepared to be mildly inconvenienced." "Lynleit." She put the pen down. "How much has to change?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can give you a difference you already understand. When I left the Academy, I took my books home and thought I would begin all the work I'd been postponing." "And did you?" "I spent the first morning drafting a request to conduct it." Lynleit laughed once, then pressed a hand against her ribs. "To whom?" "An excellent question. I had nowhere to send it." "You could have sent it to me. I'd have approved it." "You would have corrected my handwriting." "Both. I'm generous." "I had stopped being a professor on paper. I was still waiting for someone to permit the next experiment. That habit took longer to notice. Longer still to stop." Lynleit picked up the pen again. "So handing in your resignation wasn't the whole change." "No. Nor would taking the title away from me now put me back where I was. I have done the work. Made mistakes I couldn't assign to the Academy. Paid for them myself." "And you still give examinations over the phone." "Some habits are worth keeping." Lynleit looked at the two names. "Trauma could do it." "It can. So can a religious conversion, grief, parenthood. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older theological records concerning curses that attach themselves to personal identity rather than flesh or soul. His conclusion was disturbingly similar. The Church had encountered analogous phenomena before. Not identical curses, but conditions in which an entity remained attached to a person's psychic continuity. Conversion sometimes worked. Marriage occasionally worked. Surviving war sometimes worked. Parenthood had worked once. A profound confession followed by absolution had produced partial success in another case. Mikhail explained this patiently while Lynleit took notes. Then she reached the practical question. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her. Lynleit waited. The priest appeared to consider several centuries of theology. Then he said, completely straight-faced: "Just have sex, loser." Silence. Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood. "Lynleit." She grabbed her coat. "There are theological reasons." She headed for the door. "Lynleit." She opened it. "The important part is what happens when two people who have spent years maintaining separate identities voluntarily cross a boundary that neither can afterward pretend was never crossed." Lynleit slowly turned around. "If there is already sufficient attachment between you, physical intimacy may produce exactly the discontinuity you need. Body, trust, vulnerability, future expectation, shame, desire, identity. Several layers of the psyche move at once." "And if there isn't sufficient attachment?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Her expression became murderous. Mikhail shrugged. "Which is why I recommend choosing your partner carefully." She left. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit wrote them side by side. "Join them," Natalia said. "Now cross yours out." The pen stopped. "On the paper, Lynleit." "I know. I was enjoying the lesson." "If I gave that sheet to someone who knew Kyrien, could they still find you?" "Through him." "And if you crossed out his name instead?" "They could ask me." "There. "And ours recognizes the people who killed it." "Yes. Usually you hear stories about a creature hiding its life in an egg, or an animal, or a locked box. Killing the body doesn't finish the job." Lynleit turned the pen over. "This one hid its death in us." "Exactly." She stopped drawing. "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." Leave space underneath." "For the translation?" "For your objections. The ego isn't the whole mind. It's the part around which you arrange what you consciously call yours. "Then the memory is doing very well." Lynleit wrote the definition. "So the curse doesn't need every memory intact." "That would be my first objection to erasing them. You might lose a year and still make the same choices for the same reasons. We need to know what it would take for its old description of you to stop being enough." "Can you measure that?" "I once thought I could. I kept a notebook of my decisions for three weeks. Every choice, followed by the reason I thought I'd made it." "How many notebooks?" "Too many. I was very pleased with them." "Always a warning." "Eventually I noticed that the woman in the notebooks was wonderfully reasonable. She never ate because she was bored. Never postponed a letter because she disliked the recipient. She had excellent reasons for everything." "You should introduce us." "I couldn't. I'd made her up. By the time I wrote down a choice, I'd already tidied it." Lynleit smiled and pushed the reports aside. "What did you try instead?" "I wrote down what I expected to do before I did it. Then what actually happened, including the little things I wanted to leave out. Tea, letters, unfinished work. The two columns disagreed much more often." "And that worked?" "It showed me where to look. It didn't explain every disagreement. Some days I was simply tired." Lynleit divided the space below the quotation into two columns. "Expectation and result." "Yes. For you, that means a new description of yourself is not enough. Calling yourself fearless doesn't remove a fear. Losing a title doesn't necessarily change how you make a decision. Changing clothes certainly won't help." "A pity. I could have been cured before lunch." "You're still looking for a procedure you can complete without anything happening to you." "I'm prepared to be mildly inconvenienced." "Lynleit." She put the pen down. "How much has to change?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can give you a difference you already understand. When I left the Academy, I took my books home and thought I would begin all the work I'd been postponing." "And did you?" "I spent the first morning drafting a request to conduct it." Lynleit laughed once, then pressed a hand against her ribs. "To whom?" "An excellent question. I had nowhere to send it." "You could have sent it to me. I'd have approved it." "You would have corrected my handwriting." "Both. I'm generous." "I had stopped being a professor on paper. I was still waiting for someone to permit the next experiment. That habit took longer to notice. Longer still to stop." Lynleit picked up the pen again. "So handing in your resignation wasn't the whole change." "No. Nor would taking the title away from me now put me back where I was. I have done the work. Made mistakes I couldn't assign to the Academy. Paid for them myself." "And you still give examinations over the phone." "Some habits are worth keeping." Lynleit looked at the two names. "Trauma could do it." "It can. So can a religious conversion, grief, parenthood. But none is a reliable instruction. Two people can survive the same event and make very different things of it." "We already have a confrontation with death arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." "And both Kyrien and I would have to change." "Most likely. Go back to your sheet. You crossed out one name and could still recover it through the other." "So changing only me leaves him holding the old answer." "That is the risk. Whatever happens has to change what each of you is to the other." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You gave me homework, introduced me to Carl Jung, and told me about a dead substitute king so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "I was trying to make it sound expensive. I don't intend to pay." "Think about an ordinary evening. You're absorbed in something. Someone you care about was meant to call an hour ago. You read the same sentence three times. You decide to work for another ten minutes before checking your phone." "And check it after two." "Thirty seconds, in my case. Myka was quite safe. I'd spent an hour pretending I could concentrate while I waited to hear it." "You could have called her." "I did. She asked whether I needed help with something." "Did you?" "I needed her to stop sounding so pleased with herself." Lynleit glanced at her own phone. "All right. Someone matters to you. How does that become enough to save us?" "It may not. Worrying over a missed call isn't a cure. But notice how much of an ordinary evening can already depend on someone else's safety. Now imagine finding you can't make plans for your own future without making room for that person. Even plans you never intend to show them." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "You don't have to become agreeable," Natalia added. "You may be thoroughly annoyed. The question is whether you still make the same decisions about your life once theirs has become part of it." "And whether they do the same." "Yes. That's why I'm talking about a reciprocal change. One person longing beautifully while the other carries on as before is no help to my hypothesis." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." "You're enjoying this far too much." "I'm enjoying speaking to you. I'd prefer you weren't dying." Lynleit's hand tightened around the pen. "Then keep your afternoon free. I'm going to bring you a very unreasonable objection." "I look forward to it." After the call, Lynleit copied the two names onto a clean page. Underneath she wrote: What would have to change in both? She folded Natalia's first diagram and kept it inside the notebook. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. His study smelled of wax, old wood, and something medicinal. Lynleit could not locate the last smell. Possibly it was the priest. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older Church records of curses attached to personal identity. He laid out several accounts while she took notes. Conversion had worked in some cases, marriage in others. War, parenthood, a confession followed by absolution: none had worked consistently. "So it isn't the marriage," Lynleit said. "Nor the certificate. The person afterward could no longer be described adequately as the person before." "And what would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail folded his hands over his stomach. Nearly a minute passed. Lynleit straightened in her chair. "Do you understand your problem?" he asked. "I take it you have a theory." "I do." "Then I'm listening." He closed his eyes, rose, and went to the narrow window. In the evening light his cassock was almost black. When he spoke again, his voice had acquired the measured rise and fall of a chant. "O great warrior of the Divine Whore." Lynleit blinked. Her cup stopped halfway to her mouth. "O heir to the blood that stood at Inanna's gates, made covenants beneath her sign, and returned from her altars with what others had to take by the sword." She set the cup carefully on its saucer. "Father Mikhail, I'm not sure that wording is appropriate." "All the better. You're listening." He clasped his hands behind his back. "O daughter of a line that has carried its bond with the Cult through three thousand years. Through kingdoms, wars, prohibitions, reforms, and an inexhaustible supply of people convinced they had finally put an end to it." Lynleit lowered her eyes to the tea. "O heir to a tradition in which desire was power, intimacy could seal a bargain, the body could speak, and a bed could matter more to politics than a throne." "Father Mikhail." It was a very polite request. He looked at her, waited, and continued. "And here sits its representative. Educated. Disciplined. Dangerous. Entirely familiar with her ancestry." Her fingers tightened on the armrest. "And yet..." He considered the wording. Lynleit closed her eyes. "...catastrophically unsuited to the position." "I would ask you not to develop that thought." "Why?" "I doubt it will benefit either of us. Or your priesthood." "A reasonable objection." Her shoulders eased. "Overruled." Mikhail returned to the table, sat, adjusted his sleeve, and drank his tea. Then, in his ordinary voice: "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit stared at him. He took another sip. She opened her mouth, closed it, and looked away. The heat had reached her ears. "You are a priest." "An observant one." "I think we're finished." "No. That was the introduction." She glanced at the door. "Retreat is hardly becoming of a warrior of Inanna, either." "You're beginning to abuse your knowledge of my family." "I'm using the pastoral material available." "My genealogy is not pastoral material." "Everything is pastoral material when the flock is sufficiently stubborn." Lynleit clasped her hands in her lap. "An association between two traditions does not automatically oblige anyone to reproduce every cultural feature of either." Mikhail raised an eyebrow. She stopped. "How interesting." "Don't." "I haven't said anything." "Which is why I'm asking you not to." He reached for his cup. "You've prepared a defence." "A principle." "Of course." "A general principle." "And you understand the charge." "I understand that you've decided to turn genealogy into harassment." She picked up her cup again. "You can discuss murder, a coup, magical blackmail, and mass casualties in a perfectly even voice," Mikhail said. "One other human activity makes you an expert on porcelain." Lynleit looked at the saucer, then at him. "Perhaps the porcelain is behaving with more dignity than certain people present." He gave a quiet snort. "Good. Then let's leave theology out of it. You approach intimacy as an operation to be attempted after reconnaissance, risk assessment, political guarantees, and written opinions from several independent experts." "I came here about a curse." "And I am answering. If you like a man, you investigate him. If you like him a great deal, you begin counterintelligence." Her lips pressed together. "And when it becomes personal enough that neither is helping, you declare the matter irrelevant." Lynleit looked toward the window. Mikhail let her. "Thank you for the diagnosis." "An observation." "It has been noted." "In the voice of an official sending a document to an archive nobody will ever open." She set the cup down. This time she left it there. "You seem to have confused my embarrassment with a treatment." "No. You asked whether something could change both of you enough for the curse to lose its hold. If an attachment already exists, physical intimacy might do that. What you trust him with, what you expect from him afterward, what he can no longer pretend you are to him. You would both have to change." "And if the attachment isn't sufficient?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Lynleit picked up her pen. "So you cannot promise anything." "No. I can tell you why this is a possibility. I cannot make it safe by explaining it until you stop blushing." She wrote something, shut the notebook, and stood. "I think that is more than enough spiritual guidance for one visit." "You're leaving again." "I'm concluding the audience." "This is my study." Lynleit straightened her jacket. "All the more reason." She went to the door. "Lynleit." "What?" "You do understand why this is so funny?" Her hand stayed on the handle. "Unfortunately." "Then we have reached an understanding." She opened the door and looked back. Her face was composed again. "If you ever call me a warrior of the Divine Whore in front of anyone else, I will find a canonically permissible way to make your life considerably less pleasant." Mikhail considered this. "Better." "What?" "Some passion in that threat." She shut the door hard enough to rattle the cups. In the corridor, Lynleit opened her notebook. SEX? occupied most of the page. She nearly tore it out. In the study Mikhail waited until her footsteps had receded, then looked at the door. "Three thousand years of continuity." He took a sip. "And the result. A virgin." He sighed. "A disgrace to the institution." He went on drinking his tea. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

One person longing beautifully while the other carries on as before is no help to my hypothesis." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." "You're enjoying this far too much." "I'm enjoying speaking to you. I'd prefer you weren't dying." Lynleit's hand tightened around the pen. "Then keep your afternoon free. I'm going to bring you a very unreasonable objection." "I look forward to it." After the call, Lynleit copied the two names onto a clean page. Underneath she wrote: What would have to change in both? She folded Natalia's first diagram and kept it inside the notebook. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. His study smelled of wax, old wood, and something medicinal. Lynleit could not locate the last smell. Possibly it was the priest. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older Church records of curses attached to personal identity. He laid out several accounts while she took notes. Conversion had worked in some cases, marriage in others. War, parenthood, a confession followed by absolution: none had worked consistently. "So it isn't the marriage," Lynleit said. "Nor the certificate. The person afterward could no longer be described adequately as the person before." "And what would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail folded his hands over his stomach. Nearly a minute passed. Lynleit straightened in her chair. Mikhail watched her with that particular priestly calm which sometimes preceded consolation, and sometimes something entirely unacceptable. "Do you understand your problem?" he asked. "I take it you have a theory." "I do." "Then I'm listening." He closed his eyes, rose, and went to the narrow window. In the evening light his cassock was almost black. When he spoke again, his voice had acquired the measured rise and fall of a chant. "O great warrior of the Divine Whore." Lynleit blinked. Her cup stopped halfway to her mouth. "O heir to the blood that stood at Inanna's gates, made covenants beneath her sign, and returned from her altars with what others had to take by the sword." She set the cup carefully on its saucer. "Father Mikhail, I'm not sure that wording is appropriate." "All the better. You're listening." He clasped his hands behind his back. "O daughter of a line that has carried its bond with the Cult through three thousand years. Through kingdoms, wars, prohibitions, reforms, and an inexhaustible supply of people convinced they had finally put an end to it." Lynleit lowered her eyes to the tea. She knew where this was going. There was still a possibility that he would stop out of common decency. Mikhail continued. "O heir to a tradition in which desire was power, intimacy could seal a bargain, the body could speak, and a bed could matter more to politics than a throne." "Father Mikhail." It was a very polite request. He looked at her, waited, and continued. "And here sits its representative." "Educated." He raised one finger. "Disciplined." A second. "Dangerous." A third. "Entirely familiar with her ancestry." Lynleit said nothing. "And yet..." He paused, apparently searching for the correct theological term. Lynleit closed her eyes. Mikhail noticed. "...catastrophically unsuited to the position." Her eyes opened. "I would ask you not to develop that thought." "Why?" "I doubt it will benefit either of us. Or your priesthood." "A reasonable objection." Her shoulders eased. "Overruled." Mikhail returned to the table, sat, adjusted his sleeve, and drank his tea. Then, in his ordinary voice: "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit stared at him. Mikhail drank his tea. She continued staring. He lowered the cup. "What?" She opened her mouth, then closed it. "You understood," he said. "I understood quite enough." "Excellent." "I didn't say I agreed." "I didn't ask whether you agreed." "You are a priest." "An observant one." "I think we're finished." "No. That was the introduction." She glanced at the door. "Retreat is hardly becoming of a warrior of Inanna, either." "You're beginning to abuse your knowledge of my family." "I'm using the pastoral material available." "My genealogy is not pastoral material." "Everything is pastoral material when the flock is sufficiently stubborn." Lynleit clasped her hands in her lap. "An association between two traditions does not automatically oblige anyone to reproduce every cultural feature of either." Mikhail raised an eyebrow. She stopped. "How interesting." "Don't." "I haven't said anything." "Which is why I'm asking you not to." He reached for his cup. "You've just supplied your own defence." "I stated a principle." "Of course." "A general principle." "Naturally." Lynleit looked at him. Mikhail remained perfectly composed. "Then you understand the charge." "I understand that you've decided to turn genealogy into harassment." She picked up her cup again, but did not drink. Mikhail watched. "Interesting." Her hand stopped. "What is?" "You can discuss murder, a coup, magical blackmail, and mass casualties in a perfectly even voice." She slowly returned the cup to its saucer. "One other human activity makes you an expert on porcelain." Lynleit looked at the saucer, then at him. "Perhaps the porcelain is behaving with more dignity than certain people present." He gave a quiet snort. "Good. Then let's leave theology out of it. You approach intimacy as an operation to be attempted after reconnaissance, risk assessment, political guarantees, and written opinions from several independent experts." "I came here about a curse." "And I am answering. If you like a man, you investigate him. If you like him a great deal, you begin counterintelligence." Her lips pressed together. "And when it becomes personal enough that neither is helping, you declare the matter irrelevant." Lynleit met his eyes, then looked away. For once, Mikhail did not comment. He drank his tea. "Thank you for the diagnosis." "An observation." "It has been noted." "In the voice of an official sending a document to an archive nobody will ever open." She glanced at the cup. This time she left it alone. "You seem to have confused my embarrassment with a treatment." "No. You asked whether something could change both of you enough for the curse to lose its hold. If an attachment already exists, physical intimacy might do that. What you trust him with, what you expect from him afterward, what he can no longer pretend you are to him. You would both have to change." "And if the attachment isn't sufficient?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Lynleit picked up her pen. "So you cannot promise anything." "No. I can tell you why this is a possibility. I cannot make it safe by explaining it until you stop blushing." "It is considerably easier for you to dispute three thousand years of religious continuity than admit to a thoroughly present-day problem." She wrote something, shut the notebook, and stood. "I think that is more than enough spiritual guidance for one visit." "You're leaving again." "I'm concluding the audience." "This is my study." Lynleit straightened her jacket. "All the more reason." She went to the door. "Lynleit." "What?" "You understand why this is so funny?" Her hand remained on the handle. Several seconds passed. "Unfortunately," she said, very quietly. "Then we have reached an understanding." She opened the door and looked back. Her face was composed again. "If you ever call me a warrior of the Divine Whore in front of anyone else, I will find a canonically permissible way to make your life considerably less pleasant." Mikhail considered this. "Better." "What?" "Some passion in that threat." She shut the door hard enough to rattle the cups. In the corridor, Lynleit opened her notebook. SEX? occupied most of the page. She nearly tore it out. In the study Mikhail waited until her footsteps had receded, then looked at the door. "Three thousand years of continuity." Another sip. "And the result." He sighed. "A virgin." A pause. "A disgrace to the institution." He went on drinking his tea. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail
