entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 After jointly destroying a Holumn, Lynleit and Kyrien inherit one fatal curse written across both identities and search for a way to survive without sacrificing either life. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both of their identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining half reconstructs the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects that answer and searches Magiarchal, medical, theurgical, academic, and Church records for another form of identity discontinuity. Natalia identifies the attachment as sympathetic recognition of the ego and proposes profound reciprocal transformation as a possible alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds Natalia and Mikhail's proposed treatment from Kyrien. Lynleit initiates an awkward sexual encounter and Kyrien responds. Their reciprocal change makes the curse unable to recognize the exact pair of identities that destroyed the Holumn, causing the entanglement to fracture. Lynleit hiding the notebook page suggests that she still cannot discuss the attempt openly with Kyrien. inferred Doom Has an Address After the killing For several nights after they destroyed the Holumn, Lynleit blamed her exhaustion on the fight. Then small cuts stopped closing. Sleep left her as tired as she had been before it. Kyrien began pausing on stairs. He waited for her at the landings, which might have been considerate if she had not seen him trying to recover his breath. The examinations gave them weeks. Suppressing the curse in Lynleit brought brief relief. It returned through Kyrien. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. Whatever had followed them out of the fight was attached to both of them. One could survive if the other died first. "No," Lynleit said. She took the reports away and began calling people who had not yet given her that answer. The Magiarchal records led her to physicians, prohibited theurgical procedures, and arguments about what counted as a person. Memory erasure would not work. Neither would a coma. Destroying magical capacity offered no reliable prospect, and having someone declared dead would change nothing. Eventually she called Natalia. The former professor Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "I'm reading," she said. "You sent six reports." "The last two are the same treatment. On different patients." "I noticed." Lynleit leaned against the desk. Her hand had begun trembling again. She put the telephone in the other one. "The Holumn transferred its death to whoever killed it," Natalia said. "You killed it together. That's why treating either of you separately fails." "They've established that." "They've established what happens. I'm asking what it recognizes." Lynleit looked at the reports. "Us." "Your bodies? Your names? The people you understand yourselves to be?" She had used that tone in lectures. Lynleit had once liked being the student who could answer her. "The ego," she said. "Good. Now tell me why it has to be destroyed." "Because it keeps reconstructing the curse." "And death is the only thing that can change a person?" Lynleit stopped looking at the reports. Natalia spoke about substitute kings, human-shaped vessels used in purification rites, and stories in which a life was hidden outside its body. Lynleit let her finish the first example, interrupted the second, and had to ask her to repeat the third. "These aren't your curse," Natalia said. "But the point of attachment isn't always where you'd expect. Something can recognize a role or a relationship. In this case it recognizes the two people responsible for one act." "Could we make it recognize someone else?" "You need to stop being the people it recognizes." "Memory erasure doesn't work." "Because your memories aren't all of you. Nor is your title, or your name, or the description you'd give a stranger. Jung's ego isn't the whole psyche either, but it is a useful place to begin: the conscious sense of who you are. That can change without killing you." "How much would we have to change?" "That I don't know." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "Conversion," Natalia continued. "Grief. Parenthood, sometimes. An experience that makes your old assumptions impossible to live by. The trouble is getting there deliberately, and getting both of you there before the curse restores what you've changed." "We're already confronting death." "I was hoping for something you could survive." "Then suggest it." Natalia went quiet. "No," Lynleit said. "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit took the telephone away from her ear and looked at it. "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am." "You've taken me through death rituals and Carl Jung to tell me to fall in love?" "You asked for an alternative." "I asked for something we can do." "And I can't prescribe it. You can't pretend your way out of this. But if you already matter enough to each other, there may be something to work with." Lynleit looked toward the door. "How would we know?" "You'd have to risk finding out." There were faster possibilities, Natalia admitted. She declined to describe them. "Go speak to a priest." A second opinion Father Mikhail had records Natalia could not consult. He laid them out while Lynleit took notes. Conversion had broken one attachment. Marriage had broken another. Other accounts concerned war, parenthood, and a confession followed by absolution that had only partly succeeded. Lynleit put a mark beside the partial result. "So confession isn't enough." "In that case, no." "And marriage?" "Neither is a certificate." She looked up. "These people changed," he said. "The records tell us when. They don't give us a rite that will make it happen to you." The list occupied most of a page. She had already crossed out more than half of it. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her notebook, then at her. "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood and took her coat. "Lynleit. There are theological reasons." She reached the door. "Sex is not the important part." Her hand remained on the handle. "If the attachment is already there, acting on it may change what you are to each other. Enough to break the recognition. I cannot promise you that it will." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you will merely have had sex." She left before he could add anything. In the corridor she discovered that she had written SEX? across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. Days Kyrien knew the prognosis and the failed treatments. When he asked about her research, she told him she was still checking something. She checked it against a Magiarchal text, then a thaumaturgical paper. Neither gave her a dependable way to measure the change. Both gave her reasons to keep thinking about it. She tried to imagine explaining the proposed treatment to Kyrien. She got as far as his expression and shut the notebook. By then he tired after ordinary errands. She had to steady her wrist to write. Their remaining time was measured in days. The evening Kyrien noticed the second change of clothes. "Are we going somewhere?" "No." "Then why..." "Is there something wrong with this?" He stopped asking. Later she corrected him over something that needed no correction and spent several minutes avoiding his eyes. "Is this about the curse?" A cushion hit him in the face. He lowered it. "Lynleit." "Don't." "I asked a question." "Ask another one." She had expected to recognize the right moment. Instead they sat beside each other on the sofa, tired and frightened, discussing something she could not keep her mind on. Kyrien said her name. She looked at him. Then she moved closer before she could find another reason to wait. He was surprised. She gave him time to understand, and he answered her. The encounter that followed was sudden and awkward, with little of the composure she had imagined bringing to it. The curse became unstable while they were together. For several seconds they felt it searching for something in them, returning to the same place and failing to settle. Its hold fractured. Neither had cast a spell. Their attachment had changed both identities enough to disrupt the curse's recognition. The encounter had brought that change about; it had no curative power of its own. They survived. Lynleit still had the page in her notebook. She folded it under the next one before Kyrien could see. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

That was the first mistake. Lynleit and Kyrien did not understand what they were fighting until after they had already killed it. Destroying the creature completed the final part of its mechanism: its own terminal condition passed to whoever had caused its death. They had destroyed it together. There was still only one curse, attached to both of them. Their bodies began to weaken. Sleep stopped restoring them properly, and minor injuries healed too slowly. Lynleit found her magecraft increasingly exhausting. Kyrien began stopping on stairs. Within days, ordinary exertion had become difficult for both of them. The Magi who examined the curse gave them several weeks. Attempts to suppress it produced a second discovery. Removing it from Lynleit brought relief only until the attachment to Kyrien restored it. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. One of them could survive if the other died first. Lynleit rejected the answer. She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "This is older than your Holumn," she said at last. "Not the creature itself. The mechanism. People have been inventing versions of it for thousands of years." Lynleit leaned back against the desk. "Such as?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. If an omen predicted the king's death, they could install another man in his place and let the omen fall on him instead. The important part wasn't biology. It was identity. For the duration of the rite, that man occupied the position the omen recognized as king." "Comforting." "It gets worse. Japanese purification rites used human-shaped substitutes to receive pollution or misfortune from a person. Folklore is full of beings whose life is hidden somewhere outside their bodies. An egg, an animal, a box, a tree. Destroying the body does nothing because the actual point of attachment is elsewhere." Lynleit frowned. "You're saying the Holumn did the same thing." "Almost. It inverted the principle." Natalia's voice became more focused. "It hid its death in the people who killed it." Lynleit said nothing. "And then there is the old logic of sympathetic magic," Natalia continued. "Things that have been joined remain connected after separation. Hair, blood, possessions, names, vows. Primitive language for a phenomenon your Magi would dress up with considerably more mathematics." "So when Kyrien and I destroyed it together..." "You didn't each receive half a curse. That would be easier. You became two coordinates of the same one." Lynleit looked down at her hand. "If I suppress mine, his restores it." "Because the structure still resolves correctly. Kyrien exists. You exist. Both of you remain sufficiently identical to the people who performed the act. The curse checks its address and finds both occupants still at home." "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. People just become lazy when death works reliably." Lynleit closed her eyes. "Natalia." "I'm serious." "Then explain." Another pause. "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." "Natalia." "The ego," Natalia said. "That's where I would begin. Jung describes it as 'a complex of ideas which constitutes the centre of my field of consciousness.' Not the whole psyche. The conscious sense of identity. The part that says this is me, this happened to me, this is what I want, this is where I end and the rest of the world begins." Lynleit straightened slightly. Natalia continued. "If the curse attached itself to that structure, then biological death is merely the most absolute way of disrupting it. It isn't necessarily the only way." Lynleit was quiet now. "You think the ego can change enough that the curse stops recognizing it." "Exactly." "How much?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can tell you what would not be enough. New clothes. A new title. Hypnosis. Memory tampering at the surface level. Pretending to become someone else. The change would have to reach the architecture beneath ordinary self-description." "What kind of change?" "The kind after which a person can truthfully say that the one who entered an event and the one who emerged from it are not psychologically identical." Lynleit looked toward the floor. "Trauma," Natalia said. "Religious conversion. Surviving something that forces a complete reorganization of one's values. Grief can do it. Parenthood sometimes does it. A genuine confrontation with death certainly can." "We already have one of those arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "And you think both Kyrien and I would have to change?" "Most likely. The curse is relational. Altering one coordinate might destabilize it, but if the other remains intact it may simply reconstruct the original pattern. You need to damage the relation itself." "Damage?" "Change, if you prefer a nicer word." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You spent the last ten minutes explaining Assyrian death rituals, sympathetic magic, external souls and Carl Jung so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "Natalia." "Love is one of the few ordinary human experiences capable of reorganizing identity at several levels simultaneously. Future, loyalty, fear, attachment, self-image, boundaries. People begin making decisions as though another person has partially entered the structure of the self." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "If the Holumn's curse is anchored to where each of you draws the boundary between self and other," Natalia continued, "then a sufficiently profound reciprocal attachment could distort that boundary enough to break the original configuration." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." Lynleit eventually hung up with considerably more knowledge and considerably less dignity than she had possessed before making the call. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older theological records concerning curses that attach themselves to personal identity rather than flesh or soul. His conclusion was disturbingly similar. The Church had encountered analogous phenomena before. Not identical curses, but conditions in which an entity remained attached to a person's psychic continuity. Conversion sometimes worked. Marriage occasionally worked. Surviving war sometimes worked. Parenthood had worked once. A profound confession followed by absolution had produced partial success in another case. None of these things were magical rituals in themselves. The common element was transformation. An old organization of the self ceased to be sufficient. Something new replaced it. Mikhail explained this patiently while Lynleit took notes. Then she reached the practical question. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her. Lynleit waited. The priest appeared to consider several centuries of theology. Then he said, completely straight-faced: "Just have sex, loser." Silence. Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood. "Lynleit." She grabbed her coat. "There are theological reasons." She headed for the door. "Lynleit." She opened it. "Sex is not the important part." She stopped. Mikhail remained seated. "The important part is what happens when two people who have spent years maintaining separate identities voluntarily cross a boundary that neither can afterward pretend was never crossed." Lynleit slowly turned around. "If there is already sufficient attachment between you, physical intimacy may produce exactly the discontinuity you need. Body, trust, vulnerability, future expectation, shame, desire, identity. Several layers of the psyche move at once." "And if there isn't sufficient attachment?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Her expression became murderous. Mikhail shrugged. "Which is why I recommend choosing your partner carefully." She left. Only in the corridor did Lynleit realize that she had written SEX? in enormous letters across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.subtitle: Chapter 08 · Later in Arc 1
entries.text: The Bench under the Lamp · v1 Chapter 08 · Later in Arc 1 An evening walk leaves Lynleit and Kyrien beneath a park lamp. A joke about their failed attempt becomes a private encounter, followed by an unexpected request for his flask. Lynleit and Kyrien walk through the quarantined park after work, lose their way, and stop at a bench beneath a lamppost. Kyrien takes one small drink from his flask after the long day and returns it to its usual pocket. Their comfortable proximity and teasing bring up the failed curse encounter months earlier. Lynleit has spent the intervening months researching intimacy; the opportunity on the bench is spontaneous. They kiss, and the scene cuts away before the private encounter. The cut away and Lynleit's later claim of successful research indicate that their intimacy has progressed beyond the failed attempt. inferred Lynleit calls the research successful, and they leave the bench before Kyrien asks whether she intends to win arguments this way. Her delayed request for whiskey and refusal to explain suggest an unexpected practical consequence without undoing her satisfaction. inferred Kyrien hands her the flask without pressing for an explanation, and they continue walking. The Bench under the Lamp The path divided again. Lynleit stopped at the fork and looked back. Kyrien was looking back too. "That is unhelpful," she said. "I didn't put it there." They had finished work before the light began to fail. The park still lay between them and a sensible end to the evening. Neither had been particularly diligent about finding the shortest way through it. Kyrien took out his flask. One small drink, then the cap went back on. Lynleit waited while he returned it to the same pocket. "Medicine?" "Long day." She chose the left path. He followed without offering a better one. After a while, a lamppost appeared between the trees. Beneath it stood a bench with a dry seat. Kyrien sat down. "We've established one thing," Lynleit said. "That you chose left?" "That this path has a bench." He moved his elbow. She sat beside him, closer than the available space required, and leaned back. Beyond the light, the path continued into trees they had already spent too much of the day looking at. Her shoulder rested against his. Neither moved it. "You could admit you don't know the way," he said. "I know several ways. I'm choosing between them." "You've tried that answer before." She turned her head. "When?" He looked at her for a moment. "The evening you wouldn't explain anything." "You'll have to be considerably more specific." "The curse." Lynleit studied a loose thread at her cuff. The curse had been gone for months. His memory, unfortunately, had made a complete recovery too. "We survived." "I noticed." "Then your complaint seems poorly founded." "It was a question." She let her hand fall between them. He glanced at it, then back at her face. There had been quite a lot of reading since that evening. Some of it had been useful. Some had disagreed so confidently with the rest that she had wanted to mark it and send it back. None of it had suggested a park bench. "What?" Kyrien asked. "Nothing." "You're looking at me." "You are very near." "You sat there." She smiled at that, reluctantly. Then she kissed him. For a moment, he remained as still as he did before committing to a bad hand of cards. She drew back enough to look at him. "You can stop calculating," she said. "I was going to say that to you." This time, when she leaned toward him, he met her halfway. Afterward They remained beneath the lamp a little longer. Lynleit straightened her cuff. Kyrien watched her with an expression she would have liked to preserve for later reference. "Research was a success," she said. "Thanks for your participation." He looked down at the bench, then at her. "Research." "You're welcome." She stood and checked that she had everything. He took a little longer to get up. "We should probably determine where we are." "Now?" "You were the one who stopped walking." They left the lamp behind. For several minutes Lynleit was excellent company. She did not object when he chose a turning. She even allowed him to finish a sentence about their route. "Is this how you're going to win arguments from now on?" "You wish. Not a chance." He made no attempt to contest the result. They walked farther. Lynleit swallowed, frowned briefly, and continued. A few steps later the frown returned. She stopped. "Give me your whiskey." "Why?" "You don't need to know." His hand went to the familiar pocket. He passed her the flask without another question. She drank, screwed the cap back on, and returned it. "This way," she said. Kyrien followed. Lynleit,Kyrien

entries.title: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge · v1 · Archived
entries.subtitle: Chapter 05 · Part I · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge · v1 · Archived Chapter 05 · Part I · Unknowing Convergence A covert MSF inspection of apparently unmanned river shipments collapses when the Drowned Choir attacks from below, leaving Kyrien to witness Lynleit's forbidden water walking from the quarantined bank. Sherie and Drake ask Lynleit to assemble a loyal team and inspect recurring night traffic on the Vilen river. Several surveillance nights produce no boats while small oddities emerge from the quarantined park. After the failed watches, Lynleit repeatedly challenges Kyrien to short card games and they learn each other's physical tells. Their unfinished rematches and attention to breath, hands, and pauses imply an attraction neither character names or allows to displace the operation. inferred Felix freezes the bridge cameras and remains on the city bank as fallback while Reiner leads Lynleit, Kyrien, Maren, and Ivo down onto the boats. When a boat shifts, Kyrien briefly steadies Lynleit near the concealed Sparrow holster and releases her before she asks. The empty boats, drowned hands, and pale girl imply that the contraband crews were taken before the interception. inferred Reiner, Maren, and Ivo reach the city bank with Felix's fallback line while Kyrien is forced toward the quarantined park bank. The drowned hands tear away Lynleit's blue suede jacket and drag her underwater until fury releases blue flame through the river. The river surface holds beneath Lynleit's palm, knee, and boots, allowing her to stand above hands that cannot cross it. The pale girl's silence and tilted head imply that Lynleit's survival contradicts the rule by which the Drowned Choir takes people. inferred Kyrien's careful denial and continued silence imply that he has chosen to protect Lynleit's forbidden ability before either of them openly trusts the other. inferred Lynleit crosses the held surface to the park bank and later sits back to back with Kyrien for warmth among the trees. Chapter 05: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge Working draft based on the confirmed river operation. Exact dialogue, further oddities during the unsuccessful watches, and the meaning of the girl's refusal to pursue Lynleit remain provisional. The Fifth Watch The bridge was closed at the park end. On the southern bank, a low riverside district faced the water through mature trees and garden fences. Old wooden villas stood beside modest masonry houses, their windows scattered across the slope. The nearest main road lay beyond them. Lamps threw pale circles across the pavement, and civil safety cameras watched the bridge from both approaches. On the northern bank, the same bridge ended at a locked path into the quarantined park. No lamps remained lit beyond the barrier. Trees had grown into a single black mass behind it. Drake's reports described small boats passing on the darkest nights, without navigation lights, visible cargo, or anyone at the controls. The timing looked deliberate. Contraband remained a possibility. Sherie and Drake had asked Lynleit for a team capable of observing the boats without turning the investigation into an official MSF operation. The plan was narrow. Felix would freeze the bridge cameras for as long as he could preserve a convincing loop, maintain communications, and remain on the city side as the fallback if the river team lost its exit. Reiner would secure the descent ropes. Lynleit, Reiner, Kyrien, Maren, and Ivo would board from above, inspect the boats, and leave by ropes at the next bridge. They were not to seize cargo, stop a suspect, or remain after the camera window closed. The first watch produced nothing. The second ended when Felix warned that the camera loop had begun to drift out of time with the traffic lights. On the third, a branch broke somewhere inside the park before the wind reached the trees. Kyrien turned toward the sound. Lynleit noticed him turning and looked as well. Neither said anything. On the fourth, one of the frozen camera feeds showed a pale interruption on the park path. Felix blamed compression damage. When he restored the live image, the path was empty. They had no authority to investigate the park, no safe way to extend the camera window, and no proof that either incident meant anything. Every night ended with the same order from Lynleit. "Restore the cameras. We leave." The second night had left Lynleit and Kyrien waiting inside the maintenance van while Felix restored the live feeds and Reiner recovered the anchors. Felix kept a worn deck of cards in a side compartment. Kyrien found it first. Lynleit sat opposite him. He won the first short game without speaking more than the rules required. "Again," she said. The rematch continued on the third night. Lynleit watched his hands until Kyrien asked whether she intended to look at her own cards. She did not answer. Before one reckless play, his breathing stopped for a beat. He won anyway. On the fourth night, she noticed the same pause and smiled before placing an ordinary card. Kyrien looked at her instead of the table. The hesitation was brief, but his next play was the safer one. "You changed the conditions," he said. "The cards are unchanged." He began watching her hands after that. By the end of the night, he had found the small movement of her thumb that came before a committed decision. They dealt another hand before the fifth camera window opened. Felix called them to position before either could finish it. Kyrien left his cards face down on the metal shelf. Lynleit left hers opposite them. By the fifth watch, nobody expected the boats. Felix sat inside a maintenance van on the city side with a compact terminal across his knees. The bridge cameras were displayed in four muted panes. Each showed a version of the previous several minutes with no MSF officers in it. "The loop is clean," he said through the earpieces. "Please do something before I have to put it back." Reiner tested the last anchor point with both hands. "Window." Felix gave him the remaining time. "Shorter than yesterday," Reiner said. "Yesterday had fewer buses. I was not consulted about the timetable." Lynleit stood against the inner rail and watched the black water below. She had chosen a fitted blue suede jacket instead of her usual coat because it would interfere less with ropes and wet timber. It still concealed the Sparrow carried above her tailbone, but did nothing against the cold rising from the river. The current caught fragments of city light and stretched them until they broke. Kyrien waited several paces away. He had no MSF insignia and no recognized place in the formation. Felix had assigned him no task that could not be watched by someone else. "If they do not appear tonight, we end the pattern," Lynleit said. "Because the operation has failed?" Kyrien asked. "Because repeating an intrusion after the target has noticed it is not surveillance." Felix looked up from the terminal. "That almost sounded directed at someone." Kyrien did not answer. Reiner lifted one hand. The bridge fell silent. Something had entered the far edge of the river. At first Lynleit saw only the interruption it made in the reflected lights. Then the first boat separated from the dark, followed by another and another. They were small, weathered wooden craft with dark tarps stretched across shallow holds. Their lamps were off. Fixed rudders kept their bows aligned while the current carried most of their weight toward the bridge. Nobody stood at the controls. Felix stared at the feed, then at the river itself. "Those are our boats." "I can see them," Reiner said. "There is nobody aboard." "That is what we are here to establish." Lynleit watched the distance close. "Positions." The officers moved. The Descent Reiner went over the rail first, paying out the rope in short, even lengths. Maren and Ivo followed on the adjacent line. Felix stayed with the terminal inside the locked maintenance van, watching the camera loop and every signal the descending team still transmitted. Kyrien waited until Lynleit reached the rail. "You first," he said. "Is that concern?" "If I go first, Felix may cut the rope." Felix's voice arrived through both earpieces. "The possibility has been evaluated." Lynleit swung over the side. The river moved beneath her boots. The lead boat passed under the bridge at the expected angle, steady enough that Reiner landed near its center without shifting its course. The others divided themselves between the following boats. Lynleit released the rope last and absorbed the impact through her knees. Kyrien landed behind her. His weight rolled the boat farther than Reiner's landing had. Lynleit's footing shifted on the wet boards. Kyrien caught her at the waist from behind. The heel of his hand met the leather edge of the Sparrow holster beneath her jacket. Lynleit's hand went to the rail instead of the pistol. Kyrien released her before she had recovered her balance completely. The boat continued forward. There was no pilot. There was no passenger. Lynleit pulled back the tarp. The hold was empty. No mechanism visible from the deck explained how the boat had kept its route beyond the fixed rudder and the current. Its shallow interior carried the practical alterations of a craft used to move things without inviting inspection. Tonight there was no cargo to inspect. Reiner's voice came from the first boat. "Empty." The second team confirmed the same. Felix opened the restricted channel. "Nothing in any of them? Check under the boards." Lynleit crouched beside the controls. The metal was wet. So was the deck. Nothing proved that a living person had occupied the boat recently. She looked back at the tarp. Someone had covered an empty hold. The park passed on their right. From the water, the trees appeared closer than they had from the bridge. Their lowest branches extended over the bank and hid the path behind them. Kyrien stopped breathing for one beat. Lynleit looked toward him before he turned to the trees. "What?" Lynleit asked. "Nothing." Maren shifted toward the gunwale. "There is something beside us." Reiner answered at once. "Do not lean out." She had already looked down. Her right leg vanished over the side. There was no splash large enough to explain the force. Her hip struck the gunwale, both hands caught the rail, and the rest of her body followed as if the river had taken hold of her boot. Reiner crossed from the lead boat before anyone else moved. He caught her wrist. For a moment his weight held her above the surface. Then his shoulder jerked downward. "Line," he ordered. Ivo threw it from the next boat and braced against a thwart. The boats had begun to separate, not quickly, but in different directions. The rope snapped tight between them. The woman in the water tried to kick toward the hull. Her face changed. "Something has my legs." Reiner pulled hard enough to bring her shoulder against the side. The water pulled harder. His footing broke, and he went in beside her. The river ceased to behave like water shared by bodies of different weight. It took each person according to a separate direction. Ivo entered to reach Reiner. Kyrien cut the slack before the line could take Lynleit with it, but the boat rolled beneath both of them. The gunwale struck her thigh. A moment later the deck was gone from under her feet. Cold closed around the team. Two Shores The city bank was the assigned emergency route. It had steps, lamps, and streets where an extraction vehicle could approach without crossing the quarantine. Reiner forced Maren toward it. When something pulled her legs down, he hooked an arm beneath her shoulders and kicked hard. Ivo reached them from the side. Together they gained a metre, lost half of it, and gained it again. Felix kept the communications channel open from the city bank. "City side. Do not fight for the boats. City side." The order gave the officers one direction when the river seemed determined to give each of them another. Hands caught at boots, ankles, and calves. Most of the officers felt only pressure and fingers where no person could remain submerged. They kicked free without seeing what they struck. Felix left the van only when the operation had already collapsed. He carried the fallback line down to the embankment steps and threw it toward the first heads he could distinguish. Reiner reached the wall and lifted Maren high enough for Felix to catch her from above. Ivo followed in fragments, coughing river water and helping pull Reiner beyond the edge. "It was hands," Maren said. Felix knelt beside her. "What was?" "On my legs. Someone was holding my legs." Reiner looked back at the river. Lynleit was not among them. Neither was Kyrien. The force beneath the water had turned Kyrien away from the city bank. He stopped spending strength on a direction the river would not permit and chose the nearer ground. The park bank offered mud, exposed roots, and a wall of unlit trees. He caught the lowest root with both hands and pulled himself out beneath the branches. The quarantine waited behind him. He remained low and moved inside the tree line. From there, he could see the broken formation of boats and the heads of the officers reaching the opposite shore. He could not see Lynleit. Then the river struck the underside of the surface from below. Beneath Lynleit knew how to swim. That knowledge survived for the first several seconds. She turned toward the nearest light, drove one arm forward, and tried to bring her legs behind her. Her right ankle stopped. Fingers closed around it. Another hand caught her calf. A third pressed against the back of her knee. They did not seize her in one direction. They climbed. She kicked and felt a wrist bend beneath her heel. The grip did not release. Her jacket dragged in the current and made every movement heavier. The surface was still visible. She could not reach it. Her fear of drowning had existed since childhood. Training had given it procedures: control the breath, identify the current, discard weight, choose a direction. The hands made each instruction useless. They were not a current. They did not tire. They had no single body against which leverage mattered. One closed around her other ankle. Others seized the suede jacket and pulled its hem over her hips, turning the fitted garment into another grip against her escape. The river pulled her farther from the light. She kicked again. It had steps, lamps, and streets where an extraction vehicle could approach without crossing the quarantine. Reiner forced Maren toward it. When something pulled her legs down, he hooked an arm beneath her shoulders and kicked hard. Ivo reached them from the side. Together they gained a metre, lost half of it, and gained it again. Felix kept the communications channel open from the city bank. "City side. Do not fight for the boats. City side." The order gave the officers one direction when the river seemed determined to give each of them another. Hands caught at boots, ankles, and calves. Most of the officers felt only pressure and fingers where no person could remain submerged. They kicked free without seeing what they struck. Felix left the van only when the operation had already collapsed. He carried the fallback line down to the embankment steps and threw it toward the first heads he could distinguish. Reiner reached the wall and lifted Maren high enough for Felix to catch her from above. Ivo followed in fragments, coughing river water and helping pull Reiner beyond the edge. "It was hands," Maren said. Felix knelt beside her. "What was?" "On my legs. Someone was holding my legs." Reiner looked back at the river. Lynleit was not among them. Neither was Kyrien. The force beneath the water had turned Kyrien away from the city bank. He stopped spending strength on a direction the river would not permit and chose the nearer ground. The park bank offered mud, exposed roots, and a wall of unlit trees. He caught the lowest root with both hands and pulled himself out beneath the branches. The quarantine waited behind him. He remained low and moved inside the tree line. The water nearest the bank was visible beneath the branches. Farther out, mist broke the boats into separate glimpses. At the city steps he made out heads below a moving light, then lost them again. He could not see Lynleit. Then the river struck the underside of the surface from below. Beneath Lynleit knew how to swim. That knowledge survived for the first several seconds. She turned toward the nearest light, drove one arm forward, and tried to bring her legs behind her. Her right ankle stopped. Fingers closed around it. Another hand caught her calf. A third pressed against the back of her knee. They did not seize her in one direction. They climbed. She kicked and felt a wrist bend beneath her heel. The grip did not release. Her jacket dragged in the current and made every movement heavier. The surface was still visible. She could not reach it. Her fear of drowning had existed since childhood. Training had given it procedures: control the breath, identify the current, discard weight, choose a direction. The hands made each instruction useless. They were not a current. They did not tire. They had no single body against which leverage mattered. One closed around her other ankle. Others seized the suede jacket and pulled its hem over her hips, turning the fitted garment into another grip against her escape. The river pulled her farther from the light. She kicked again. The grip tightened. In the panic she wanted to hurt whatever was holding her, even if she had to turn and go deeper to reach it. Lynleit twisted downward instead of up. Blue flame broke from both hands and spread through the water without steam or loss of colour. It caught the drowned wrists as if the river were air. The hands burned beneath the surface. Fingers opened. Others caught at her sleeves, her boots, and the edge of the jacket until the suede tore free and disappeared among them. She tore upward through them. Her head broke the surface. Air entered as pain. She coughed, reached for anything that might hold her, and found nothing. Her palm struck the water and met resistance where her weight should have broken through. The surface bowed beneath her like stretched cloth, then held. Lynleit pressed down. She brought one knee onto the same impossible resistance, planted a boot, and pushed herself upright. Water ran from her ash-black hair across her face. Her breath would not slow. The river yielded by a few centimetres beneath each step but no longer admitted her body. Hands filled the darkness beneath her. Some were pale. Some had lost the shape of living hands. Small ones reached between larger ones. They opened and closed beneath the soles of her boots, pressing against the underside of the surface. None passed through it. Lynleit stood above them. From the trees, Kyrien watched without moving. The water ahead of Lynleit swelled. Hair appeared first, flattened against a white forehead. Then came a face with fishing line drawn through both eyelids. The knots were neat. Water dripped from them. The girl rose until the river released the upper half of her dress. Dead fish had been fastened together in overlapping rows, their bodies colourless, their mouths opening as the current passed through them. She faced Lynleit. The drowned hands continued reaching below. The girl said nothing. Lynleit could not tell whether sewn eyes were capable of looking at her, but she felt the attention settle. The girl's head tilted slowly to one side. Lynleit glanced down at her own boots, then back at the girl. She did not dare move yet. The Park Bank The girl did not pursue when Lynleit moved. Lynleit placed one foot before the other, testing the surface each time before trusting it. The water depressed beneath her boots and recovered behind them. She backed toward the park bank until mud and reeds replaced the impossible support beneath her feet. Kyrien found her beyond the lowest branches, where the bank rose into the trees. She had lost the blue suede jacket. Her blouse and the holster above her tailbone were soaked through, her ash-black hair clung to her cheeks and throat, and she was still breathing as if the hands remained around her legs. He removed his jacket. It was as wet as everything else and therefore useless. "A thoughtful gesture," Lynleit said. "I reconsidered it." "Sensibly." They moved under the trees, away from the exposed bank. Through gaps between the trunks and drifting mist, they could still see parts of the city embankment across the water. Felix and Reiner were gathering the officers beneath the bridge lights. A cough reached them from that direction. Lynleit looked back, but could not tell who had coughed. Lynleit stopped at the base of a broad tree and sat. Kyrien lowered himself behind her. They settled back to back, shoulders touching through soaked clothes, each lending the other the little warmth that remained. For a while neither spoke. His breathing was slower than hers but not yet steady. Once, it stopped for the same brief interval she had learned across the cards. Lynleit looked across the river toward the officers gathering under Felix's light. "You came ashore on this side," Lynleit said. "It was closer." "So you could see the river." "Parts of it." She waited. "Did you see anything strange?" she asked. "The boats had no crews. Something tried to drown all of us. We are sitting inside a quarantined park in wet clothes." "That is not what I asked." "It is what happened." Lynleit turned her face slightly, not enough to look at him. "And nothing else?" "Nothing I can explain." Lynleit let her head rest back against his shoulder. "Then do not invent an explanation," she said. "I was not planning to." Across the river, Felix's light moved along the embankment. Reiner stood at the edge, looking toward the park. Kyrien saw the search before Lynleit did. He remained still for another moment, keeping his back against hers while her breathing slowed. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner,Sherie,Drake

entries.text: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge · v4 · Current Chapter 05 · Part I · Unknowing Convergence The River Choir, Part I. Kyrien checks the exits, endures four failed watches and boards the empty boats on the fifth. When the river takes hold of the team, the forbidden bank is the only ground he can reach. Kyrien inspects the bridge, locked park barrier and city steps before the covert boat operation. Four failed watches exhaust the camera windows; a breaking branch and a pale camera interruption remain unexplained. Lynleit and Kyrien play repeated card games during operational downtime. He watches her hands; she watches his fingers and face. Their attention to each other begins to exceed what either needs to win a card game. inferred On the fifth watch, heavy mist interrupts the view across the river. Three wooden boats arrive with fixed rudders and empty tarp-covered holds. Felix stays ashore while Reiner, Maren, Ivo, Lynleit and Kyrien descend by rope. Kyrien steadies Lynleit at the waist when the boat shifts and releases her as she catches the rail. Maren is pulled over the side. Reiner tries to hold her, then enters the water; Ivo follows to help. Lynleit puts on black gloves and rolls up her sleeves. Kyrien cuts a snagged line before their boat rolls. Kyrien feels fingers holding his leg but cannot see their source. Reiner, Maren and Ivo move towards the city steps while he struggles towards the park roots. Kyrien reaches the mud on the park bank without understanding the attack. The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge The River Choir, Part I. Kyrien. The city side I checked the other end of the bridge before I checked the ropes. There was a locked barrier across it. Behind that, a path went into the park and disappeared between trees. The notice on the barrier was large enough to read from the middle of the bridge. It said the area was closed. It didn't say where you should go if you happened to come out of the river on that side. Reiner found me looking at it. “Our exit is downstream.” “I saw.” “Then check this one.” He put a rope into my hand. I checked it. He watched until I had finished, took it back, and checked it himself. I didn't object. If I had been responsible for somebody I hadn't chosen, I would have done the same. The bridge joined the city to the quarantined park. On our side there were houses, a street, steps down to the embankment. A bus passed beyond the gardens often enough that I began recognizing the sound before its lights appeared. On the other side there was the barrier and then nothing lit. You could stand in the middle and hear someone's television through an open window behind you while looking at a place nobody was supposed to enter. Lynleit had brought me to inspect boats. That was the work, as she explained it. Small wooden craft had been passing at night without lights, and nobody watching from the banks had seen anyone aboard. Drake had information he wouldn't hand over through the usual channels. Sherie had helped persuade Lynleit to supply people instead. I had seen the envelope change hands at their meeting. I hadn't heard everything said over it. Afterwards Lynleit gave us the part we needed: watch, board, look, leave. We weren't making arrests. We weren't bringing a boat home. We weren't following anything into the park. “If there's somebody aboard?” I asked. “Report it before you approach.” “If they approach us?” “Then the inspection is over.” Felix was sitting in the open van, feeding a cable beneath his terminal. He glanced up at that. “An unusually short assignment. You should enjoy it.” I asked Lynleit where we would come out. She showed me the next bridge downstream. Reiner would arrange the lines there before we started. If we couldn't use them, the city embankment had steps. Felix would remain with the van, the cameras and the fallback line. The park was on the wrong side of every part of the plan. That much was clear. I didn't particularly like having the current choose when we reached the exit, but I could follow the arrangement. I wanted to see the steps for myself. Lynleit came with me while Reiner and the others worked on the ropes. The lower steps were dark with water. I counted them from the pavement, then went down far enough to see where the wall began to overhang. There was a narrow ledge beside the bottom step. Farther along, there was nowhere obvious to put a foot. “You can swim?” she asked. “Yes.” “Reiner will ask you again.” “He already did.” She leaned on the upper rail, looking past me at the river. Her usual long coat moved against the iron. A little water had gathered on the rail under her hand, and she wiped it off with her thumb without looking down. “Is there something you don't like?” she asked. “These aren't visible from the bridge.” “Felix will be here if we need them.” “I mean to somebody in the water.” She looked at the steps again. This time she came down two of them. “A light from here,” she said. “Not from the road.” I nodded. She stayed a moment longer. I could hear Reiner calling from above. She heard him too, but she was still looking at the water when she answered. I had agreed to work for her. That didn't mean I thought she told me everything. There were things about my release, the people she could influence, and the work itself that she answered carefully or didn't answer at all. But she had listened about the steps. I found it useful to keep those two observations separate. What we did while nothing happened The first night, nothing came down the river except rubbish. I watched a pale container approach for so long that I could still see its shape when I looked away. It caught behind one of the bridge supports, turned once and stayed there. Felix asked whether I intended to arrest it. I didn't answer. A few minutes later he asked if it had resisted. Lynleit ended the watch when the camera window ran out. Reiner recovered the equipment. We drove away without a chase, a discovery, or anything to justify how carefully we had got there. The second night ended earlier. Felix said his loop was slipping out of time with the traffic lights. I couldn't see the fault until he pointed out the same car passing twice behind a changing reflection. Once he showed me, it was obvious. “How long?” Reiner asked. Felix gave him a time. Lynleit said, “Restore the cameras. We leave.” Nobody argued for another few minutes. I liked that. It would have been easy to begin treating the limit as negotiable because the boats hadn't obliged us. Reiner still had work on the bridge, so I waited in the van. My phone had a message confirming that my mother was home and had eaten. I read it twice, sent a reply, and put the phone away before Lynleit climbed in. She took the seat across from me, leaving the side door open. Felix's cards were in a compartment beside my knee. The box had worn through at one corner. I took them out because there was nothing useful to watch from inside the van and because watching Felix work seemed to annoy him more than was worth the effort. “Those are mine,” he said. “I assumed.” “Don't bend them.” Several were already bent. I dealt around the worst one. Lynleit put her gloves beside her on the seat and accepted a hand. We agreed on a short game. No money. Felix said he wanted a share if there was money. Lynleit told him to finish what he was doing. I won. She looked at the last card I had put down, then at my hand, as though the part she wanted to examine might still be there. “Again.” Reiner shut the van door before we could deal. She remembered on the third night. I hadn't thought she would forget, but I was pleased she brought it up first. That watch had been worse than the others without giving us anything we could use. A branch broke inside the park. I turned towards it before the wind reached the trees along the water. Lynleit turned a moment after me. We both stood looking through the barrier, listening to the leaves begin moving. It could have been rotten timber. It could have been somebody stepping where the ground gave way. Nothing followed it. “What was that?” she asked. “A branch.” “Yes, thank you.” She waited. I had nothing better to give her. We had no reason to cross the barrier. We left it where it was and watched for boats. They didn't come. By the time we got back into the van, I still wanted to know why I had turned so quickly. Lynleit sat opposite me and tapped the cards. For the first few hands she watched my fingers more than the cards on the shelf between us. “You have cards of your own,” I said. She looked down at them, as though checking my claim, and carried on watching me. I won that game too. On the last play I took a risk I didn't need to take. I remember that because she moved her attention from my hand to my face just before I put the card down. She didn't say anything. I thought she had noticed the card I was protecting. I began keeping my hand flatter. On the fourth night, Felix had a pale mark on one of the camera panes. It was near the park entrance. Not the whole shape of a person. A narrow interruption beside the path, too light against the trees. He went back over the loop and found it again. “Compression,” he said. “Show us the live feed,” Lynleit said. He did. The path was empty. I looked from the screen to the barrier outside. There wasn't a white sign in that position. I asked how old the loop was. Felix told me, then told me that an image defect didn't become a visitor just because I disliked it. “I didn't say it was a visitor.” “You were preparing to.” Lynleit asked him to keep the frame. She didn't send anyone into the park. When the watch ended, she gave the same order about the cameras and sat down to finish our rematch. I had a chance to end it quickly. She watched me consider the play. Then she smiled and put down an ordinary card. I looked at her for longer than I should have. Not long. Long enough to lose the count I had been keeping. I played the safer card. “You changed the conditions,” I said. “The cards are unchanged.” I counted again from what I could see. She waited with the same small smile, enjoying the wait. I wanted to beat her rather more than the game deserved. After that I watched her hands. She moved her thumb along the edge of a card before committing herself. It wasn't every move, and when I thought I had found an easy way to read her, I lost a hand. I had mistaken impatience for a decision. She laid the winning card down and looked at me until I collected it. Felix reached between us for a lead he needed. We both moved our cards out of his way without stopping. He looked from her to me, unplugged the lead and went back to his screen. We were still playing when Reiner returned. On the fifth night there was a hand left unfinished on the shelf. Mine were face down. Hers were opposite. Felix called us out before either of us could make the other finish. The fifth watch The drive had been clear. On two earlier nights fog had slowed us before we reached the river, but this time I could see the houses at the top of the slope. Below the bridge it was different. The mist lay in broad stretches over the water. A reflection would disappear in it and return farther down with no lamp visible above. I checked the steps again. Felix's line was ready. Reiner made me repeat which bank I would use if I couldn't regain a boat. “City side,” I said. “Even if the park looks closer.” I looked across. Roots projected over the water there. They were easier to see than the steps. Lynleit wore a short blue suede jacket that night. I noticed because I had been expecting her to lift the long coat clear of the ropes. She tested the reach of both arms before settling against the rail. The holster at her lower back stayed covered when she bent. “If they do not appear tonight, we end the pattern,” she said. “Because the operation has failed?” “Because repeating an intrusion after the target has noticed it is not surveillance.” Felix said something about that being directed at someone. I let him have it. I was looking at the fixed reflection under the bridge. There was another reflection beside it that hadn't been there before. Reiner raised his hand. A boat came out of the mist. Then another. Then a third, close enough behind the second that I first took its bow for something tied to the stern. They were low wooden craft with dark tarps over the holds. No lights, no visible load. The first turned a little in the current, corrected, and passed under a pale patch from the bridge lamp. I could see the rudder held in position. I couldn't see anyone controlling it. Felix looked away from his terminal towards the real water. “Those are our boats.” “I can see them,” Reiner said. “There is nobody aboard.” “That is what we are here to establish.” I watched the gap between the first two boats. It widened under the support and narrowed again beyond it. They weren't tied together. At least there was no line above the water. If there was someone beneath the tarp, they were willing to come under the bridge without looking where they were going. Lynleit leaned over far enough to check beneath our ropes. She looked back at Reiner. He nodded. “Positions,” she said. He went first. His descent made the boat look steadier than I expected. He got his feet down near its centre, bent his knees, and let the line slide clear. Maren and Ivo followed onto the second boat. Lynleit waited for the third. I stood back from the rail. “You first.” “Is that concern?” “If I go first, Felix may cut the rope.” His answer arrived through the earpiece. “The possibility has been evaluated.” She went over without answering him. I watched her find the boat and followed. From above, the boards had looked merely wet. With my weight on them they shifted and the whole boat rolled. Lynleit was still moving her foot clear of the descent line. Her shoulder went back. I caught her at the waist, and the heel of my hand struck the hard leather edge beneath her jacket. She caught the rail. I let go. For a moment I was aware of exactly where my hand had been. Then the rope slid out of reach and we were moving away from the bridge. Under the tarps There was nobody at the stern. I checked there first, although there was nowhere for a person to hide except under the covering we could both see. Lynleit drew the tarp back. It sagged into the hold. I expected boxes low enough to be covered without showing a shape, or someone lying flat with a weapon pointed up at us. There was nothing. A little water, ribs of timber, the underside of the boards. “Empty,” Reiner said from the first boat. Ivo answered from the second. The same. Felix asked us to check underneath. I crouched while Lynleit held the tarp clear. One of the boards lifted at the edge. I got my fingers beneath it and raised it far enough to look. Water moved below. I lowered it carefully; it would have been a stupid place to trap a hand. “Anything?” she asked. “Water.” She looked herself. I moved so she could get the angle without leaning over me. The boats still looked as though somebody had prepared them to carry something. The alterations were useful ones: a hold you could cover quickly, nothing projecting high enough to catch the eye from the street. I could understand a crew hiding before a bridge. I couldn't understand why they would cover nothing and then abandon all three craft in the same stretch of current. I looked back upstream. The bridge was receding behind the mist. There wasn't a swimmer following us that I could see. “How long until the next bridge?” Lynleit asked. Felix told her. Reiner said we would be ready for the lines. I checked the side facing the park. Low branches covered the bank, and the mist made them look detached from their trunks. The nearer ones were visible against the water. Beyond them there was only a grey darkness where the path ought to be. Something held my attention there. I stopped breathing to listen. Lynleit looked at me before I turned my head fully. “What?” “Nothing.” I meant nothing I could point to. She didn't like the answer. Neither did I. I kept looking for a break in the movement of the leaves. Maren spoke from the next boat. “There is something beside us.” Reiner told her not to lean out. She had already moved. I saw her shoulder above the tarp, her hand on the side. Then her hip struck the wood and her foot was gone. I didn't see anything rise to take it. Reiner crossed the gap while it was still narrow. He caught her wrist and went down on one knee. She was hanging against the side, trying to bring her other leg back into the boat. For a second he held her there. “Line.” Ivo threw it. Lynleit told him where to brace. I grabbed the loose portion that came across our deck before it could slide beneath my foot. Maren said something was holding her legs. I thought of a submerged cable. I looked for tension in the water, a snag pulling her behind the moving hull. There wasn't one I could identify. Her body went down almost straight beneath her hands. Reiner's shoulder jerked. The boat rolled towards him. Ivo pulled from the other side, but the first boat was already moving away without anybody on it. The distance between us changed while they were trying to use it. Lynleit was giving directions beside me. I saw black gloves and her sleeves pushed back. I didn't ask about them. Reiner went in, and Maren disappeared beneath the side of the boat. Ivo entered the water after them. The loose line slid over our gunwale. I had it in my hand when the next pull came. It ran across Lynleit's boot and drew tight around a fitting. The boat began to turn towards the pull. I had my knife out before I could decide whether I was cutting away something we would need. There wasn't time to untie it. I cut the line beside the fitting, and the freed length went into the river. The boat rolled back under us. Its side hit my thigh. I reached for wood and found the wet tarp instead. The nearer ground I went in with my mouth open. I remember being angry about that before I understood anything else. I had seen it coming and still hadn't kept my mouth shut. The cold made me draw up my knees. My jacket dragged across my shoulders. I pushed it away from my throat, kicked and found air. Felix was saying, “City side. Do not fight for the boats. City side.” I turned towards the lamps. Reiner had an arm under Maren's shoulders. Ivo was close to him. I could see them in pieces, a head, a raised forearm, water across someone's face. They were making progress towards the steps. I tried to follow. Something closed around my ankle. It felt like a hand. I didn't want to decide that while I was swallowing water. I kicked down, expecting whatever had snagged me to loosen if I changed the angle. The pressure moved higher instead. There was a separate pressure against the back of my knee. I went under again. I couldn't see anything useful. My eyes stung, and the lights above had become long pale strokes. I brought my other foot against the grip, kicked and turned. I was free for one stroke. That stroke took me farther from the city. When I got my head up, Lynleit's boat was on its side. I saw her face beside it, then an arm reaching past the boards. I tried to call her name. Water broke against my mouth before I could finish. I could have spent the rest of my strength swimming towards where she had been. I tried for long enough to find that I wasn't getting closer. Something pulled beneath my left leg. My shoulders turned while I was still trying to go straight. I stopped fighting for the lamps and looked the other way. The roots on the park bank were nearer. I had noticed them from the bridge because they projected over the water. Now I could distinguish the one that forked near its end. Behind it was mud, a slope, trees. I couldn't see anything waiting there. I also couldn't see anything holding my leg. I kicked towards the root. For two strokes I moved. On the third my leg stopped again and my face went under. I bent towards it, got a hand against my own trouser leg, and found fingers through the cloth. I couldn't get a useful grip on them. I drove my heel across them and kicked for the pale fork I had last seen above me. I came up short of it. My first reach caught leaves. They tore away in my hand. I let the current take me a little farther, though every part of me wanted to go straight at the bank. The thicker root was downstream of the leaves. I reached again, caught it with my fingertips and got my other hand over it before I slipped. There was no bottom beneath my feet. I had both arms bent, my chest against the root, and nothing to push on. I tried to pull higher and nearly lost the hold. Across the water a light moved down the steps. Felix shouted a name I couldn't make out. Somebody answered. The sound gave me enough of an ordinary direction to stop trying everything at once. I put my right hand farther along the root. It was thicker there. I pulled until I could get an elbow over it, then brought my knee up towards the mud. Something dragged at my shoe. I kicked without looking down. This time my knee found ground. I pressed it into the bank and pulled again. Continue to Part II: The Water Beneath Her Feet Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner,Sherie,Drake

entries.subtitle: Chapter 02 · The Quarantine
entries.text: The Last Man Out · v1 · Archived Chapter 02 · The Quarantine Captain Heyk leads a specially equipped unit into Vilen's sealed park and becomes its sole survivor. Public disappearances force police to close the park before the government seals it even from them. Captain Heyk leads a specially equipped paramilitary unit into the park. Forces the unit cannot understand or explain massacre the squad. Heyk becomes the sole survivor and is evacuated by the Ducal Guard under Drake's orders. Grief for his squad follows him into a new role as a Ducal Guard field agent and bodyguard serving Drake and Sherie. Chapter 02: The Last Man Out Placeholder draft built from confirmed quarantine events. Exact action, dialogue, and the force inside the park remain undefined. The Public Cordon The park cannot be erased from public attention. Citizens vanish first. Private investigators and police officers disappear when they go looking for them. Families know who has not come home, and the absence of bodies makes every ordinary explanation less convincing. Police enforce the first quarantine to prevent more people from entering. Gas, poison, or another harmful substance remains possible, but no theory explains why nothing is recovered. Eventually the government seals the park even from the police. The Unit Captain Heyk enters with a specially equipped paramilitary unit tasked with investigating the park in full protective gear. They expect an environmental hazard, a criminal operation, or something else that training can name. The unit is massacred by forces Heyk cannot understand or explain. He becomes the sole survivor. The Evacuation The Ducal Guard removes Heyk from the park under Drake's orders. What warning reaches Drake, how the evacuation succeeds, and what follows Heyk out remain unresolved. Heyk survives with grief for the squad he lost and no language adequate to describe the cause. He is later recruited into the Ducal Guard as a field agent and bodyguard serving Drake and Sherie's interests. Heyk,Drake,Sherie

entries.title: The Name Left Behind
