entries.text: The Name Left Behind Chapter 04 · Unknowing Convergence Natalia follows a missing name through the city archive and finds her niece Myka protecting the last surviving clue. Natalia finds a missing page hidden from every archive index. Myka reveals an unaltered copy carrying Fionn's name beside a future date. The archive erases the evidence while Natalia attempts to preserve it. Chapter 04: The Name Left Behind Placeholder draft. Replace this chapter when final story material is available. Missing Entry Natalia noticed the gap because the archive insisted there was none. A page number had been removed from every index, leaving the sequence perfect and the history incomplete. The missing name led her back to the Magi Academy, where her niece Myka had hidden the last unaltered copy inside a student spellbook. The Witness Fionn's name appeared in the margin beside a date that had not happened yet. Myka refused to explain how the record had been written. Someone entered the archive below them. The shelves began correcting themselves one book at a time. End Record Natalia photographed the page before it turned blank. The image preserved every word except the name she had come to find. Natalia,Myka,Fionn

entries.title: The Nameless Street
entries.subtitle: Chapter 06 · Divided Attention
entries.text: The Nameless Street Chapter 06 · Divided Attention Lynleit loses Felix during a walk after lunch and follows a child's cries through an impossible street. Lynleit and Felix take an ordinary walk through central Vilen after lunch. Lynleit finds herself alone, dizzy, and unable to navigate a street that does not obey the surrounding city. A little girl loses a red balloon and runs away crying. Lynleit catches the balloon and follows the girl's cries through the labyrinth. The girl leads Lynleit to a broken fence above the body of a dead boy, then pushes her from the ledge. Lynleit wakes on a city bench while Felix tries to revive her from an apparent fainting episode. The girl's smile and sudden push suggest that her crying was a lure. inferred Chapter 06: The Nameless Street Working draft based on the confirmed Nameless Street encounter. Exact dialogue, the route Lynleit and Felix take after lunch, and the sensory details of the street remain provisional. After Lunch Felix had spent most of lunch explaining why a senior officer's secure telephone was not secure. He continued after they left the restaurant, even though Lynleit had stopped answering him. "The problem," he said, "is that people confuse being important with being difficult to overhear." "You demonstrated this to him?" "I demonstrated it to myself. Telling him would have made him unhappy." "And not telling him?" "Keeps both of us happy." They walked without destination because neither had to return immediately. The older part of central Vilen rose and folded around them. Narrow streets bent between plastered facades and old brick. Timber gates opened into courtyards too deep to see from the road. Iron balconies hung above steep passages, and flights of stone steps connected streets built at different heights. A roof could appear level with the pavement on one side of a hill and three storeys below it on the other. He bought a folded newspaper from a street stall and carried it under one arm. Lynleit suspected he had no intention of reading it. They turned past a small square where children chased pigeons around a dry fountain. Felix said something about coffee. Lynleit did not hear the end of the sentence. The Street Without a Name She was alone. She looked back for Felix. The square was gone too. Lynleit stopped. Her head continued moving. The walls leaned and corrected themselves. A pressure behind her eyes made distance difficult to judge. She placed one hand against cold plaster and waited for the dizziness to settle. It did not. She had drunk no alcohol. Nobody at lunch had approached their table closely enough to drug her. She tested the thought twice because both conclusions felt remote, as though they belonged to someone reasoning in another room. "Felix?" Her voice travelled down the street and returned too softly. No answer came. There were no people at the windows. No voices behind the doors. No laundry moved above the courtyards. The street was not abandoned. Its doors were painted, its windows clean, and flowers stood in boxes beneath several sills. It appeared maintained by residents who had all agreed to leave a moment before she arrived. Lynleit began walking. The lane descended beneath an arch and opened onto a triangular courtyard. Three passages left it. She chose the widest one and emerged beside the same arch from the opposite direction. She returned to the courtyard and took the passage with stone steps. It climbed for longer than the hill could contain. At the top, the pavement sloped downward toward a row of doors whose numbers were not arranged in order. One bore a brass six. The next bore eighteen. The third had no number, only four empty holes where a plate had been removed. Lynleit tried to remember whether the old city had a street like this. She searched the corners of the buildings for a street sign. The headache sharpened. She heard a child crying. The Red Balloon A little girl stood at the far end of the lane. She wore a light coat buttoned to the throat. One hand held the string of a red balloon. Its color was the only clean color Lynleit had seen since losing Felix. The girl looked at her. For a moment neither moved. Then the string slipped from the girl's hand. The balloon rose slowly. Its thread dragged across the edge of a balcony, cleared the ironwork, and drifted down the street rather than into the open sky. The girl cried out and ran after it. She turned through a narrow passage and vanished. Lynleit reached for the thread as it passed. It caught across her fingers with almost no weight. "Wait." The girl did not return. Her crying continued somewhere beyond the passage. The passage narrowed until her shoulders almost touched both walls. It opened at the top of another stairway, then divided between a covered arcade and an alley descending beneath houses. The crying came from the arcade. She followed it. At the next turn the sound came from below. At the next, from behind her. The girl never appeared. Lynleit saw only the red balloon above her hand, brushing stone whenever the street bent too sharply. The thread gave her something straight to hold while the city refused every other direction. She crossed a small bridge between two buildings and found herself beneath it a minute later. She passed a blue door three times, although she never repeated a turn. A church tower appeared between the roofs, first ahead of her, then behind her, then close enough that she should have been able to touch its wall. No bell sounded from it. The crying weakened into broken breaths. "I have it," Lynleit called. "Stop running." Her own voice sounded intoxicated. She could no longer keep one shoulder from striking the walls. The headache pulsed with her steps, and the pavement rose under her feet at angles that made no physical sense. The Broken Fence The passage ended on a terrace above the lower city. An old fence ran along its edge. Several sections had been repaired with newer timber. One had broken outward and left an opening above a sudden drop. The girl stood there. She was no longer crying. She looked down through the broken fence with her hands resting at her sides. Lynleit approached carefully. The red balloon pulled upward behind her. "You should not stand there." The girl did not turn. Lynleit followed her gaze. A boy lay below. His body had come to rest against the base of a retaining wall. One arm was folded beneath him. His face was turned far enough away that Lynleit could not see it, but nothing in the angle of his neck belonged to a living child. Her hand opened. The red thread slid from her fingers. The balloon climbed above the terrace, passed the roofs, and became smaller against the colorless sky. Lynleit looked at the girl. The girl was smiling. Lynleit tried to step back. Her heel caught against the uneven pavement. The headache surged hard enough to empty the strength from her legs. The girl placed both hands against her. The broken fence passed beneath Lynleit's hands. Stone, roofs, and pale sky changed places. She saw the boy below growing larger. Then a white sheet struck her across the face. The Bench "Lynleit." The sheet struck her again. "If you are dead, this is going to become extremely inconvenient." She opened her eyes. Felix stood over her, violently fanning her with the folded newspaper. Behind him, the ordinary city moved without concern. People crossed the square. A bus braked somewhere beyond the buildings. The dry fountain was close enough for Lynleit to hear children running around it. She was lying across a bench. Felix stopped fanning. "There you are." Lynleit sat up too quickly and gripped the edge of the bench while the square tilted. "How long?" "Long enough for three strangers to decide I had murdered you and one to offer advice on reviving you." "Where did you find me?" Felix looked at the bench. "Here." "I mean before." His expression changed. The playfulness withdrew without leaving his face entirely. "You were beside me. Then you stopped answering. I thought you were ignoring me with unusual commitment." He crouched in front of her. "You took two steps toward the bench and collapsed." Lynleit looked past him. The old streets climbed behind the square exactly as they had before lunch. She could identify every entrance. None led toward the terrace, the blue door, or the silent church tower. No red balloon crossed the sky. Felix asked what she had seen. Lynleit pressed two fingers against the place behind her eyes where the pain was fading. "A street," she said. Felix waited. "Which street?" She looked at the folded newspaper in his hand, then at the city around them. "It did not have a name." The answer sounded less credible once spoken aloud. Felix did not laugh. Lynleit,Felix,Fionn,Helena

entries.title: The Shared Night · v1 · Superseded
entries.subtitle: Unplaced Chapter · Unplaced
entries.text: The Shared Night · v1 · Superseded Unplaced Chapter · Unplaced A shared-dream investigation becomes painfully personal when Sherie discovers that Felix remembers the same nights. Natalia refuses to mistake a dream for a confession. Independent reports describe corresponding dream memories, including violence, grief and intimate encounters, without corresponding bodily injuries. Natalia briefs the group on the Oneiric Confluence and rejects treating dream behaviour as a confession. Sherie discovers that Felix remembers their recurring sexual dreams. Their discussion exposes the difference between remembered participation and freely chosen action. Lynleit and Kyrien describe a shared house, rain, tea, cards, two bedrooms and a cat. Sherie and Felix agree to test whether they can resist the dream. Acknowledging their attachment helps them regain choice, although the pressure returns before easing again. Once they can step away, Sherie deliberately kisses Felix. They wake, exchange messages and arrange coffee. The Shared Night The first indication that something had gone wrong was not screaming. It was embarrassment. By nine in the morning, three separate government departments had received complaints from people insisting that somebody else had entered their dreams. By eleven, the number was twenty-seven. By lunch, nobody wanted to put anything in writing. A customs officer in Vilen swore that his supervisor had shot him six times inside a railway station that did not exist. The supervisor remembered doing it. Two university students separately described spending an entire night searching the same impossible library for a room numbered zero. A married accountant refused to explain his dream after learning that his secretary remembered it too. The secretary submitted her resignation before breakfast. A retired woman on Orsin Street reported drinking tea with a neighbour she had barely spoken to in twenty years. The neighbour remembered the tea, the green cups, the rain outside and the name of the dead husband they had discussed. There were no injuries. No missing people. No unexplained physical marks. Only memories. That made the incident worse. By the third night, the phenomenon had acquired the provisional designation HI-009. The following morning, Natalia stood beside the incident board with a stack of reports nobody wanted read aloud. Natalia objected to the nickname everyone else had already started using. "The Shared Night sounds like a romance novel." Lynleit looked at the incident board. "What would you call it?" "Nothing yet." "You need something." "I need evidence." Felix, leaning against the edge of the table, raised a hand. "The Dream Orgy." Natalia looked at him over her glasses. "No." "Statistically, you haven't ruled it out." "No." Yulia said, "Technically, it's not an orgy if it's only two people doing it." Felix turned. "Why do you know that?" "Because words have definitions." "That sounded disturbingly professional." "I investigate crimes. Precise terminology matters." Hiyu leaned forward. "So what's the minimum occupancy for an orgy?" "More than two." "Three?" "Definitions vary." Sherie said nothing. That was sufficiently unusual that Lynleit noticed. Sherie stood near the tall window with her arms folded, blonde hair pinned into its usual elaborate arrangement, expression composed, boots perfectly aligned beneath her. Felix looked at her once. Sherie immediately looked at him. Felix looked away. Kyrien noticed that too. Nobody said anything. Natalia returned to the board. "We have enough reports to establish provisional rules." She wrote as she spoke. "Subjects fall asleep normally. We have no common physical location, no confirmed magical vector, no shared object and no evidence of deliberate targeting. When two affected people encounter each other inside the phenomenon, both awaken with substantially corresponding memories." "At the same time?" Reiner asked. "Their sleep often overlaps. That does not tell us whether the dreams follow the same clock. We have matching accounts, not a shared watch." Reiner frowned. "Substantially?" "Peripheral discrepancies. Colour. Distance. Sometimes sequence. One person remembers six windows, another remembers seven. But conversations, major actions and emotionally charged events remain unusually consistent." Felix scratched his cheek. "That seems bad." "It is socially catastrophic." "I meant magically." "That too." Sherie shifted one shoulder against the window. Natalia continued. "The environments themselves appear composite. Memory contributes. Expectation contributes. So do fear, attachment, shame, resentment, fantasy, unresolved conflict." Hiyu, who had somehow been allowed into the meeting despite nobody remembering inviting him, brightened. "So the dream is negotiated." Natalia looked at him. "That is one possibility." "Only one?" "Negotiation implies participants who know what they are doing. I see no evidence for that." Hiyu looked delighted. "So it may be self-organizing." "Possibly." Yulia, beside him, said, "He tried to murder me with a filing cabinet." Hiyu turned. "I was testing something." "You threw it down a staircase." "It was a dream." "You shouted 'empirical method' first." Hiyu considered that. "That does sound like me." Natalia pointed at both of them. "Exactly the problem." Yulia stared. Natalia lowered her hand. "Not the filing cabinet specifically." She placed the pen against the board. "The mistake everyone keeps making is assuming that dream behaviour works like testimony. It does not." Sherie's eyes shifted toward her. Natalia continued. "A dream image is not a witness under oath. If you dream of killing someone, the dream has not automatically discovered your secret intention to kill them. If you dream of sleeping with someone, the dream has not automatically uncovered a hidden wish to do so." Felix nodded. "Good." Natalia glanced at him. "I was not acquitting anybody." Felix stopped nodding. Natalia continued. "The psyche dramatizes. It creates situations in which emotional relationships become visible. Sex may indeed represent sexual desire. Sometimes remarkably straightforward sexual desire." Sherie looked away. "But sex can also dramatize closeness, possession, surrender, rivalry, dependence, intrusion, curiosity, fear of intimacy, fear of abandonment, even hostility." Lynleit nodded knowingly. "So sometimes dreaming of having sex with someone just means you miss having them around." Natalia turned slowly. "Not exactly." Lynleit paused. "But that's basically what you said." "No." "It was the general direction." "The general direction is how people end up turning psychology into fortune cookies." Felix covered a smile. Lynleit frowned. Natalia leaned against the desk. "Suppose a person has been absent from your life and the dream responds with sexual intimacy. Missing them may be part of the emotional field. But you cannot then translate the image into a sentence saying, 'Sex equals missing someone.' The image chose sex rather than conversation, dinner, an embrace, a funeral, an argument or simply sitting beside them." Lynleit listened. "That choice matters." "So you look at why the dream chose that image." "You look at the image itself. You look at the people involved. You look at the emotions before, during and after it. You ask what kind of relationship the dream created. Who approached whom. Who resisted. Who surrendered. Who was embarrassed. Who was relieved. What changed afterward." Hiyu said, "So you interrogate the dream." Natalia shook her head. "You observe it before you interrogate it. Otherwise you only force the answer you expected into its mouth." Lynleit folded her arms. "So my explanation wasn't wrong." "It was incomplete." "That is less satisfying." "Education often is." Sherie suddenly asked, "What happens if the people know?" The room became quieter. Natalia looked at her. "Know what?" "That they're sharing the dream." Felix stopped scratching his cheek. Sherie did not look at him. Natalia capped the pen. "Several subjects discovered it accidentally. Awareness does not terminate the phenomenon." "And control?" "We don't know." Sherie nodded once. Too casually. Natalia's eyes narrowed. "Why?" "No reason." Felix made the mistake of exhaling. Sherie's gaze snapped toward him. He immediately found something fascinating on the opposite wall. Natalia looked between them. "Have either of you experienced a recurring dream?" Felix said, "No." Sherie said, "Potentially." They spoke simultaneously. Silence. Sherie turned her head very slowly. Felix closed his eyes. Lynleit leaned back in her chair. Kyrien looked down at the table, perhaps out of mercy. Natalia removed her glasses. "Good. We're making progress." Sherie stared at Felix. "Potentially," Felix corrected. She did not blink. Natalia asked, "Recurring location?" Sherie answered without looking away from him. "A room." Felix's shoulders tightened. Natalia picked up her pen. "Describe it." "Red furniture." Felix moved. Barely. Sherie saw it. "Large windows." Natalia wrote. "What outside?" Sherie hesitated. She had never told anybody. Felix said, very quietly: "Black water." Sherie froze. The pen stopped moving. Felix seemed to realize what he had done approximately half a second after doing it. Sherie turned toward him. Completely. The room ceased existing for her. Felix gave her a cautious smile. "Morning." Sherie crossed the distance between them. "You." Felix moved behind the table. "Sherie." "You knew." "I suspected." "How long?" "Define knew." She circled the table. Felix circled the other way. "Felix." "The second night." Sherie stopped. "The second?" "That was when the windows changed." "You knew on the second night?" "I thought maybe I was dreaming about your dream." "That sentence does not improve your position." Felix continued moving. Sherie followed. Lynleit looked at Natalia. Natalia quietly closed her notebook. Sherie pointed across the table. "You pervert." Felix stared. "Me?" "Yes, you." "I am also asleep during these events." "And you said nothing." "What exactly was I supposed to say?" Sherie changed direction suddenly. Felix nearly collided with Reiner. "'Good morning, Sherie. Interesting weather. By the way, last night I remember you taking all your clothes off and demanding that I fuck you against a wall that was somehow underwater.'" Hiyu's eyes widened. Yulia covered her face. Reiner looked toward the ceiling. Sherie stopped again. "You remember that?" Felix's expression changed. That was the wrong answer. Sherie's face went red. "You remember all of it." Felix pointed at Natalia. "She just said shared memory is part of the phenomenon." "You knew." "Yes." "You witnessed me." "I participated." "You witnessed me participating." "So did you." "That is completely different." "How?" "It was me." Felix stared. Sherie realized what she had said. Kyrien looked down again. Lynleit pinched the bridge of her nose. Sherie thrust one finger toward Felix. "I am tired of you doing me in the ass." A cup hit the table. Reiner had been drinking. He coughed once. Hiyu whispered, "This meeting improved tremendously." Yulia elbowed him. Felix held both hands up. "I am not doing anything to you." "Every night." "In a dream." "My dream." "Apparently also mine." Sherie looked ready to kill him. Felix stepped behind Kyrien. Kyrien moved aside. Felix stared at him. "Really?" Kyrien said, "I'm not getting involved." Sherie advanced. Felix retreated. "You could at least change the scenario." "I don't control it." "You are very active for somebody who claims no responsibility." "So are you." Sherie's face coloured further. "Felix." "What?" "Stop remembering things." "I would love to." Lynleit finally raised one hand. "You know, dreaming about having sex with someone doesn't necessarily mean you're attracted to them." Sherie turned. Lynleit continued with the grave confidence of somebody who had recently learned something complicated and was looking forward to using it. "The subconscious sometimes uses sex when what it really cares about is closeness. Or missing somebody. Or wanting them around. It can even happen with people you don't consciously want sexually at all. Lost friends. Someone you've been separated from. Family sometimes, apparently." Natalia slowly turned toward her. Lynleit noticed. "What?" "Continue." Lynleit became suspicious. "I was basically finished." "Good." Sherie stared. "Miss?" She pointed at Felix. "I talk to him practically every day." Felix said, "Talking?" Sherie turned. "All you do is bully me and call me names. Like just now." "Please stop putting your thing into my ass." Kyrien asked, "Would it be better if he put it somewhere else?" The room went silent. Sherie slowly turned toward him. Kyrien appeared to realize he had said the thought aloud. Felix bent over the table laughing. Yulia made a choking noise. Even Reiner's mouth twitched. Sherie pointed at Kyrien. "You." He raised both hands. "It was a question." "Never speak to me again." "Understood." Sherie turned back to Felix. "Do you know how many nights I've had these dreams already? I'm exhausted." Felix straightened, still grinning. "You complain as if I'm intentionally doing it. Plus, it's just a dream." "Can you at least change your kinks?" "I never had a kink like that." Sherie blinked. Felix blinked. They both looked at Natalia. Natalia sighed. Lynleit, still refusing to surrender her lecture, said: "If two psyches are linked, then maybe you can't really say whose intention belongs to whom. The dream mixes both of you together. Feelings, suppressed ideas, expectations. It turns into one messy concoction." Natalia looked at her. Lynleit looked back. "What?" "You copied that." "I did not." "That is almost exactly how I explained composite dream fields to you last month." "I reached the same conclusion independently." "You used the phrase 'messy concoction.'" "It's a useful phrase." Natalia sighed again. "But the basic direction is correct." Lynleit looked vindicated. Natalia immediately ruined it. "The dream is still not merely a mixture." Lynleit frowned. Natalia returned to the board. "If two minds are genuinely connected, we may be looking at an emergent imaginal field. Think of it as a third room built out of two houses." Felix stopped laughing. Natalia drew two circles, then a third between them. "Material comes from both people. Memories. Complexes. Desires. Fears. Bodily expectations. But once the shared dream begins, the resulting world can develop patterns neither participant consciously designed." Sherie looked at the circles. "So the dream itself can start doing things." "In a sense." "That sounds alarmingly alive." "Dreams already behave more autonomously than people like admitting. Magecraft may simply be giving that autonomy a shared stage." Natalia marked three places on the board. "That is one explanation. Another is that familiar impulses have become harder to refuse. A third is that the Holumn selects and intensifies something until the dreamers cannot ignore it. We do not yet know which explains which report." "It could be all three," Hiyu said. "It could. That is not evidence that it is." Hiyu leaned forward. "So if Sherie keeps dreaming that Felix prefers her ass..." Sherie picked up the cushion. Hiyu leaned back. Natalia continued as though he had not spoken. "This is why assigning responsibility becomes difficult. One action might originate primarily from Sherie's psyche. Another from Felix's. Another from an association both share. Another may emerge because the dream has already established a pattern and continues developing it." Felix's face changed. Confusion first. Then dawning horror. Then delight. "Wait a minute." Sherie immediately disliked that face. "No." "So the ass thing could be entirely your kink." Sherie's mouth opened. Felix pointed at her, scandalized. "All this time you've been blaming me." "Oh God." "And your subconscious is the one doing it." "Felix." "I didn't even know I liked that." "Shut up already." "Maybe I still don't." "Felix." "Maybe Dream Sherie keeps putting the idea in my head." Sherie reached for the nearest cushion. Felix saw it. He saw Sherie's face. Some instinct that should have protected him from himself failed completely. "And honestly..." Sherie froze. Felix tilted his head. "I bet it wouldn't look or feel that good in the real world." Silence. Not ordinary silence. The kind in which eight intelligent adults simultaneously understood that somebody had just stepped onto a landmine and was apparently proud of the noise. Sherie very slowly lowered the cushion. Felix's smile weakened. Lynleit stared at him. Kyrien looked away. Natalia removed her glasses. Yulia covered her mouth. Hiyu whispered: "Oh, no." Sherie spoke with astonishing calm. "What did you just say?" Felix reconsidered several life choices at once. "I said the dream probably exaggerates physical sensation." "No, you didn't." "That was the psychological content of the statement." "You said my ass probably wouldn't look as good in real life." Felix blinked. "I said look or feel." Hiyu made a noise somewhere between a cough and a strangled laugh. Yulia hit him in the ribs. Sherie's face went crimson. "You unbelievable fucking pervert." Felix raised both hands. "You were the one complaining about it." "That does not authorize a comparative review!" "I haven't reviewed anything." "You just hypothesized!" "Scientifically." "Do not use science." Natalia said, "Agreed." Felix turned toward her. "You're supposed to be neutral." "I am neutral. That was simply a terrible use of the word scientifically." Sherie advanced. Felix retreated behind Kyrien again. Kyrien immediately moved aside. Felix stared at him. "Again?" Kyrien said, "This one is entirely your fault." Sherie pointed at Felix from across the table. "So now you're imagining what my ass would look like in reality?" Felix opened his mouth. Lynleit said quickly: "Don't." Felix closed it. Sherie narrowed her eyes. "Oh, now you develop judgment." Felix said, "I'm learning." "Too slowly." She lifted the cushion. Felix backed away. "To be fair, you introduced the topic." Sherie threw it. The cushion hit him directly in the face. He caught it on the rebound. "Violence," he said. "More unconscious material." Sherie went for another. Natalia raised her voice. "Enough." The room settled. Felix kept the cushion. Sherie sat down with the rigid posture of somebody refusing to acknowledge that she had just discussed recurring dream sodomy and the hypothetical real-world quality of her own ass in front of seven colleagues. "Please stop conducting legal research into my dream sex." Yulia looked up. "Then stop introducing disputed terminology into an evidentiary meeting." Hiyu leaned toward Yulia. "I think he wants empirical verification." The second cushion hit him instead. Nobody had time to explain why a government briefing room contained two cushions. Natalia put her glasses back on. "Lynleit's stolen explanation was useful." "I did not steal it." "But incomplete." Lynleit looked offended. Natalia returned to the incident board. "The shared dream does not provide a confession. It gives us an image." Felix said, "An extremely graphic image." Sherie glared. Natalia ignored both. "Images can tell the truth without telling it literally." Sherie's expression changed slightly. Natalia noticed. "If you want to understand why this particular dream keeps returning, asking 'Which one of us secretly wants this exact sexual act?' is too narrow." Felix slowly lowered the cushion. "What do we ask instead?" Natalia considered. "What happens between you in the dream?" Sherie folded her arms. "Things." "Yes, Sherie. We have established that." Yulia covered another laugh. Natalia continued. "Who initiates?" Sherie and Felix pointed at each other. Natalia watched them. "Useful." "It is him." "It is absolutely her." "Who provokes whom?" Both began speaking. Natalia raised one hand. They stopped. "Also useful." Sherie frowned. "Why?" "Because the argument itself may matter more than the mechanics." Felix glanced at Sherie. Natalia tapped the board. "You keep describing the dream in terms of provocation, retaliation, humiliation, attention, loss of control and who gets to determine what happens next." Sherie became very still. "That sounds less sexual when you say it." "It is still sexual." Felix smiled. Sherie elbowed him. Natalia continued. "But perhaps sexuality is the form through which the relationship becomes impossible to ignore." Nobody spoke for several seconds. Natalia looked between them. "A dream may exaggerate something because waking consciousness has become too skilled at minimizing it." Sherie looked at the floor. Felix looked at Sherie. Sherie noticed. "Don't." "I didn't say anything." "You looked." Natalia pointed at them. "Exactly." Felix looked away. Sherie crossed her arms tighter. Natalia continued. "Now, that still does not prove romantic attraction." Sherie looked relieved. Felix looked mildly disappointed. Natalia noticed both reactions. She said nothing about them. "Attraction may be present. So may annoyance. Dependency. Habit. Curiosity. Fear of being ignored. Fear of being known too well. The dream may contain contradictions simultaneously." "So the person we are awake is a mask?" Sherie asked. "The mask belongs to you too. Your restraint is you. Your anger is you. Your kindness is you. Your appetite is you. Your horror at the appetite is also you. Do not confuse sincerity with totality." Natalia put down the pen. "A capacity revealed is not necessarily an intention confessed. Neither of you has established whose preference produced a particular act." Lynleit nodded. "So basically they have a lot of unresolved tension." Natalia looked at her. Lynleit shrugged. "That's what I said in fewer words." "Yes." "Was it wrong?" "No." Lynleit smiled. "It was merely imprecise." Her smile disappeared. Natalia capped the pen. "The psyche is under no obligation to simplify itself for us." Sherie muttered, "Mine could make an effort." Felix said, "Maybe it already simplified as much as possible." Sherie hit him with the cushion. Again. Natalia eventually turned toward Lynleit. "You have experienced the phenomenon too." Lynleit's expression changed. Sherie noticed instantly. That was enough. "Oh?" Lynleit said nothing. Sherie leaned forward. "Oh, this is interesting." Kyrien looked toward the window. Sherie's eyes moved between them. "No." Felix followed. Then Hiyu. Then Yulia. Within seconds, everybody was staring at Lynleit and Kyrien. Lynleit crossed her arms. "It was different." Sherie smiled. "How?" "Nothing happened." Kyrien said, "Something happened." Lynleit looked at him. "You are not helping." Sherie leaned across the table. "What happened?" Lynleit stared at her. Sherie smiled wider. "Teehee." Lynleit looked away. Felix whispered, "Oh, she hates this." Sherie whispered back, "Good." Natalia asked, "Shared environment?" Kyrien nodded. "A house." Sherie waited. Lynleit said, "Near water." Sherie waited harder. Kyrien continued. "It was raining." Sherie's expression collapsed. "That's it?" Lynleit looked irritated. "What were you expecting?" Sherie gestured violently between herself and Felix. "This." Felix nodded. "Fair." Kyrien said, "There was tea." Sherie stared. Felix stared. Sherie looked at Lynleit. "You got tea?" Lynleit's face reddened slightly. "It was a dream." "You got rain and tea?" "There were cards." Felix looked genuinely wounded. "You got cards too?" Sherie slapped the table. "I got sodomy." Reiner left the room. Nobody stopped him. They heard him laughing in the corridor. Lynleit's face had gone completely red now. "There was nothing sexual about it." Natalia looked at Kyrien. He hesitated. "There were two bedrooms upstairs." Lynleit turned. "You did not need to mention that." Sherie immediately sharpened. "Why two?" "I don't know." Kyrien added, "And a cat." Felix leaned back. "A cat." "Yes." Sherie looked toward the ceiling. "Of course they get domestic symbolism." Lynleit muttered, "I hate all of you." Sherie pointed at her. "No. You have no standing to complain. Your subconscious gave you tea." Natalia tapped the board with her pen. "This contrast is useful." Sherie turned. "For whom?" "For us." "Not for me." "Their dream organizes intimacy differently." Lynleit looked at Natalia. Natalia continued. "It creates a house. Weather outside. Warmth inside. Food. Repetition. Separate rooms that still belong to one shared structure." Kyrien looked thoughtful. Sherie said, "And a cat." "And a cat." "What does the cat mean?" Natalia looked at her. "I have no idea." Sherie stared. Natalia shrugged. "Perhaps it means cat." Hiyu smiled. "I like this methodology." Natalia ignored him. Lynleit said, "But the house obviously represents stability." Natalia turned. "Perhaps." "And safety." "Perhaps." "And the two bedrooms mean boundaries." "Possibly." Lynleit looked pleased. Natalia added: "Or one of you remembers a house with two bedrooms." Lynleit frowned. Natalia continued. "Do not murder an image by making it symbolic too quickly. The house first has to remain a house." Lynleit sat back. "So what do we know?" "That the dream placed you together in a domestic environment neither of you appears to have found threatening." Lynleit nodded. "That you drank tea." "Yes." "Played cards." "Yes." "And did not attempt to escape from one another." Lynleit looked toward Kyrien. Kyrien was already looking at her. Sherie saw. "Oh." Lynleit turned. "Don't." Sherie held both hands up. "Teehee." Natalia continued. "The emotional tone matters. Their dream emphasizes sustained proximity without urgency." Sherie gestured between herself and Felix. "And ours emphasizes what, exactly?" Natalia paused. Felix smiled cautiously. Natalia said: "Urgency." Sherie sighed. "Provocation." Felix nodded. "Competition." Sherie looked offended. "Mutual attention." That landed. Sherie went still. Felix noticed. Natalia noticed him noticing. Sherie noticed Natalia noticing Felix noticing. She hated everyone in the room. Natalia looked away first. "Possibly also a difficulty tolerating emotional ambiguity." Sherie looked at Felix. Felix looked at her. Both immediately looked elsewhere. Natalia smiled very slightly. "The dream solves ambiguity by making everything physical." No one answered. Hiyu whispered, "That is elegant." Yulia whispered back, "Don't encourage her." Natalia resumed writing. "The mechanism appears to magnify psychic pressure until it becomes narratively visible. Ordinary dreams already do this. The Holumn appears to externalize the process into a shared imaginal space." "Can it stop doing that?" Sherie asked. "Sometimes recognition changes the pressure," Natalia said. "An unconscious content does not need to seize consciousness as violently once consciousness agrees to see it. That does not tell us how reliably it works here." Lynleit nodded. "So once you admit what's bothering you, the dream stops forcing you." "Sometimes." "That's what I said." "No. You made it sound like plumbing." Natalia crossed out the empty title at the top of the board and wrote The Oneiric Confluence. Felix inspected it. "Less catchy." "More accurate." Sherie muttered, "My imaginal space has very little subtlety." Felix said, "Maybe your psyche believes in clear communication." She hit him with the cushion. Again. Felix caught up with her in the corridor twenty minutes later. Sherie heard him before she saw him. "Sherie." She kept walking. "Sherie." "Pervert." "You're still doing that?" "Yes." "I was unconscious." "So was I." "Exactly." "That does not make it better." "It should." "It doesn't." Felix increased his pace until he walked beside her. Sherie ignored him. They crossed two windows in silence. Felix said, "I really didn't know the first night." Sherie kept walking. "The second night was when I knew something was wrong." Still nothing. "Because you remembered something." Sherie slowed. Felix noticed. "What?" He scratched the back of his neck. "In the first dream you said something." Sherie's stomach tightened. "What?" Felix looked uncomfortable. "That if I laughed, you'd kill me." "That sounds normal." "You said it again the next day." Sherie stopped. Felix stopped too. She looked at him. "When?" "Over lunch. You dropped your fork." Sherie remembered. Felix had made a joke. She had looked at him and said exactly that. Sherie's face changed. "You knew then." "I suspected then." "And you said nothing." Felix leaned against the wall. "You want to know why?" "Yes." "I thought you'd react like this." Sherie stared. Felix gestured at her entire body. "This." "You deserved it." "I hadn't done anything." "Dream you had." Felix opened his mouth. Closed it. "Fine." Sherie started walking again. Felix followed. After several steps he said, "You know I remember the other parts too." Sherie stopped so abruptly he nearly walked into her. "What other parts?" His expression softened. That frightened her much more than the teasing had. "The parts between." Sherie said nothing. Felix looked toward the window. "You kept falling asleep on me." Her lips parted slightly. "After." "Yes." She looked away. Felix continued. "You always complained that the room was cold." "It was." "There was no temperature." "It felt cold." "You stole the blanket." "You deserved it." "For what?" Sherie had no answer. Felix smiled. She hated that smile now because it was gentle. "And once," he said, "you woke up inside the dream and asked if I was still there." Sherie looked at him. He stopped smiling. "You remember?" Of course she remembered. She remembered the red room after everything obscene had ended, the impossible black water beyond the windows, Felix beneath her cheek, his heartbeat much too real for a dream. She had asked the question without thinking. He had answered yes. Sherie crossed her arms again. "That proves nothing." "I didn't say it did." "You were about to." "No." "You had the face." "What face?" "The hopeful one." Felix almost smiled again. Sherie pointed. "That." He lowered his head. "Fine." They stood in the corridor. Sherie looked at the floor. "How many nights?" "Three." She looked up. "Three?" Felix winced. "Four." "Felix." "The first barely counts." "You lying bastard." "I was trying to preserve my life." "What happened on the fourth?" He looked at her. Sherie immediately remembered. "Oh." Felix nodded. "Oh." She went red again. Felix politely looked at the ceiling. Sherie covered her face with one hand. "I hate magic." "That's more of a Lynleit sentence." "Tonight." Felix looked at her. Sherie lowered her hand. "We test it." "How?" "No sex." Felix stared. "In the dream." "I understood that." "No touching." "Fine." "No kissing." "Fine." "No grabbing me." "Fine." "And absolutely no ass." Felix looked wounded. "Why are you telling me?" "Because apparently one of our subconsciouses needs supervision." "You still think it's mine." Sherie pointed at him. "Don't." Felix raised both hands. "All right." Sherie started walking again. Felix followed. After several steps: "What if Dream Sherie starts it?" Sherie did not turn around. "I will wake up and kill you." "That seems unfair." "Then pray." Sherie did not sleep. At eleven she read. At midnight she made tea. At one she reorganized two drawers that did not need reorganizing. At two she considered calling Natalia. At two fifteen she rejected the idea because explaining why she feared sleeping would require explaining that she and Felix had made an agreement about dream sex. At two forty she sat upright on the sofa. At some point between then and three, she ceased being awake. The red room was waiting. Sherie opened her eyes. She was standing. Fully dressed. That alone felt suspicious. Felix stood twenty feet away. Also dressed. They stared at one another. Neither moved. Sherie lifted one finger. "Don't." Felix said, "I'm not doing anything." "Good." "I'm literally standing still." "Continue." The room was quieter than usual. Black water pressed against the enormous windows as though the room had sunk beneath some sea without drowning. The red sofa sat between them. One lamp burned. No door. Sherie looked down at herself. Her clothes were exactly right. Blouse. Skirt. Tights. Jacket. Shoes. Everything. Felix looked down at his suspenders and blue tie. "This is encouraging." "Don't say that." "Why?" "You'll provoke it." "The room?" "The thing." Felix looked upward. "Can it hear us?" Sherie glared. "Excellent question to ask inside it." "Sorry." They stood still. Thirty seconds passed. A minute. Sherie began to feel ridiculous. Felix looked equally uncomfortable. "Maybe knowing changes it," he said. "Maybe." Sherie looked toward the sofa. Felix noticed. "No." "I wasn't doing anything." "You looked at it." "So did you." "Because you looked." "You looked first." Sherie's eyes narrowed. Felix sighed. "This is already more exhausting than the sex." "Do not mention sex." "Right." Silence. Sherie became aware of something stranger. The room was not pushing her. On previous nights, desire had simply arrived like gravity. Touch him. Tease him. Get closer. Make him react. The thought and the action had been almost the same thing. Now there was space between them. She could feel impulses. They did not own her hands. Sherie slowly looked at Felix. He looked back. "You feel it too," she said. "Yeah." "What?" Felix hesitated. "That's a trap." "Answer." "No." "Felix." "You first." Sherie folded her arms. "I want to slap you." "That one might just be normal." She almost smiled. Almost. "And..." Felix waited. Sherie looked toward the black water. She hated this room. She hated the Holumn. She hated Natalia. She particularly hated Felix for standing there patiently enough that she might accidentally become honest. "And I don't like when you're gone." Felix's expression changed. Sherie immediately pointed. "Do not." "I didn't say anything." "You made a face." "I have a face." "That one." Felix looked down. Sherie's heart was beating much harder than it had during the first several dreams. That was unfair. Sex had been easier. Felix said, "I miss you too." Sherie frowned. "I see you all the time." "That's what you said earlier." "It's true." "I know." "Then how can you miss me?" Felix thought about it. "Sometimes you're in the room and I still feel like you're somewhere else." Sherie stared at him. The black water moved beyond the windows. No waves. Only pressure. Something in the room loosened. Sherie felt it physically, like a muscle unclenching. Felix looked around. "You felt that?" "Yes." They both went quiet. Sherie whispered, "Natalia." "What about her?" "She said the dream dramatizes pressure." Felix nodded. "So?" Sherie looked around the room. "Maybe saying it changes the relationship to the image." Felix waited. Sherie frowned, trying to remember Natalia's exact explanation. "If something stays unconscious, you just enact it. Once you recognize it..." She hesitated. Felix said, "You have a choice?" Sherie nodded slowly. "Something like that." Natalia would undoubtedly correct the wording. Sherie could almost hear her already. Recognition does not destroy the image. It gives consciousness somewhere to stand in relation to it. Sherie looked toward Felix. "So if we stop pretending we don't know what the pressure is..." "The dream doesn't need to scream it at us?" "Maybe." Felix considered that. "That's almost disappointing." Sherie's eyes narrowed. "Teehee." The sound escaped before she meant it to. Felix smiled. Sherie immediately became annoyed. "Don't." "You teeheed." "I did not." "You did." "It was involuntary." "Sure." The room shifted. Both stopped. The sofa had moved. Neither had seen it move. It now sat directly behind Sherie. She looked at it. Felix looked at it. "No," Sherie said. The lamp went out. Felix said, "That seems bad." The black water outside the windows began glowing faintly from beneath. Sherie looked down. Her hands were trembling. Not from fear. "Felix." "Yeah." "The compulsion is coming back." "I know." "What do you want?" He looked at her. The room pressed closer around them. Felix said, "You." Sherie inhaled. "That is extremely unhelpful." "You asked." "I meant psychologically." "You said be honest." She stared. The red sofa touched the backs of her knees. Sherie did not remember stepping backward. Felix had somehow crossed half the room. He stopped himself. Both looked down at the distance between them. Two metres. One and a half. Sherie said, "Don't move." "I'm trying." "Try harder." "You try harder." "I am." "You're coming toward me." "The floor is tilted." "It is not." "It feels tilted." Sherie looked down. The floor was perfectly level. Felix said, "This is ridiculous." "Yes." "I hate Holumns." "Yes." The distance became one metre. Sherie's breathing changed. Felix noticed. She noticed him noticing. That familiar little current passed between them. Sherie hated how reassuring it felt. "Felix." "Yeah?" "If this room makes me do something humiliating..." "You'll blame me." "Yes." "Obviously." Half a metre. Sherie looked at his mouth. Felix saw. She looked away. "Don't." "You did that." "Shut up." Twenty centimetres. Felix whispered, "Sherie." "What?" "I'm not sure the room is moving us anymore." She froze. So did he. They stood almost touching. Sherie looked down. Nothing moved. No pressure. No invisible force. No sudden impulse commanding her hands. Just Felix. Her heartbeat. His breath. The black water behind the glass. Sherie could step away. She knew she could. Felix knew it too. That changed everything. Sherie looked up at him. He did not move. For once, he did not offer the hopeful smile. He waited. Sherie stared for several seconds. Then caught his tie. Felix's eyebrows rose. "This still the Holumn?" Sherie pulled him closer. "Obviously." "Right." "Completely beyond my control." "Of course." She kissed him. Slowly. No dream urgency. No filthy choreography arriving before thought. No furniture rearranging itself around them. Just a kiss. Felix's hand moved toward her waist. Stopped before touching. Sherie felt the hesitation. She took his wrist and put the hand there herself. His fingers closed around her. The room remained still. When they separated, Felix looked at her. Sherie immediately looked offended. "Not a word." "I didn't say anything." "You were going to." "No." "The face." He laughed quietly. Sherie pressed her forehead against his chest. "That definitely wasn't in the plan." "No." "The Holumn did it." "Sure." "Felix." "Absolutely." She stayed there. The red sofa remained unused behind them. After a while, Felix said: "So about the ass thing." Sherie punched him in the stomach. The dream ended. Sherie woke sitting upright on the sofa. Morning light. No red room. No black water. No Felix. She stared at the wall. Then at her hand. She could still remember the texture of his tie. Her phone buzzed. One message. Felix. GOOD MORNING. Sherie stared. Another appeared. FOR THE RECORD, I ACCEPT THAT THE HOLUMN FORCED YOU TO KISS ME. Sherie typed: DIE. Three dots appeared immediately. ALSO I THINK WE PROVED CONSCIOUS RECOGNITION REDUCES THE COMPULSION. NATALIA WILL WANT TO KNOW. Sherie stared at that one longer. Then: IF YOU TELL NATALIA ABOUT THE KISS I WILL ACTUALLY KILL YOU. Felix: RESEARCH FRAUD. Sherie: NATIONAL SECURITY. Felix: SAME THING WHEN DIPLOMATS DO IT? Sherie put the phone face down. It buzzed again. She refused to look. Then looked. SLEEP WELL? Sherie hated him. She hated the Holumn. She hated herself slightly. She typed: BETTER. Stopped. Deleted it. Typed: MY ASS STILL HURTS BECAUSE OF YOU. Deleted that too. Finally: COFFEE. 10. DON'T BE LATE. His answer arrived immediately. MISS ME ALREADY? Sherie threw the phone across the sofa. Then, despite herself, buried her face in the pillow and laughed. "Teehee." Downstairs, somewhere beyond the house, the city was waking from another night full of dreams that belonged to more than one person. Somewhere, two customs officers were probably avoiding each other. Somewhere, Yulia was preparing to murder Hiyu in waking life for what he had done with another filing cabinet. Somewhere, Lynleit was drinking tea and refusing to look at Kyrien. And somewhere inside an incident report Natalia had not yet finished writing, the first useful hypothesis concerning HI-009 was beginning to take shape: Conscious recognition did not destroy the dream image. It changed the dreamer's relationship to it. For a while, naming the pressure had let them refuse it. It had returned once already. Natalia would want to know why it had eased again, and whether anyone else could repeat what they had done. The image remained. Desire remained. Embarrassment remained. The black water remained. Choice had simply reappeared beside them. Natalia would consider that distinction important. Sherie would consider one other distinction considerably more alarming. The Holumn had stopped forcing her. She had kissed Felix anyway. Natalia,Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Sherie,Reiner
