entries.text: The Shared Night · v2 · Current Unplaced Chapter · Unplaced A shared-dream investigation becomes painfully personal when Sherie discovers that Felix remembers the same nights. Natalia refuses to mistake a dream for a confession. Independent reports describe corresponding dream memories, including violence, grief and intimate encounters, without corresponding bodily injuries. Natalia briefs Lynleit, Kyrien, Felix, Sherie and Reiner on the Oneiric Confluence and rejects treating dream behaviour as a confession. Sherie discovers that Felix remembers their recurring sexual dreams. Their discussion exposes the difference between remembered participation and freely chosen action. Lynleit and Kyrien acknowledge a shared experience without recounting it to the group. Sherie and Felix test whether they can resist the dream. Recognizing a pressure briefly restores choice, but its return prevents them from treating recognition as a reliable cure. When they can step away, Sherie does so. They keep their agreement not to touch or kiss, then arrange coffee after waking. The Shared Night The first indication that something had gone wrong was not screaming. It was embarrassment. By nine in the morning, three separate government departments had received complaints from people insisting that somebody else had entered their dreams. By eleven, the number was twenty-seven. By lunch, nobody wanted to put anything in writing. A customs officer in Vilen swore that his supervisor had shot him six times inside a railway station that did not exist. The supervisor remembered doing it. Two university students separately described spending an entire night searching the same impossible library for a room numbered zero. A married accountant refused to explain his dream after learning that his secretary remembered it too. The secretary submitted her resignation before breakfast. A retired woman on Orsin Street reported drinking tea with a neighbour she had barely spoken to in twenty years. The neighbour remembered the tea, the green cups, the rain outside and the name of the dead husband they had discussed. There were no injuries. No missing people. No unexplained physical marks. Only memories. That made the incident worse. By the third night, the phenomenon had acquired the provisional designation HI-009. The following morning, Natalia stood beside the incident board with a stack of reports nobody wanted read aloud. Natalia objected to the nickname everyone else had already started using. "The Shared Night sounds like a romance novel." Lynleit looked at the incident board. "What would you call it?" "Nothing yet." "You need something." "I need evidence." Felix, leaning against the edge of the table, raised a hand. "The Dream Orgy." Natalia looked at him over her glasses. "No." "Statistically, you haven't ruled it out." "No." Sherie said nothing. That was sufficiently unusual that Lynleit noticed. Sherie stood near the tall window with her arms folded, blonde hair pinned into its usual elaborate arrangement, expression composed, boots perfectly aligned beneath her. Felix looked at her once. Sherie immediately looked at him. Felix looked away. Kyrien noticed that too. Nobody said anything. Natalia returned to the board. "We have enough reports to establish provisional rules." She wrote as she spoke. "Subjects fall asleep normally. We have no common physical location, no confirmed magical vector, no shared object and no evidence of deliberate targeting. When two affected people encounter each other inside the phenomenon, both awaken with substantially corresponding memories." "At the same time?" Reiner asked. "Their sleep often overlaps. That does not tell us whether the dreams follow the same clock. We have matching accounts, not a shared watch." Reiner frowned. "Substantially?" "Peripheral discrepancies. Colour. Distance. Sometimes sequence. One person remembers six windows, another remembers seven. But conversations, major actions and emotionally charged events remain unusually consistent." Felix scratched his cheek. "That seems bad." "It is socially catastrophic." "I meant magically." "That too." Sherie shifted one shoulder against the window. Natalia continued. "The environments themselves appear composite. Memory contributes. Expectation contributes. So do fear, attachment, shame, resentment, fantasy, unresolved conflict." She placed the pen against the board. "The mistake everyone keeps making is assuming that dream behaviour works like testimony. It does not." Sherie's eyes shifted toward her. Natalia continued. "A dream image is not a witness under oath. If you dream of killing someone, the dream has not automatically discovered your secret intention to kill them. If you dream of sleeping with someone, the dream has not automatically uncovered a hidden wish to do so." Felix nodded. "Good." Natalia glanced at him. "I was not acquitting anybody." Felix stopped nodding. Natalia continued. "The psyche dramatizes. It creates situations in which emotional relationships become visible. Sex may indeed represent sexual desire. Sometimes remarkably straightforward sexual desire." Sherie looked away. "But sex can also dramatize closeness, possession, surrender, rivalry, dependence, intrusion, curiosity, fear of intimacy, fear of abandonment, even hostility." Lynleit nodded knowingly. "So sometimes dreaming of having sex with someone just means you miss having them around." Natalia turned slowly. "Not exactly." Lynleit paused. "But that's basically what you said." "No." "It was the general direction." "The general direction is how people end up turning psychology into fortune cookies." Felix covered a smile. Lynleit frowned. Natalia leaned against the desk. "Suppose a person has been absent from your life and the dream responds with sexual intimacy. Missing them may be part of the emotional field. But you cannot then translate the image into a sentence saying, 'Sex equals missing someone.' The image chose sex rather than conversation, dinner, an embrace, a funeral, an argument or simply sitting beside them." Lynleit listened. "That choice matters." "So you look at why the dream chose that image." "You look at the image itself. You look at the people involved. You look at the emotions before, during and after it. You ask what kind of relationship the dream created. Who approached whom. Who resisted. Who surrendered. Who was embarrassed. Who was relieved. What changed afterward." Lynleit said, "So you interrogate the dream." Natalia shook her head. "You observe it before you interrogate it. Otherwise you only force the answer you expected into its mouth." Lynleit folded her arms. "So my explanation wasn't wrong." "It was incomplete." "That is less satisfying." "Education often is." Sherie suddenly asked, "What happens if the people know?" The room became quieter. Natalia looked at her. "Know what?" "That they're sharing the dream." Felix stopped scratching his cheek. Sherie did not look at him. Natalia capped the pen. "Several subjects discovered it accidentally. Awareness does not terminate the phenomenon." "And control?" "We don't know." Sherie nodded once. Too casually. Natalia's eyes narrowed. "Why?" "No reason." Felix made the mistake of exhaling. Sherie's gaze snapped toward him. He immediately found something fascinating on the opposite wall. Natalia looked between them. "Have either of you experienced a recurring dream?" Felix said, "No." Sherie said, "Potentially." They spoke simultaneously. Silence. Sherie turned her head very slowly. Felix closed his eyes. Lynleit leaned back in her chair. Kyrien looked down at the table, perhaps out of mercy. Natalia removed her glasses. "Good. We're making progress." Sherie stared at Felix. "Potentially," Felix corrected. She did not blink. Natalia asked, "Recurring location?" Sherie answered without looking away from him. "A room." Felix's shoulders tightened. Natalia picked up her pen. "Describe it." "Red furniture." Felix moved. Barely. Sherie saw it. "Large windows." Natalia wrote. "What outside?" Sherie hesitated. She had never told anybody. Felix said, very quietly: "Black water." Sherie froze. The pen stopped moving. Felix seemed to realize what he had done approximately half a second after doing it. Sherie turned toward him. Completely. The room ceased existing for her. Felix gave her a cautious smile. "Morning." Sherie crossed the distance between them. "You." Felix moved behind the table. "Sherie." "You knew." "I suspected." "How long?" "Define knew." She circled the table. Felix circled the other way. "Felix." "The second night." Sherie stopped. "The second?" "That was when the windows changed." "You knew on the second night?" "I thought maybe I was dreaming about your dream." "That sentence does not improve your position." Felix continued moving. Sherie followed. Lynleit looked at Natalia. Natalia quietly closed her notebook. Sherie pointed across the table. "You pervert." Felix stared. "Me?" "Yes, you." "I am also asleep during these events." "And you said nothing." "What exactly was I supposed to say?" Sherie changed direction suddenly. Felix nearly collided with Reiner. "'Good morning, Sherie. Interesting weather. By the way, last night I remember you taking all your clothes off and demanding that I fuck you against a wall that was somehow underwater.'" Reiner looked toward the ceiling. Sherie stopped again. "You remember that?" Felix's expression changed. That was the wrong answer. Sherie's face went red. "You remember all of it." Felix pointed at Natalia. "She just said shared memory is part of the phenomenon." "You knew." "Yes." "You witnessed me." "I participated." "You witnessed me participating." "So did you." "That is completely different." "How?" "It was me." Felix stared. Sherie realized what she had said. Kyrien looked down again. Lynleit pinched the bridge of her nose. Sherie thrust one finger toward Felix. "I am tired of you doing me in the ass." A cup hit the table. Reiner had been drinking. He coughed once. Felix held both hands up. "I am not doing anything to you." "Every night." "In a dream." "My dream." "Apparently also mine." Sherie looked ready to kill him. Felix stepped behind Kyrien. Kyrien moved aside. Felix stared at him. "Really?" Kyrien said, "I'm not getting involved." Sherie advanced. Felix retreated. "You could at least change the scenario." "I don't control it." "You are very active for somebody who claims no responsibility." "So are you." Sherie's face coloured further. "Felix." "What?" "Stop remembering things." "I would love to." Lynleit finally raised one hand. "You know, dreaming about having sex with someone doesn't necessarily mean you're attracted to them." Sherie turned. Lynleit continued with the grave confidence of somebody who had recently learned something complicated and was looking forward to using it. "The subconscious sometimes uses sex when what it really cares about is closeness. Or missing somebody. Or wanting them around. It can even happen with people you don't consciously want sexually at all. Lost friends. Someone you've been separated from. Family sometimes, apparently." Natalia slowly turned toward her. Lynleit noticed. "What?" "Continue." Lynleit became suspicious. "I was basically finished." "Good." Sherie stared. "Miss?" She pointed at Felix. "I talk to him practically every day." Felix said, "Talking?" Sherie turned. "All you do is bully me and call me names. Like just now." "Please stop putting your thing into my ass." Kyrien asked, "Would it be better if he put it somewhere else?" The room went silent. Sherie slowly turned toward him. Kyrien appeared to realize he had said the thought aloud. Felix bent over the table laughing. Even Reiner's mouth twitched. Sherie pointed at Kyrien. "You." He raised both hands. "It was a question." "Never speak to me again." "Understood." Sherie turned back to Felix. "Do you know how many nights I've had these dreams already? I'm exhausted." Felix straightened, still grinning. "You complain as if I'm intentionally doing it. Plus, it's just a dream." "Can you at least change your kinks?" "I never had a kink like that." Sherie blinked. Felix blinked. They both looked at Natalia. Natalia sighed. Lynleit, still refusing to surrender her lecture, said: "If two psyches are linked, then maybe you can't really say whose intention belongs to whom. The dream mixes both of you together. Feelings, suppressed ideas, expectations. It turns into one messy concoction." Natalia looked at her. Lynleit looked back. "What?" "You copied that." "I did not." "That is almost exactly how I explained composite dream fields to you last month." "I reached the same conclusion independently." "You used the phrase 'messy concoction.'" "It's a useful phrase." Natalia sighed again. "But the basic direction is correct." Lynleit looked vindicated. Natalia immediately ruined it. "The dream is still not merely a mixture." Lynleit frowned. Natalia returned to the board. "If two minds are genuinely connected, we may be looking at an emergent imaginal field. Think of it as a third room built out of two houses." Felix stopped laughing. Natalia drew two circles, then a third between them. "Material comes from both people. Memories. Complexes. Desires. Fears. Bodily expectations. But once the shared dream begins, the resulting world can develop patterns neither participant consciously designed." Sherie looked at the circles. "So the dream itself can start doing things." "In a sense." "That sounds alarmingly alive." "Dreams already behave more autonomously than people like admitting. Magecraft may simply be giving that autonomy a shared stage." Natalia marked three places on the board. "That is one explanation. Another is that familiar impulses have become harder to refuse. A third is that the Holumn selects and intensifies something until the dreamers cannot ignore it. We do not yet know which explains which report." "This is why assigning responsibility becomes difficult. One action might originate primarily from Sherie's psyche. Another from Felix's. Another from an association both share. Another may emerge because the dream has already established a pattern and continues developing it." Felix's face changed. Confusion first. Then dawning horror. Then delight. "Wait a minute." Sherie immediately disliked that face. "No." "So the ass thing could be entirely your kink." Sherie's mouth opened. Felix pointed at her, scandalized. "All this time you've been blaming me." "Oh God." "And your subconscious is the one doing it." "Felix." "I didn't even know I liked that." "Shut up already." "Maybe I still don't." "Felix." "Maybe Dream Sherie keeps putting the idea in my head." Sherie reached for the nearest cushion. Felix saw it. He saw Sherie's face. Some instinct that should have protected him from himself failed completely. "And honestly..." Sherie froze. Felix tilted his head. "I bet it wouldn't look or feel that good in the real world." Silence. Not ordinary silence. The kind in which six intelligent adults simultaneously understood that somebody had just stepped onto a landmine and was apparently proud of the noise. Sherie very slowly lowered the cushion. Felix's smile weakened. Lynleit stared at him. Kyrien looked away. Natalia removed her glasses. Sherie spoke with astonishing calm. "What did you just say?" Felix reconsidered several life choices at once. "I said the dream probably exaggerates physical sensation." "No, you didn't." "That was the psychological content of the statement." "You said my ass probably wouldn't look as good in real life." Felix blinked. "I said look or feel." Sherie's face went crimson. "You unbelievable fucking pervert." Felix raised both hands. "You were the one complaining about it." "That does not authorize a comparative review!" "I haven't reviewed anything." "You just hypothesized!" "Scientifically." "Do not use science." Natalia said, "Agreed." Felix turned toward her. "You're supposed to be neutral." "I am neutral. That was simply a terrible use of the word scientifically." Sherie advanced. Felix retreated behind Kyrien again. Kyrien immediately moved aside. Felix stared at him. "Again?" Kyrien said, "This one is entirely your fault." Sherie pointed at Felix from across the table. "So now you're imagining what my ass would look like in reality?" Felix opened his mouth. Lynleit said quickly: "Don't." Felix closed it. Sherie narrowed her eyes. "Oh, now you develop judgment." Felix said, "I'm learning." "Too slowly." She lifted the cushion. Felix backed away. "To be fair, you introduced the topic." Sherie threw it. The cushion hit him directly in the face. He caught it on the rebound. "Violence," he said. "More unconscious material." Sherie went for another. Natalia raised her voice. "Enough." The room settled. Felix kept the cushion. Sherie sat down with the rigid posture of somebody refusing to acknowledge that she had just discussed recurring dream sodomy and the hypothetical real-world quality of her own ass in front of five colleagues. "Please stop conducting legal research into my dream sex." Natalia put her glasses back on. "Lynleit's stolen explanation was useful." "I did not steal it." "But incomplete." Lynleit looked offended. Natalia returned to the incident board. "The shared dream does not provide a confession. It gives us an image." Felix said, "An extremely graphic image." Sherie glared. Natalia ignored both. "Images can tell the truth without telling it literally." Sherie's expression changed slightly. Natalia noticed. "If you want to understand why this particular dream keeps returning, asking 'Which one of us secretly wants this exact sexual act?' is too narrow." Felix slowly lowered the cushion. "What do we ask instead?" Natalia considered. "What happens between you in the dream?" Sherie folded her arms. "Things." "Yes, Sherie. We have established that." Natalia continued. "Who initiates?" Sherie and Felix pointed at each other. Natalia watched them. "Useful." "It is him." "It is absolutely her." "Who provokes whom?" Both began speaking. Natalia raised one hand. They stopped. "Also useful." Sherie frowned. "Why?" "Because the argument itself may matter more than the mechanics." Felix glanced at Sherie. Natalia tapped the board. "You keep describing the dream in terms of provocation, retaliation, humiliation, attention, loss of control and who gets to determine what happens next." Sherie became very still. "That sounds less sexual when you say it." "It is still sexual." Felix smiled. Sherie elbowed him. Natalia continued. "But perhaps sexuality is the form through which the relationship becomes impossible to ignore." Nobody spoke for several seconds. Natalia looked between them. "A dream may exaggerate something because waking consciousness has become too skilled at minimizing it." Sherie looked at the floor. Felix looked at Sherie. Sherie noticed. "Don't." "I didn't say anything." "You looked." Natalia pointed at them. "Exactly." Felix looked away. Sherie crossed her arms tighter. Natalia continued. "Now, that still does not prove romantic attraction." Sherie looked relieved. Felix looked mildly disappointed. Natalia noticed both reactions. She said nothing about them. "Attraction may be present. So may annoyance. Dependency. Habit. Curiosity. Fear of being ignored. Fear of being known too well. The dream may contain contradictions simultaneously." "So the person we are awake is a mask?" Sherie asked. "The mask belongs to you too. Your restraint is you. Your anger is you. Your kindness is you. Your appetite is you. Your horror at the appetite is also you. Do not confuse sincerity with totality." Natalia put down the pen. "A capacity revealed is not necessarily an intention confessed. Neither of you has established whose preference produced a particular act." Lynleit nodded. "So basically they have a lot of unresolved tension." Natalia looked at her. Lynleit shrugged. "That's what I said in fewer words." "Yes." "Was it wrong?" "No." Lynleit smiled. "It was merely imprecise." Her smile disappeared. Natalia capped the pen. "The psyche is under no obligation to simplify itself for us." Sherie muttered, "Mine could make an effort." Felix said, "Maybe it already simplified as much as possible." Sherie hit him with the cushion. Again. Natalia eventually turned toward Lynleit. "You have experienced the phenomenon too." Lynleit glanced at Kyrien. Sherie sat forward. "Oh?" "It wasn't like theirs," Lynleit said. "I had gathered that," Natalia said. "What can you tell me?" Kyrien waited for Lynleit to answer. "Not here." Natalia picked up a fresh sheet and left it blank. "Then separately." Sherie opened her mouth. Felix nudged the cushion toward her. For once, she let the question go. [WRITER: The particulars of Lynleit and Kyrien's connected dream are not settled. Develop a nonsexual, painful or emotionally exposing experience that draws them closer unintentionally. Mutual childhood disclosures are one possible approach, not established events. Do not restore the earlier house, tea, bedrooms or cat as confirmed dream content.] Sherie gestured between herself and Felix. "And ours emphasizes what, exactly?" Natalia paused. Felix smiled cautiously. Natalia said: "Urgency." Sherie sighed. "Provocation." Felix nodded. "Competition." Sherie looked offended. "Mutual attention." That landed. Sherie went still. Felix noticed. Natalia noticed him noticing. Sherie noticed Natalia noticing Felix noticing. She hated everyone in the room. Natalia looked away first. "Possibly also a difficulty tolerating emotional ambiguity." Sherie looked at Felix. Felix looked at her. Both immediately looked elsewhere. Natalia smiled very slightly. "The dream solves ambiguity by making everything physical." No one answered. Natalia resumed writing. "The mechanism appears to magnify psychic pressure until it becomes narratively visible. Ordinary dreams already do this. The Holumn appears to externalize the process into a shared imaginal space." "Can it stop doing that?" Sherie asked. "Sometimes recognition changes the pressure," Natalia said. "An unconscious content does not need to seize consciousness as violently once consciousness agrees to see it. That does not tell us how reliably it works here." Lynleit nodded. "So once you admit what's bothering you, the dream stops forcing you." "Sometimes." "That's what I said." "No. You made it sound like plumbing." Natalia crossed out the empty title at the top of the board and wrote The Oneiric Confluence. Felix inspected it. "Less catchy." "More accurate." Sherie muttered, "My imaginal space has very little subtlety." Felix said, "Maybe your psyche believes in clear communication." She hit him with the cushion. Again. Felix caught up with her in the corridor twenty minutes later. Sherie heard him before she saw him. "Sherie." She kept walking. "Sherie." "Pervert." "You're still doing that?" "Yes." "I was unconscious." "So was I." "Exactly." "That does not make it better." "It should." "It doesn't." Felix increased his pace until he walked beside her. Sherie ignored him. They crossed two windows in silence. Felix said, "I really didn't know the first night." Sherie kept walking. "The second night was when I knew something was wrong." Still nothing. "Because you remembered something." Sherie slowed. Felix noticed. "What?" He scratched the back of his neck. "In the first dream you said something." Sherie's stomach tightened. "What?" Felix looked uncomfortable. "That if I laughed, you'd kill me." "That sounds normal." "You said it again the next day." Sherie stopped. Felix stopped too. She looked at him. "When?" "Over lunch. You dropped your fork." Sherie remembered. Felix had made a joke. She had looked at him and said exactly that. Sherie's face changed. "You knew then." "I suspected then." "And you said nothing." Felix leaned against the wall. "You want to know why?" "Yes." "I thought you'd react like this." Sherie stared. Felix gestured at her entire body. "This." "You deserved it." "I hadn't done anything." "Dream you had." Felix opened his mouth. Closed it. "Fine." Sherie started walking again. Felix followed. After several steps he said, "You know I remember the other parts too." Sherie stopped so abruptly he nearly walked into her. "What other parts?" His expression softened. That frightened her much more than the teasing had. "The parts between." Sherie said nothing. Felix looked toward the window. "You kept falling asleep on me." Her lips parted slightly. "After." "Yes." She looked away. Felix continued. "You always complained that the room was cold." "It was." "There was no temperature." "It felt cold." "You stole the blanket." "You deserved it." "For what?" Sherie had no answer. Felix smiled. She hated that smile now because it was gentle. "And once," he said, "you woke up inside the dream and asked if I was still there." Sherie looked at him. He stopped smiling. "You remember?" Of course she remembered. She remembered the red room after everything obscene had ended, the impossible black water beyond the windows, Felix beneath her cheek, his heartbeat much too real for a dream. She had asked the question without thinking. He had answered yes. Sherie crossed her arms again. "That proves nothing." "I didn't say it did." "You were about to." "No." "You had the face." "What face?" "The hopeful one." Felix almost smiled again. Sherie pointed. "That." He lowered his head. "Fine." They stood in the corridor. Sherie looked at the floor. "How many nights?" "Three." She looked up. "Three?" Felix winced. "Four." "Felix." "The first barely counts." "You lying bastard." "I was trying to preserve my life." "What happened on the fourth?" He looked at her. Sherie immediately remembered. "Oh." Felix nodded. "Oh." She went red again. Felix politely looked at the ceiling. Sherie covered her face with one hand. "I hate magic." "That's more of a Lynleit sentence." "Tonight." Felix looked at her. Sherie lowered her hand. "We test it." "How?" "No sex." Felix stared. "In the dream." "I understood that." "No touching." "Fine." "No kissing." "Fine." "No grabbing me." "Fine." "And absolutely no ass." Felix looked wounded. "Why are you telling me?" "Because apparently one of our subconsciouses needs supervision." "You still think it's mine." Sherie pointed at him. "Don't." Felix raised both hands. "All right." Sherie started walking again. Felix followed. After several steps: "What if Dream Sherie starts it?" Sherie did not turn around. "I will wake up and kill you." "That seems unfair." "Then pray." Sherie did not sleep. At eleven she read. At midnight she made tea. At one she reorganized two drawers that did not need reorganizing. At two she considered calling Natalia. At two fifteen she rejected the idea because explaining why she feared sleeping would require explaining that she and Felix had made an agreement about dream sex. At two forty she sat upright on the sofa. At some point between then and three, she ceased being awake. The red room was waiting. Sherie opened her eyes. She was standing. Fully dressed. That alone felt suspicious. Felix stood twenty feet away. Also dressed. They stared at one another. Neither moved. Sherie lifted one finger. "Don't." Felix said, "I'm not doing anything." "Good." "I'm literally standing still." "Continue." The room was quieter than usual. Black water pressed against the enormous windows as though the room had sunk beneath some sea without drowning. The red sofa sat between them. One lamp burned. No door. Sherie looked down at herself. Her clothes were exactly right. Blouse. Skirt. Tights. Jacket. Shoes. Everything. Felix looked down at his suspenders and blue tie. "This is encouraging." "Don't say that." "Why?" "You'll provoke it." "The room?" "The thing." Felix looked upward. "Can it hear us?" Sherie glared. "Excellent question to ask inside it." "Sorry." They stood still. Thirty seconds passed. A minute. Sherie began to feel ridiculous. Felix looked equally uncomfortable. "Maybe knowing changes it," he said. "Maybe." Sherie looked toward the sofa. Felix noticed. "No." "I wasn't doing anything." "You looked at it." "So did you." "Because you looked." "You looked first." Sherie's eyes narrowed. Felix sighed. "This is already more exhausting than the sex." "Do not mention sex." "Right." Silence. Sherie became aware of something stranger. The room was not pushing her. On previous nights, desire had simply arrived like gravity. Touch him. Tease him. Get closer. Make him react. The thought and the action had been almost the same thing. Now there was space between them. She could feel impulses. They did not own her hands. Sherie slowly looked at Felix. He looked back. "You feel it too," she said. "Yeah." "What?" Felix hesitated. "That's a trap." "Answer." "No." "Felix." "You first." Sherie folded her arms. "I want to slap you." "That one might just be normal." She almost smiled. Almost. "And..." Felix waited. Sherie looked toward the black water. She hated this room. She hated the Holumn. She hated Natalia. She particularly hated Felix for standing there patiently enough that she might accidentally become honest. "And I like having you around. I would rather this didn't make that difficult." Felix's expression changed. Sherie immediately pointed. "Do not." "I didn't say anything." "You made a face." "I have a face." "That one." Felix looked down. Sherie's heart was beating much harder than it had during the first several dreams. That was unfair. Sex had been easier. Felix said, "I like having you around too." "Good. Then we ought to be capable of spending ten minutes in a room without giving Natalia another report." "She'll want a report if nothing happens." "An extremely short one." Sherie looked past him at the window. She did not want him watching her absence as though it were something she had done to him. Depending on his presence herself would be worse. There was work tomorrow. She wanted to be able to see him tomorrow. The black water moved beyond the windows. No waves. Only pressure. Something in the room loosened. Sherie felt it physically, like a muscle unclenching. Felix looked around. "You felt that?" "Yes." They both went quiet. Sherie whispered, "Natalia." "What about her?" "She said the dream dramatizes pressure." Felix nodded. "So?" Sherie looked around the room. "Maybe saying it changes the relationship to the image." Felix waited. Sherie frowned, trying to remember Natalia's exact explanation. "If something stays unconscious, you just enact it. Once you recognize it..." She hesitated. Felix said, "You have a choice?" Sherie nodded slowly. "Something like that." Natalia would undoubtedly correct the wording. Sherie could almost hear her already. Recognition does not destroy the image. It gives consciousness somewhere to stand in relation to it. Sherie looked toward Felix. "So if we stop pretending we don't know what the pressure is..." "The dream doesn't need to scream it at us?" "Maybe." Felix considered that. "That's almost disappointing." Sherie's eyes narrowed. "Teehee." The sound escaped before she meant it to. Felix smiled. Sherie immediately became annoyed. "Don't." "You teeheed." "I did not." "You did." "It was involuntary." "Sure." The room shifted. Both stopped. The sofa had moved. Neither had seen it move. It now sat directly behind Sherie. She looked at it. Felix looked at it. "No," Sherie said. The lamp went out. Felix said, "That seems bad." The black water outside the windows began glowing faintly from beneath. Sherie looked down. Her hands were trembling. Not from fear. "Felix." "Yeah." "The compulsion is coming back." "I know." "What do you want?" He looked at her. The room pressed closer around them. Felix said, "You." Sherie inhaled. "That is extremely unhelpful." "You asked." "I meant psychologically." "You said be honest." She stared. The red sofa touched the backs of her knees. Sherie did not remember stepping backward. Felix had somehow crossed half the room. He stopped himself. Both looked down at the distance between them. Two metres. One and a half. Sherie said, "Don't move." "I'm trying." "Try harder." "You try harder." "I am." "You're coming toward me." "The floor is tilted." "It is not." "It feels tilted." Sherie looked down. The floor was perfectly level. Felix said, "This is ridiculous." "Yes." "I hate Holumns." "Yes." The distance became one metre. Sherie's breathing changed. Felix noticed. She noticed him noticing. That familiar little current passed between them. Sherie hated how reassuring it felt. "Felix." "Yeah?" "If this room makes me do something humiliating..." "You'll blame me." "Yes." "Obviously." Half a metre. Sherie looked at his mouth. Felix saw. She looked away. "Don't." "You did that." "Shut up." Twenty centimetres. Felix whispered, "Sherie." "What?" "I'm not sure the room is moving us anymore." She froze. So did he. They stood almost touching. Sherie looked down. Nothing moved. No pressure. No invisible force. No sudden impulse commanding her hands. Just Felix. Her heartbeat. His breath. The black water behind the glass. Sherie could step away. She knew she could. Felix knew it too. That changed everything. Sherie stepped sideways. Felix stayed where he was. Nothing dragged her back. She walked around the sofa and rested her hands on its back. The black water pressed against the windows. "Stay there," she said. "I am." "Excellent. You can follow instructions." "I was beginning to doubt it." She laughed before she could stop herself. He smiled, and she looked down at the upholstery until hers had gone. "The plan still applies," she said. "No touching." "And no kissing." "I remember." "Try remembering that before the next briefing." Felix lowered himself onto the floor, well away from the sofa. "What are you doing?" "Making it harder to wander." Sherie considered him, then sat at the far end of the sofa. "That may be your best idea today." "Please include it in the report." She stayed at her end. He stayed on the floor. When the light changed behind the water, neither could decide whether it had grown brighter or merely nearer. Sherie woke sitting upright on her own sofa. Morning light. No red room. No black water. Her phone buzzed. Felix. GOOD MORNING. STILL FOLLOWING INSTRUCTIONS. Sherie typed: A HISTORIC DEVELOPMENT. His answer came almost immediately. NATALIA WILL WANT TO KNOW. She looked at the message for a while. ABOUT THE PRESSURE. NOT YOUR OPINIONS. RESEARCH CENSORSHIP. NATIONAL SECURITY. SAME THING WHEN DIPLOMATS DO IT? Sherie put the phone down, then picked it up again. COFFEE. 10. DON'T BE LATE. WILL THERE BE A BRIEFING? NOT IF YOU BEHAVE. She sent it and went to put the kettle on. There were papers to read before ten. Natalia,Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Sherie,Reiner

entries.title: The Water Beneath Her Feet
entries.subtitle: Chapter 05 · Part II · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: The Water Beneath Her Feet Chapter 05 · Part II · Unknowing Convergence The River Choir, Part II. Lynleit recounts the failure from the empty hold, the hands beneath the river, and her escape using an ability she has kept hidden. Lynleit questions the empty holds and prepares to end the inspection when Maren is pulled overboard. She puts on both protective gloves and rolls both sleeves, but holds her flame while rescuers are too close to Maren. The overturned boat separates her from the team. She sees the city-bound swimmers and Kyrien struggling towards the park. Hands seize her boots and jacket underwater. Her practiced swimming cannot free her, and her childhood fear of drowning returns. Blue flame burns the submerged grips. The light exposes hands of different sizes and states of decay; her ordinary blue suede jacket tears away. The river supports her palm, knee and boots. She recognizes an ability she has secretly practiced at night. Lynleit fears the Church discovering an act that resembles a forbidden miracle, while still wanting to hear her team. A silent girl emerges in a dress of dead fish, her eyelids sewn shut with fishing line. Her fingertips touch the water. The tilted head and stillness suggest that the girl cannot readily account for Lynleit standing above the hands. inferred The submerged hands cannot reach through the surface beneath Lynleit. She tests her steps backwards towards the park without discovering why. Lynleit reaches the mud, climbs by a branch and calls Kyrien. She does not know that he watched her crossing. The Water Beneath Her Feet The River Choir, Part II. Lynleit. Part I: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge An empty hold Kyrien was holding a wet board so that I could look underneath it. I remember wishing he would move his fingers. They were close to the edge, and if the boat lurched he would lose the use of them for the rest of the night. There was water beneath the board. Nothing else that I could see. I touched his wrist, he shifted his hand, and we lowered it together. Ahead, Reiner had finished inspecting the first boat. Maren and Ivo were checking the second. Nobody had found a person or a cargo. We had waited through four unsuccessful watches to board three empty boats. “Anything at the controls?” I asked. “Fixed rudder,” Reiner said. “Maren?” “Same.” Felix asked us to check under the boards. I told him we had. I wanted another answer from somebody, preferably an ordinary one. People sometimes went to considerable trouble to move nothing. There could be a reason for the empty holds. But the tarps had been fastened down. Somebody had finished that work before the boats reached us. I looked at the part of the tarp still hanging from my hand. The edge had soaked through. I couldn't tell whether that had happened here or farther upstream. The water was quiet enough to hear it striking the bows. We had passed beyond the bridge lights. On the city side the lamps showed through mist without their posts; on the park side I could still make out branches above the bank. They were much closer than I liked. “How long until the next bridge?” Felix gave me the remaining interval. Reiner confirmed that we would be ready to leave. I had agreed to inspect the traffic, not keep going until I could explain it. I knew that. I was already preparing to tell the others to stop lifting things and face downstream when Kyrien held his breath. It was the same little pause I had noticed over the cards. I looked at him before he turned towards the trees. “What?” “Nothing.” I didn't think he meant it. He was listening, and I wanted him to tell me what he was listening for. An objection I could examine would have been better than watching his face and trying to manufacture one. I had asked these people to come. They had accepted the small operation I could describe, with its camera window and exit lines. Reiner's confidence had helped me give the order to descend. It hadn't cured my unease. Now there was nothing in the boats, Kyrien was looking away from the exit, and I was wondering whether I had heard reassurance as an answer to a different question. Maren spoke before I could ask him again. “There is something beside us.” “Do not lean out,” Reiner said. She had already looked. Her hip struck the gunwale. I saw her fingers close over the edge, one hand after the other, and her leg disappear below it. The boat tipped, but not enough to account for the way she had moved. Reiner crossed to her and caught her wrist. She kicked with her free leg, trying to get a knee against the boards. I told Ivo to brace where he was rather than add his weight to their side. He threw the line Reiner called for. “Something has my legs,” Maren said. I couldn't see it. I could see what it was doing to her. I let the tarp fall and pulled the black leather gloves from my belt. The first went on badly. I had to push my fingers to the ends. I rolled that jacket sleeve and the blouse cuff beneath it above my wrist, then did the same with the other sleeve as I pulled on the second glove. Kyrien was gathering the loose line beside me. I told him to keep it clear of his feet. I didn't use the flame. Reiner's arm was beside Maren's face; Ivo was leaning across them. If I put fire where she was being held without seeing the grip, I could burn the people trying to free her. I needed them apart. I needed a view of what was under the side. Reiner pulled her shoulder up. For a moment I thought he had her. Then he went forward, both of them struck the water, and Ivo entered after them. “Felix. Fallback. Now.” “Moving.” The line crossed our boat and tightened. Kyrien cut it beside the fitting. I felt the release through my feet, followed by the boat's return in the other direction. I reached for the rail. The gunwale struck my thigh before my hand found it. I hit the river on my side. Where I could still swim I had shut my mouth. That was the one thing I had done in time. My jacket filled and pulled across my shoulders. I turned beneath it, opened my eyes and found a pale strip above me. I kicked towards it. There was no pain yet, only cold and the thickness of my own clothes in the water. My head came out beside the overturned boat. I caught a board, drew a breath and looked for the others. Reiner had Maren. Ivo was moving towards them. Felix was calling the city bank over the radio. Kyrien surfaced farther from me than I expected. I saw him turn towards the lights. “City side,” I tried to say. The water slapped the boat and came over my mouth. I coughed, tightened my hold and tried again. Reiner was already doing it. I didn't need to tell him twice. I needed to get myself clear of the hull before it rolled over me. I pushed away and started swimming. I could swim. I had practised because I was afraid of drowning, not because practice had made me stop being afraid. I knew how to turn, how to stop wasting a kick, how to use a breath instead of snatching at the next one. For the first few strokes I was still doing those things. Then my right ankle stopped. My body kept moving while my foot didn't. It brought my face down into the water. I drew the leg up, expecting to pull free of something, and felt pressure close around the calf as well. I got my mouth above water and called for Reiner. I don't know whether he heard. He was occupied with Maren, and between one blink and the next they were farther away. I kicked at the pressure with my other foot. For an instant I could move again. I turned onto my side to look behind me and saw Kyrien struggling towards the park. He was no longer trying to follow the others. I wanted to tell him there were steps on the city side. Of course he knew. He had been the one to insist on looking at them. I stopped trying to give him an order he was already unable to follow. Something closed around my other ankle. I could still see the hull beside me. I reached for it and got two fingers over its edge. The wood cut into them through the glove. I pulled, but the boat came towards me instead of holding me up. My face went beneath it. I let go before it covered my head. That was the last choice which felt like one of the swimming exercises I knew. Beneath There were fingers against my boot. I could see them now. The leather had drawn tight under the grip. A thumb lay along the lacing, and the rest of the hand curved around my ankle. I followed it with my eyes, wanting an arm, a shoulder, something I could strike and understand. There was another hand behind it, then another beneath my knee. Whatever bodies they belonged to were lower than I could see. I kicked. A wrist bent beneath my heel. It should have made a difference. The fingers didn't open. My hair floated in front of my face. I swept it away and reached upwards with the same hand, as though clearing my sight might also have brought the surface nearer. The light was still there. I could see the underside of the water moving. Bubbles went up past my fingers and continued after my hand had stopped. I remember being furious with the bubbles. They had no difficulty going where I wanted to go. A grip closed higher on my leg. Another caught the jacket at my waist. Its hem pulled tight across my back and then up, bunching beneath my arms. I couldn't bring one arm forward properly. I tried to shrug out of it and felt a pull at the other sleeve. I had chosen the shorter jacket because of the ropes. I had tested my reach in it on the bridge. Now I couldn't get it off. My chest wanted me to breathe. I pressed my lips together and pulled at the fabric. There was a hand where the sleeve met the shoulder. I caught its wrist, tried to force it away and saw the fingers dig farther into the suede. The fear had been with me since childhood. It didn't return as a useful memory. There was no complete scene to look at, no voice giving advice. I wanted somebody above me to notice that I hadn't come up. I wanted a hand that would pull in the other direction. I reached again. Nothing was close enough. The gloves made my own hands dark against the reaching ones. I had them on. That was useful. I tried to think about that, about something I had actually managed to do, while another grip found the top of my boot. I couldn't keep pulling upwards. They were multiplying beneath me, or I was sinking into more of them. I couldn't tell which. The loose parts of my clothes and hair streamed towards the surface while my body went down. I looked along my legs and saw hands at different angles, holding wherever there was room. One was small enough to close over only part of my wrist when I reached down. I tried to wrench away from that one first. I don't know why its size was worse. It was holding just as hard. I wanted to hurt them. The thought was much simpler than anything I had been trying to do. I turned down instead of up and caught the wrist at my knee with both hands. Blue flame ran between my fingers. I had expected resistance, a hiss, a waste of the little strength I had left. The flame held its colour in the water. It moved over the wrist beneath my glove, and the fingers opened. I kicked that leg free. Another hand found it. I put the flame there too. The light showed me more than I wanted to see. Hands with swollen fingers. A hand whose nails seemed too long because there was so little left around them. Smaller ones reaching between the others. They crowded into the space I was trying to leave. I couldn't fight them one at a time. I called more flame than I could shape neatly, spread my hands and pushed it through the grips nearest my body. The burning fingers released. Something still held my jacket. I twisted against it until a seam gave, then another. The suede pulled away from my shoulder and disappeared below my elbow. I didn't try to keep it. There was space to kick. I used it before I had finished looking. My foot struck a wrist, passed it, struck nothing. I pulled water down with both arms. The flame remained around the hands below me, blue between the moving fingers, and I kept going towards the pale strip above. I don't know how much of the last stroke was swimming. I remember reaching too soon. I remember my hand still in water when I thought it should have been in air. Then my face broke through. I tried to take an entire breath at once and coughed it away. My next breath hurt. I reached out for the boat, for a rope, for anything at the height of my shoulders. There was nothing there. My palm struck the surface. It held. Above it I pressed down before I dared think about what I was doing. The water bowed under my hand, deep enough for it to feel as though I was about to slip through. Then the pressure steadied. I knew that resistance. I had felt it alone at night, where nobody was close enough to see me practising. Knowing it did not make me trust it with hands still moving below my feet. I brought one knee up. It took too long. My leg shook, and I couldn't get my weight over it without leaning farther onto the hand. I coughed again and almost lost the position. Water ran off my face onto the small hollow beneath my palm. For a little while I stayed on a hand and a knee, looking down at the place where they should have sunk. I needed both boots beneath me. I didn't want to lift anything that was already holding. I planted one foot. The surface gave and stopped. I moved the other leg, slowly, and braced with my hand until I was crouching. My wet hair hung across my face. I pushed it back with my free wrist and looked for a bank. The city lamps were distant and broken by mist. The park trees were nearer. I could see the low branches and the darkness beneath them. There was somewhere to get out. I only had to stand. Below me, a hand pressed upwards. I jerked my boot away and almost fell. The hand had not come through. Its fingers spread against the underside of the surface, and the water between us distorted the shape. More hands rose beside it. They reached under my knees and my planted foot, opening and closing without finding me. I got upright. My legs wanted to keep kicking. I had to stop them. I was standing above the river with my breath coming in ugly, short catches, and if I let myself behave as though I was still swimming I would lose my balance. There was a light moving on the city side. I looked at it, then away. I had kept this ability from everyone. The Church's distinction wasn't between something helpful and something harmful. There were things that were not permitted to look like miracles. I knew enough to practise where nobody watched. I didn't know what I would say if Felix called across the river now and asked me to explain where I was standing. I wanted him to call anyway. I wanted to hear that he had the others. Instead, the water in front of me rose around a pale forehead. At first I thought another person had come up. I took half a step towards her before I saw her eyes. Fishing line passed through the lids. Little tight stitches, with water caught against the knots. I could see them because her face was turned towards me and she wasn't far away. She didn't blink. There was no opening through which I could see an eye. I stopped moving. Her hair lay wet against her cheeks. Water ran from her chin. Beneath it, something silver-grey moved along her chest, and I thought of scales sewn onto cloth. Then one of the shapes turned enough for me to see its mouth. They were fish. Whole dead fish, overlapping, their bodies making the dress. More emerged as she rose. Their pale mouths opened with the water moving through them. I could see an eye near the waist, another lower down, each facing somewhere different. I looked back at her face. That was worse than looking at the fish, but at least it was one face. She said nothing. “Stay there,” I said. My voice was rough enough that I wasn't sure she had heard. Her head tilted. It was a small movement. I had given an order because there was nothing else ready in my mouth. She gave me no sign that it meant anything to her. I lowered my hands a little and waited. I still had the gloves on. I could call the flame again. I didn't know what it would do to her, how much I could use without losing my footing, or what would happen if she came close enough to touch me. Under the water I had needed the grips to release. Here I had a bank behind me. I could leave. I glanced down. The hands had followed the space beneath my boots. They were still held below it. I could not see a wall or a skin or anything I could name. I only knew I was above them. The girl lowered one hand towards the water. Her fingertips touched it, and a small ring spread away. I watched the ring approach my foot. It passed through the reflection beside it. Nothing struck me. Nothing let go beneath me. I had been holding my breath again, and I let a little of it out. Her head remained at that angle. Was she trying to understand what I was standing on? I couldn't even establish whether she was looking at my feet. The stitched lids faced me and gave me nothing to work with. I took a step backwards. The water sank slightly beneath the boot and held. I waited until my weight had settled before moving the other foot. The girl stayed where she was. The bank behind me I couldn't walk backwards all the way without looking. The park bank was uneven. A root I couldn't see would be enough to bring me down at the edge, after everything else. I turned my head, found a pale piece of exposed mud below the branches, and chose it. Then I looked back at the girl. She hadn't moved closer. I took another step. Water ran down inside my boots. My blouse stuck to my shoulders where the jacket had been torn away, and the cold on the wet fabric made me want to curl my arms around myself. I kept them out instead, using them for balance. Something brushed the sole of my right boot from underneath. I felt it only faintly through the yielding support. I put the foot down harder than I meant to and stopped until I was steady. There was no sense in hurrying if hurrying put me back among them. I repeated that to myself, then hurried the next step anyway. I had to stop a second time. From the city bank I heard a shout. I couldn't make out the words. I tried to count shapes around the light, but the mist and the distance made it impossible. Reiner had been moving in that direction. Felix had answered me. I held on to those two things and kept going. The girl was farther away now. That helped. Her dress was becoming one pale shape again instead of dozens of separate bodies. She still hadn't followed. I watched her while I put the next foot down. The heel met something solid that didn't yield with the rest of the water. Mud. I nearly stumbled at the change. I bent my knee, felt the slope through the sole and set my other foot beside it. My hand found a branch. I squeezed it before I trusted it, then pulled myself beneath the leaves. They struck my wet hair and caught there. I ducked, took another step and got both feet above the waterline. The slope was steep enough that I needed the branch to keep climbing. I used it. I had no intention of letting go merely because I ought to have been able to walk on land. When I looked back through the leaves, I couldn't distinguish the girl from the mist. I could still see water moving where she had stood. That didn't tell me whether she had gone under or whether I had lost the angle. I wanted to sit down. First I had to find somewhere my boots would stay put. I took one more step towards the trees and called Kyrien's name. Continue to Part III: The Wrong Bank Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner

entries.subtitle: Chapter 05 · Part III · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: The Wrong Bank Chapter 05 · Part III · Unknowing Convergence The River Choir, Part III. Kyrien watches from the trees, withholds what he has seen and helps Lynleit find a way out of the quarantined park, where something moves above the path. Kyrien reaches the park bank and hides behind a tree while searching the near water for Lynleit. He watches her rise, stand and walk on the water. The distant pale figure is visible, but its stitched eyes are not. Lynleit reaches the bank and takes his forearm to climb. They sit back to back while recovering from immersion. Kyrien deliberately avoids admitting that he saw her standing on the river. He suspects her fear of being seen without knowing the Church reason. A phone call confirms Reiner, Maren and Ivo reached the city side. Maren reports feeling hands, not seeing their source. Reiner directs them to the path and warns that the riverbank drops away before the bridge. On the wet park path Lynleit questions Kyrien again. Both admit fear; she describes the sewn eyelids and dead-fish dress to him. An elongated shape moves above the path while the supporting branches remain still. Both see it without identifying it. They keep it in sight while detouring around the bench, then reach the locked barrier and rejoin Felix and Reiner. All six regroup on the city side. Lynleit reports movement in the park, Kyrien keeps the water walking secret, and their unfinished cards are still in the van. The Wrong Bank The River Choir, Part III. Kyrien. Part II: The Water Beneath Her Feet Behind the trees My knee went into the mud, slipped, and stayed there on the second attempt. I pulled against the root until my chest was above it. After that I could drag the rest of myself out. I lay on the bank with one foot still in the water. It took me a moment to notice. I brought it up quickly and caught the heel on the root. Nothing was holding me. I checked anyway, pressing a hand around my ankle through the soaked cloth. Across the river, Felix's light was moving at the steps. I could see heads below it. Someone was coughing. Reiner was there, or a man large enough to be Reiner, helping another person over the edge. I counted three shapes and then four, but one of them might have been the same person moving. I couldn't see Lynleit. There was no sensible reason to remain flat where anything in the water could reach my legs. I crawled higher, got one foot against a tree and stood with my shoulder on the trunk. The ground felt unreliable after the river. When I looked down, it wasn't moving. I went inside the tree line and crouched behind a thick trunk. From there I could see through the lower branches without standing against the open bank. The river nearest me was visible. Farther out, the mist hid the spaces between the boats. I tried to find the one we had been on. A dark hull turned, showed me wet boards and went out of sight. I should have called. I knew that. But I hadn't identified what had taken us out of the boats, and I didn't want to announce where I had come out until I knew whether I needed to move again. I listened for her and watched the near water. Something struck it from below. I saw a gloved hand, dark hair, a face rising far enough to cough. She reached in front of her. I moved out from the trunk, looking for anything long enough to put between us. Then her shoulder came higher. I thought she had found the hull. I couldn't see it beneath her, but I had lost track of the boats. She brought a knee up, moved her foot and crouched. There was no hull. I leaned to one side to see past a branch. It changed the angle. I could see water beneath both boots, the small rings spreading from them, her hand planted ahead of her. There was no board joining the places where she rested her weight. She stood. I stayed half out of cover with my hand on the trunk. She was too far from the mud to be standing on a shelf of the bank. I had just been in that water. I knew where I had failed to find the bottom. I looked for something else beneath her. I don't know what I expected to find. Anything with an edge would have helped. The surface dipped under a boot when she moved it. Water ran away from the sole. She put her weight there and remained upright. I went back behind the tree. I didn't want her to turn and see me staring while I was still trying to decide whether I understood what I was looking at. There was another person in front of her. I had missed the arrival. The figure was pale, with long hair and a dress that reflected little pieces of light when the water moved. I couldn't see the eyes from where I was. I could see the angle of the head. It was tipped towards Lynleit. Neither of them came towards the bank for several seconds. Lynleit held her arms slightly away from her sides. She didn't look comfortable. The other figure scarcely moved at all. Lynleit said something I couldn't hear. I watched the distance between them. If the pale one closed it, I would have to do something. There was a branch beside my foot, too short to reach the water. I picked it up before deciding what use it could be. Then Lynleit stepped backwards. The other figure remained where it was. She took another step. She was walking on the water. I had run out of less difficult ways to describe it to myself. I could have called her name. Instead I watched until she reached the reeds. She caught a branch, bent beneath it and began climbing the mud. Only then did I put the piece of wood down. She called me from below the trees. “Here.” I came out where she could see me. She stopped with one hand still on the branch. “Can you stand?” I asked. “I am standing.” She tried to take the next step and had to use the branch again. I went down far enough to offer my forearm. She took it without another answer. Her grip was hard. I braced against the tree and let her do the climbing. When she was beside me, she didn't let go immediately. She was looking at my face. “The others?” “City bank. I saw people at the steps.” “How many?” “I couldn't count.” She released my arm and tried to look through the trees herself. A thoughtful gesture Her jacket was gone. Her hair stuck against her neck and shoulders; water ran from the ends of it onto her blouse. One glove was still clenched around the branch after she had let go of me. I took my jacket off. It was heavy with water. I looked at it, then at her, and lowered it before offering it. “A thoughtful gesture,” she said. “I reconsidered it.” “Sensibly.” I folded it over my forearm. My shirt was wet enough that the change made little difference except to the weight. She pulled off one glove with her teeth at the fingertips, then used the freed hand for the other. She was having trouble holding them together. “Put them away first,” I said. She looked at me. I pointed at her belt. She put them there, carefully, and rested her empty hand against the tree. I could hear someone calling from the other bank. Lynleit started towards the gap in the branches. After two steps she stopped and coughed so hard that she bent at the waist. I waited beside her. When I touched her shoulder she lifted a hand, asking me to wait too. “I need a moment,” she said. There was a broad tree a little higher up the bank. Its roots made a place to sit without sliding towards the river. We got there slowly. I went behind her because somebody ought to keep looking at the path, and because she had already taken the better place against the root. We ended up back to back. At first only our shoulders touched. She shifted, I moved my foot out of the way, and we found a position where neither of us had to hold the other upright. There wasn't much warmth in it, but there was less wind against the wet cloth. I kept my jacket across my knees. She was still coughing. When she stopped, I could feel how quickly she was breathing through the contact at my back. “Any pain?” I asked. “Several varieties.” “Something that stops you walking.” “No.” She asked me the same thing. I told her my ankle hurt but worked. She wanted to see it. I said we could do that when we were somewhere she didn't have to get up to look. She accepted that more readily than I expected. Across the river the light moved along the wall. There were gaps between the trees where I could follow it. When it vanished behind one trunk, I watched the next gap instead of standing to recover the whole view. I had seen something I could not fit into what I knew. I kept trying to put a support beneath her feet, even while remembering the water bending under them. If I had been told this by somebody else, I would have asked where he stood and what obstructed his view. I had already tried those questions on myself. Lynleit shifted against me. “You came ashore on this side.” “It was closer.” “So you could see the river.” “Parts of it.” She waited. I had stopped breathing without noticing. “Did you see anything strange?” “The boats had no crews. Something tried to drown all of us. We are sitting inside a quarantined park in wet clothes.” “That is not what I asked.” “It is what happened.” She turned slightly. I felt the movement before I saw the edge of her face. “And nothing else?” “Nothing I can explain.” It wasn't an answer to the question she wanted to ask. I knew that. She hadn't asked it either. Her head rested back against my shoulder. “Then do not invent an explanation.” “I was not planning to.” She was afraid I had seen her. That was what I made of the questions, the pause, the way she had looked at me when I came out of the trees. I didn't know why being seen was dangerous to her. For the moment I could leave her without a clear answer. I had spent enough time being invited to complete somebody else's account of an event. The light on the opposite bank stopped and swept towards us. I kept still for another moment. Her breathing had begun to slow. Then I said, “They're looking here.” She raised her head at once. The way back We moved to the gap where we could be seen without going down to the water. I called Felix's name. He turned the light, found us and kept it there. I raised a hand. Lynleit called that we were both ashore. For a moment everybody tried to speak across the river. I could hear Felix and Reiner but couldn't separate the words. Lynleit stopped trying to compete with them and looked for her phone. It had stayed in its closed pouch. Her hands were shaking enough that she couldn't open it neatly. I held the edge while she worked the fastening. The screen lit when she pressed it. I hadn't expected that small thing to be as reassuring as it was. She called Felix and put the phone between us on speaker, low enough that we both had to lean towards it. “Reiner?” she asked. “Here.” “Maren?” “Here.” Felix turned away from the phone. I heard him ask her something, then her irritated answer. He came back. “And displeased.” “Ivo?” “Here,” Ivo said himself. She closed her eyes for a moment. When she opened them, she asked whether they could walk. Maren could, but not without help yet. Reiner said he would stay with her until she was steady. There was no suggestion that anyone should get back into the river. “It was hands,” Maren said somewhere behind the phone. Felix asked what she meant. “On my legs. Someone was holding my legs.” I looked down at my ankle. Lynleit was looking at the screen. Neither of us spoke into the little silence that followed. Reiner asked where we were in relation to the bridge. I could see the side of it through two gaps upstream. Lynleit said we would take the path back to the barrier. “Stay together,” he said. “Yes.” “Not the bank. The path.” “Reiner.” “The bank drops away before the bridge.” She looked upstream along the mud and said, more quietly, “Understood.” Felix would meet us at the locked end. He had to restore the cameras before leaving the van again. For a few moments his part of the conversation was addressed to his terminal instead of us. I heard him swear, stop, and say he had it. Lynleit asked how long the walk around to the bridge would take him. “Longer if you keep asking.” “Then stop answering.” He told us to call when we could see the barrier. She ended the call and stood looking at the river with the phone still in her hand. “What?” I asked. She shook her head and put it away. I wanted to ask what she had seen from the water. I wanted to know whether the pale figure was a person, whether it had gone after the others, and whether it could come onto the bank. Every version of the first question gave away that I had been watching. I hadn't decided whether avoiding it was worth not knowing the answer. “Do we need to keep watching the river?” I asked instead. “For now.” That was enough to keep me from treating the path as safety. Along the path The path was a little higher than the place where we had rested. We climbed between roots and found paving under wet leaves. Rain had begun while we were sitting. I hadn't distinguished it from the water dripping out of the trees until it struck my face beyond them. Lynleit went first. I wrung what I could out of my jacket and carried it over my arm. It wasn't going to dry there. My sleeves were sticking at the elbows, so I pushed them up and kept the knife where I could reach it. I had no particular idea what a knife would do to anything we had encountered. I wanted to know where it was. There was a bench beside the path. Water stood on its slats. Farther ahead, around a bend we couldn't see from the bridge, a single amber lamp showed through the mist. It lit the pavement beneath it, not the trees overhead. We went towards it because the path went towards it. I watched the edge nearest the river. Lynleit kept looking back at me. The third time she did it, she stopped walking. “I think you saw something, and don't want to tell me.” I looked past her. The lamp was reflected in several shallow puddles, broken by leaves. A dark length lay among the branches over the next stretch of path. I couldn't tell whether it joined either tree. “Shouldn't we leave as soon as possible?” She watched me for another moment, then turned and gathered her wet hair with both hands. “Are you scared?” “Yes.” She glanced back again. I don't think that was the answer she had expected. “So am I,” she said. “Keep walking.” I did, though I moved to where I could see past her shoulder. She pulled the length of her hair free of her collar. Her hands kept returning to it even after it was clear. “There was a girl,” she said. I waited. “In the river.” “Did she touch you?” “No.” She looked towards the water. I could see it only in narrow pieces between the trunks. She described sewn eyelids and fish fastened into a dress. I had seen the pale figure, but not those things. Hearing them didn't help me decide what it was. “Dead fish?” “Yes.” “Was she one of the people on the boats?” “I don't know.” We hadn't found the people who ought to have been there. I didn't know if that was even the right way to ask it. “And what pulled us down?” She stopped winding her hair around her hand. “I saw hands.” “Maren said that.” “I know.” She didn't try to improve the answer. I looked at her hand tightening around the wet hair and decided not to ask her to describe them yet. The dark length above the path moved. I stopped. At first I thought I had seen a branch change position because I was walking beneath it. I moved my head back to where it had been. The shape remained in its new position. Rain fell through the gap beside it. Lynleit took another step before she noticed I wasn't with her. “Kyrien?” I lifted a hand. She waited. There was something thin stretched between two larger branches. One part of it lay close against the upper branch. The other hung lower, then drew up a little as I watched. It had an end that might have been a head. I didn't want to decide that from the shape alone. The branches didn't move with it. I could see smaller twigs against the sky. They weren't being bent under weight or shaken by what was moving between them. That was the part I kept checking. If it was someone climbing, I should have seen something carry the weight. “Don't go under that,” I said. Lynleit followed my gaze. For several seconds she stood with her back to me, looking up. I could see her fingers close and open once beside her shorts. “Where did it start?” I pointed to the upper branch without raising my arm all the way. “There. Then lower.” “I see it.” I was glad she said that. I hadn't wanted another explanation about compression or a reflection. She took a step back towards me, keeping her eyes up. The shape shifted once more. It didn't come down. It didn't speak. I heard rain, the river and a vehicle somewhere across it. I kept waiting for one of those sounds to stop so that I could hear something from above, but none did. “The girl?” I asked. “I don't know.” This time she looked at me when she said it. I nodded. We left the question there. Past the bench We couldn't stand and watch until we were too cold to move properly. I could already feel my fingers becoming slow. The path passed directly beneath the shape. To the river side, the paving dropped into roots and mud. On the other side there was enough open ground to go around the bench and rejoin the path beyond the overhanging branches. Lynleit looked at both sides before I pointed. “There,” she said. “I can keep it in sight from behind the bench.” She considered that, then moved with me rather than sending me around alone. We went slowly. I watched the ground when she watched above, and when I had found the next place to put my foot, I looked up again. Wet leaves made it difficult to tell where the soil dipped. She caught my sleeve when I stepped onto an edge that crumbled. I moved back, found a root and went past it. Neither of us made anything of it. The shape stayed among the branches. As our angle changed, one end disappeared behind the trunk. I waited until we could see past it. It was still there, or enough of it was there that I wasn't going to assume otherwise. We reached the paving beyond the bench. Lynleit kept looking back until a bend took the branches out of sight. “Did it follow?” she asked. “Not while I could see it.” We walked faster. The amber lamp dropped behind us. Ahead, the path bent towards the bridge. I recognized the angle of the rail before I saw the barrier. There was a light beyond it and a person holding it at chest height. Felix called Lynleit's name. She answered. He lowered the light enough to see her face and said something under his breath that I couldn't hear. The chain was still across the gate. Reiner was working at it from the bridge side. He had left Maren with Ivo on the city bank. He asked again whether both of us could walk. This time Lynleit said yes without sounding annoyed. I turned towards the path while they worked. From the barrier I couldn't see the bench or the lamp. I couldn't see the shape. I listened for movement following ours and heard only water falling from the leaves. The gate opened far enough for one person at a time. Lynleit went through. I followed, and Reiner pulled it shut behind me. He put the chain back. The small metal noise was more welcome than anything Felix said. Felix had a dry outer layer for Lynleit. She took it. I was glad he hadn't watched my earlier attempt. He started to ask her something, looked at the way she was holding the fastening, and asked whether she could get to the van instead. She said she could. Reiner stayed close enough to catch either of us without making us hold him. On the city side, Maren was sitting out of the wind with Ivo beside her. She looked at Lynleit, then at me, counting us as plainly as Reiner had. She raised a hand. I raised mine back. I didn't tell anyone about the water. Lynleit told Felix there had been movement above the park path. She described where, not what it was. He listened without making a joke and glanced at Reiner. Whatever they decided to do about it, it wasn't going to involve going back in that night. Inside the van, the cards were still where we had left them. I put my wet jacket on the floor instead of the shelf. Lynleit sat opposite me with Felix's dry layer around her shoulders. She looked at her unfinished hand, then at mine. “Don't turn them over,” she said. “I wasn't going to.” She watched me long enough to make it clear that this was not a general expression of trust. I slid her cards away from a drop falling off my sleeve. Then I put mine beside them and shut the box. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner
